D. 'a' is large and 'b' is small

mcqs.q: At constant pressure, at what temperature will the volume of a gas become twice what it is at 0 degrees C?
mcqs.why: By Charles's law volume is proportional to Kelvin temperature: T1 = 273 K for double volume, so T2 = 273 * 2 = 546 K.

mcqs.q: The number of molecules in 1 dm3 of water is close to:
mcqs.why: 1 dm3 of water has mass 1000 g, and moles = 1000 / 18 = 55.6 mol, so molecules = 55.6 x 6.02 x 10^23.

mcqs.q: Which pair will have the same number of molecules at STP?
options: 11.2 dm3 of O2 and 32 g of O2
44 g of CO2 and 11.2 dm3 of CO
280 cm3 of CO2 and 280 cm3 of N2O
28 g of N2 and 5.6 dm3 of oxygen
mcqs.why: At STP equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules by Avogadro's law, and both gases here have the same volume, 280 cm3.

mcqs.q: If the absolute temperature of a gas is doubled and its pressure is reduced to one half, its volume will:
mcqs.why: V is proportional to T / P, so the volume factor is 2 * 2 = 4: doubling T doubles V and halving P doubles it again.

mcqs.q: How should conditions be changed to prevent the volume of a gas from expanding when its mass is increased?
options: Temperature is increased and pressure is lowered
Temperature is lowered and pressure is increased
Temperature and pressure both are lowered
Temperature and pressure both are increased
mcqs.why: Lowering the temperature contracts the gas and increasing the pressure compresses it, and together they prevent expansion when mass is increased.

mcqs.q: The molar volume of CO2 is maximum at:
mcqs.why: Molar volume grows with temperature and falls with pressure, so among the choices the highest temperature at the lowest pressure, 127 degrees C and 1 atm, gives the maximum.

mcqs.q: What is the order of the rate of diffusion of NH3, CO2, SO2 and Cl2?
mcqs.why: By Graham's law lighter gases diffuse faster: molar masses are NH3 17, CO2 44, SO2 64 and Cl2 about 71, so the rate falls in that order.

mcqs.q: Equal masses of methane and oxygen are mixed at 25 degrees C. The fraction of the total pressure exerted by oxygen is:
mcqs.why: Take 32 g of each gas: moles of O2 = 32 / 32 = 1 and moles of CH4 = 32 / 16 = 2, so the oxygen mole fraction is 1 / (1 + 2) = 0.3333, that is 1/3 of the total pressure.

mcqs.q: Gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure mainly because:
options: The gas molecules move in one direction only
The collisions between molecules stop completely
mcqs.why: The notes identify significant intermolecular attractions at high pressure as a correct reason for non-ideal behaviour of gases.

mcqs.q: The deviation of a gas from ideal behaviour is maximum at:
mcqs.why: Deviation is greatest at low temperature and high pressure, and -10 degrees C with 5.0 atm is the lowest temperature with the highest pressure listed.

lessons.title: Fill in the Blanks
lessons.notes_html:
2(i). The product PV has the S.I. unit of joule (energy).

2(ii). Eight grams each of O2 and H2 at 27 degrees C will have total K.E. in the ratio of ______. Total kinetic energy = (3/2) nRT. Moles: O2 = 8/32 = 0.25 mol; H2 = 8/2 = 4 mol. At the same temperature, total K.E. ratio = 0.25 : 4 = 1 : 16.

2(iii). Smell of the cooking gas during leakage from a gas cylinder is due to the property of diffusion of gases.

2(iv). Equal ______ of ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure contain ______ number of molecules. Equal volumes of ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal number of molecules (Avogadro's law).

2(v). The temperature above which a substance exists only as a gas is called critical temperature.

mcqs.q: The product PV has the S.I. unit of ______ (energy).
mcqs.why: The fill-in-the-blank notes state directly that the product PV has the S.I. unit of joule, the unit of energy.

mcqs.q: Total kinetic energy of a gas is given by:
options: (1/2) mv^2 for the whole gas only
mcqs.why: The notes give the relation total kinetic energy = (3/2) nRT for n moles of gas at absolute temperature T.

mcqs.q: Eight grams of O2 contain how many moles? (O2 = 32 g/mol)
mcqs.why: Moles = mass / molar mass, so for oxygen 8 / 32 = 0.25 mol, as calculated step by step in the notes.

mcqs.q: Eight grams of H2 contain how many moles? (H2 = 2 g/mol)
mcqs.why: Moles = mass / molar mass, so for hydrogen 8 / 2 = 4 mol, as calculated step by step in the notes.

mcqs.q: Eight grams each of O2 and H2 at 27 degrees C will have total K.E. in the ratio ______ (O2 : H2).
mcqs.why: At the same temperature K.E. follows moles: O2 = 0.25 mol and H2 = 4 mol, and 4 / 0.25 = 16, giving the ratio 0.25 : 4 = 1 : 16.

mcqs.q: Smell of cooking gas during leakage from a cylinder is due to the property of ______ of gases.
mcqs.why: The notes fill this blank with diffusion: the gas molecules spread through the air, so the leakage can be smelled.

mcqs.q: Equal ______ of ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal number of molecules.
mcqs.why: The blank is volumes: equal volumes of ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal number of molecules.

mcqs.q: The statement that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules is:
mcqs.why: The notes name this statement Avogadro's law, linking equal volumes at the same temperature and pressure to equal numbers of molecules.

mcqs.q: The temperature above which a substance exists only as a gas is called ______ temperature.
mcqs.why: The notes fill this blank with critical: above the critical temperature a substance exists only as a gas.

mcqs.q: In the K.E. comparison of 8 g O2 and 8 g H2 at the same temperature, the ratio is fixed by which quantity?
options: The volume of the cylinder alone
The number of moles of each gas
mcqs.why: Total K.E. = (3/2) nRT, so at the same temperature only n differs: 0.25 mol versus 4 mol, and 4 / 0.25 = 16 fixes the 1 : 16 ratio.

lessons.title: True or False
lessons.notes_html:
3(i). Kinetic energy of molecules of a gas is zero at 0 degrees C. False

3(ii). A gas in a closed container will exert much higher pressure at the bottom due to gravity than at the top. False

3(iii). Real gases show ideal gas behaviour at low pressure and high temperature. True

3(iv). Liquefaction of gases involves decrease in intermolecular spaces. True

3(v). An ideal gas on expansion will show Joule-Thomson effect. False

mcqs.q: Statement: Kinetic energy of molecules of a gas is zero at 0 degrees C. This statement is:
mcqs.why: The notes mark this statement False: gas molecules still have kinetic energy at 0 degrees C, which is 273 K, not absolute zero.

mcqs.q: Statement: A gas in a closed container exerts much higher pressure at the bottom due to gravity than at the top. This statement is:
options: True only for heavy gases in tall columns as stated
mcqs.why: The notes mark this statement False: a gas fills its container and its pressure is not much higher at the bottom due to gravity.

mcqs.q: Statement: Real gases show ideal gas behaviour at low pressure and high temperature. This statement is:
mcqs.why: The notes mark this statement True: at low pressure and high temperature real gases approach ideal gas behaviour.

mcqs.q: Statement: Liquefaction of gases involves decrease in intermolecular spaces. This statement is:
mcqs.why: The notes mark this statement True: on liquefaction the molecules come much closer, so intermolecular spaces decrease.

mcqs.q: Statement: An ideal gas on expansion will show Joule-Thomson effect. This statement is:
mcqs.why: The notes mark this statement False: an ideal gas, with no intermolecular attractions, shows no Joule-Thomson cooling on expansion.

mcqs.q: Which pressure condition helps a real gas behave ideally?
mcqs.why: The true statement in the notes pairs ideal behaviour with low pressure and high temperature, so low pressure is the helpful condition.

mcqs.q: Which temperature condition helps a real gas behave ideally?
mcqs.why: The true statement in the notes pairs ideal behaviour with low pressure and high temperature, so high temperature is the helpful condition.

mcqs.q: At 0 degrees C, the kinetic energy of gas molecules is:
mcqs.why: The notes judge the claim of zero kinetic energy at 0 degrees C to be False, so the molecules still possess kinetic energy there.

mcqs.q: When a gas is liquefied, its intermolecular spaces:
mcqs.why: The notes mark as True that liquefaction of gases involves a decrease in intermolecular spaces as molecules pack closer together.

mcqs.q: Which gas will show no Joule-Thomson effect on expansion, according to the notes?
options: A real gas below its inversion temperature
mcqs.why: The notes mark the claim that an ideal gas shows the Joule-Thomson effect as False, so an ideal gas shows no such effect on expansion.

lessons.title: Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q4(a). What is Boyle's law of gases?
Give its experimental verification.

Boyle's law: at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of a gas is

inversely proportional to its pressure, PV = constant. Experimental verification: a

fixed mass of gas is trapped in a graduated tube over mercury (or in a syringe with

a pressure gauge); as weights are added to increase the pressure, the volume

decreases, and the product PV stays constant at constant temperature. A plot of P

against 1/V is a straight line through the origin, and a plot of PV against P is a

horizontal line.

Q4(b). What are isotherms? What happens to the positions of isotherms when they are

plotted at high temperature for a particular gas.

Isotherms are the curves of P against V for a fixed mass of gas at one constant

temperature. At higher temperatures the isotherms move away from the axes

(upwards and to the right): at a higher temperature the same volume corresponds

to a higher pressure, and the whole PV = constant curve is shifted outward, because

PV = nRT is larger.

Q4(c). Why do we get a straight line when pressures exerted on a gas are plotted

against inverse of volumes? This straight line changes its position in the graph by

varying the temperature. Justify it.

Because PV = constant at constant temperature, P = constant/V, so P is directly

proportional to 1/V and the graph is a straight line through the origin. Raising the

temperature increases the constant (PV = nRT), so the line becomes steeper: for the

same 1/V the pressure is higher. The slope of the line is therefore nRT and it

increases with temperature.

Q4(d). How will you explain that the value of the constant k in the equation PV = k

depends upon (i) the temperature of a gas (ii) the quantity of a gas.

In PV = k, the constant k = nRT, so it depends on both (i) the temperature of the

gas and (ii) the quantity (number of moles) of the gas. It is not a universal constant:

doubling the moles or doubling the absolute temperature doubles k.

Q5(a). What is the Charles's law?
Which scale of temperature is used to verify that V/T

= k (pressure and number of moles are constant)?

Charles's law: at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of a gas is directly

proportional to its absolute temperature, V/T = constant. The Kelvin (absolute) scale

is used, because only on that scale does V become zero at -273.16 degrees C and

the proportionality V proportional to T hold with a straight line through the origin.

Q5(b). A sample of carbon monoxide gas occupies 150.0 mL at 25.0 degrees C. It is

then cooled at constant pressure until it occupies 100.0 mL. What is the new

temperature?

Step 1 - Convert to Kelvin: T1 = 25.0 + 273 = 298 K. V1 = 150.0 mL, V2 = 100.0

mL.

Step 2 - Charles's law: V1/T1 = V2/T2, so T2 = T1 x (V2/V1) = 298 x (100.0/150.0).

Step 3 - T2 = 198.7 K, which is 198.7 - 273 = -74.3 degrees C.

Answer: 198.8 K, about -74.4 degrees C (matches the book's printed answer; the 0.1

K difference is rounding of 273 vs 273.16).

Q5(c). Do you think that the volume of any quantity of a gas becomes zero at -273.16

degrees C? Is it not against the law of conservation of mass? How do you deduce

the idea of absolute zero from this information?

No, the volume does not really become zero: the gas liquefies (and then solidifies)

long before -273.16 degrees C, so Charles's law stops applying. This does not break

the law of conservation of mass, because mass is not volume: the same mass

occupies a much smaller volume as a liquid. Extrapolating the straight V-T graph for

a gas to zero volume gives the intercept -273.16 degrees C, the absolute zero, the

temperature at which the volume of an ideal gas would be zero and molecular

motion would cease.

Q6(a). What is Kelvin scale of temperature?
Plot a graph for one mole of a real gas to

prove that a gas becomes liquid, earlier than -273.16 degrees C.

The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, -273.16 degrees C = 0 K, and has the same

degree size as the Celsius scale: T(K) = t(degrees C) + 273.16. A real gas does not

reach -273.16 degrees C as a gas: on cooling it liquefies first (its V-T curve bends

away from the ideal straight line and drops to the small liquid volume), so the

straight-line extrapolation, not an actual measurement, gives absolute zero.

Q6(b). Throw some light on the factor 1/273 in Charles's law.

Charles found that the volume of a gas at constant pressure increases by 1/273 of

its volume at 0 degrees C for every 1 degree C rise. That is, Vt = V0 (1 + t/273) =

V0 (273 + t)/273. The factor 1/273 is therefore the coefficient of thermal expansion

of an ideal gas: it is the fraction by which the volume grows per degree, and it is the

same for all gases because it comes from the absolute temperature scale (273 K at

0 degrees C).

Q7(a). What is the general gas equation?
Derive it in various forms.

The general gas equation is PV = nRT, obtained by combining Boyle's law (V

proportional to 1/P), Charles's law (V proportional to T) and Avogadro's law (V

proportional to n). Its forms include: PV = nRT; P = (m/M) RT/V; PM = dRT (density

form, since d = m/V); P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2 for a fixed mass; and V = nRT/P.

Q7(b). Can we determine the molecular mass of an unknown gas if we know the

pressure, temperature and volume along with the mass of that gas?

Yes. From PV = nRT, n = PV/RT, and the mass m is known, so the molar mass M =

m/n = mRT/PV. The pressure, temperature, volume and mass are all measurable, so

M follows directly.

Q7(c). How do you justify from general gas equation that increase in temperature or

decrease of pressure decreases the density of the gas?

From PM = dRT, density d = PM/RT. At constant pressure, increasing T increases the

denominator, so d decreases: the same mass occupies a larger volume. Decreasing

P decreases the numerator, so d also decreases. In words, heating a gas or lowering

its pressure spreads the same mass over a larger volume.

Q7(d). Why do we feel comfortable in expressing the densities of gases in the units of

g dm-3 rather than g cm-3, a unit which is used to express the densities of liquids

and solids?

Gas densities are very small: for example oxygen is about 1.43 g per dm3, whereas

liquids and solids are of the order of grams per cm3, a thousand times larger.

Expressing a gas density in g per cm3 would give awkwardly small numbers

(0.00143 g cm-3), while g per dm3 gives convenient numbers (1.43 g dm-3).

Q8. Derive the units for gas constant R in general gas equation: (a) when the

pressure is in atmosphere and volume in dm3. (b) when the pressure is in N m-2

and volume in m3. (c) when energy is expressed in ergs.

R = PV/nT. (a) P in atm, V in dm3: R = 0.0821 atm dm3 mol-1 K-1 (from 1 mol at

STP: 1 x 22.414 / 273). (b) P in N m-2 (Pa), V in m3: R = 8.314 N m mol-1 K-1 =

8.314 J mol-1 K-1. (c) Energy in ergs: 1 J = 10^7 erg, so R = 8.314 x 10^7 erg mol-1

K-1.

Q9(a). What is Avogadro's law of gases?

Avogadro's law: at the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of all gases

contain equal numbers of molecules (equal moles). One mole of any gas occupies

22.414 dm3 at S.T.P.

Q9(b). Do you think that 1 mole of H2 and 1 mole of NH3 at 0 degrees C and 1 atm

pressure will have Avogadro's number of particles?

Yes, approximately. Both are 1 mol of gas at the same temperature and pressure, so

by Avogadro's law both contain Avogadro's number of particles (6.02 x 10^23

molecules). Real-gas deviations are small at 0 degrees C and 1 atm, and the count

is the same for both gases.

Q9(c). Justify that 1 cm3 of H2 and 1 cm3 of CH4 at STP will have same number of

molecules, when one molecule of CH4 is 8 times heavier than that of hydrogen.

Both samples have the same volume (1 cm3) at the same temperature and

pressure, so by Avogadro's law they contain the same number of molecules. The

mass of a molecule does not enter Avogadro's law: the number of molecules

depends only on volume, temperature and pressure, not on how heavy each

molecule is. (That the CH4 molecule is 8 times heavier only means the CH4 sample

is 8 times heavier in mass, not in molecule count.)

Q10(a). Dalton's law of partial pressures is only obeyed by those gases which don't

have attractive forces among their molecules. Explain it.

Dalton's law assumes the gases in a mixture behave independently, each exerting

the pressure it would exert alone in the same volume. If the molecules attract each

other, they no longer act independently: the total pressure is changed by the

attractions, and the partial pressures do not simply add. The law is therefore exact

only for gases with negligible intermolecular attractions, that is, for ideal gases (or

real gases at low pressure and high temperature).

Q10(b). Derive an equation to find out the partial pressure of a gas knowing the

individual moles of component gases and the total pressure of the mixture.

For a mixture, the partial pressure of each gas is pi = (ni / n total) x P total, where ni

is its moles and P total is the total pressure. Derivation: each gas obeys PV = ni RT

in the same volume V at the same temperature, so pi = ni RT/V; adding all partial

pressures gives P total = (sum ni) RT/V, and dividing gives pi = (ni / n total) x P

total, that is, partial pressure = mole fraction x total pressure.

Q10(c). Explain that the process of respiration obeys the Dalton's law of partial

pressures.

Respiration obeys Dalton's law because the air in the lungs is a mixture of gases,

each contributing its own partial pressure. Inhaled air has a high partial pressure of

oxygen (about 159 mmHg) and a low partial pressure of carbon dioxide, while

venous blood has a lower oxygen and higher carbon dioxide partial pressure.

Oxygen therefore diffuses from the alveoli into the blood and carbon dioxide

diffuses the other way, each gas moving down its own partial-pressure gradient,

exactly as Dalton's law describes for a mixture.

Q10(d). How do you differentiate between diffusion and effusion?
Explain Graham's

law of diffusion.

Diffusion is the spontaneous spreading of a gas through another gas (or through

space) by random molecular motion, without a hole or barrier. Effusion is the escape

of a gas through a tiny hole (pinhole) into a vacuum or a region of lower pressure,

molecule by molecule. Graham's law of diffusion: the rate of diffusion (or effusion)

of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its density (or molar mass) at

constant temperature and pressure: r1/r2 = sqrt(M2/M1). Lighter gases diffuse

faster.

Q11(a). What is critical temperature of a gas?
What is its importance for liquefaction

of gases? Discuss Linde's method of liquefaction of gases.

The critical temperature is the highest temperature at which a gas can be liquefied

by pressure alone; above it, no amount of pressure can liquefy the gas. It matters

because a gas must be cooled to or below its critical temperature before

compression can liquefy it. Linde's method: air is compressed, cooled, and then

allowed to expand through a nozzle (Joule-Thomson expansion); the expansion cools

the gas further, and the cold gas cools the incoming compressed gas in a heat

exchanger. Repeated cycles lower the temperature until the gas liquefies, and the

liquid is collected.

Q11(b). What is Joule-Thomson effect?
Explain its importance in Linde's method of

liquefaction of gases.

The Joule-Thomson effect is the cooling (for most gases below their inversion

temperature) that occurs when a gas expands from a high pressure to a low

pressure through a nozzle or porous plug without exchanging heat with the

surroundings. In Linde's method this expansion cooling is the working step: each

expansion makes the gas colder, the cold outgoing gas pre-cools the incoming

compressed gas, and after many cycles the temperature falls below the critical

temperature and the gas liquefies.

Q12(a). What is kinetic molecular theory of gases?
Give its postulates.

Kinetic molecular theory of gases assumes: (1) a gas consists of a large number of

tiny particles in continuous random motion; (2) the particles are negligibly small

compared with the distances between them, so their own volume is negligible; (3)

there are no attractive or repulsive forces between the particles; (4) collisions

between particles and with the walls are perfectly elastic, so no kinetic energy is

lost; (5) the average kinetic energy of the particles is directly proportional to the

absolute temperature; (6) the pressure of a gas is due to the collisions of its

particles with the walls of the container.

Q12(b). How does kinetic molecular theory of gases explain: (i) Boyle's law (ii)

Charles's law (iii) Avogadro's law (iv) Graham's law of diffusion.

(i) Boyle's law: at constant temperature the kinetic energy (and hence the average

speed) is fixed; compressing the gas into a smaller volume makes the particles hit

the walls more often, so the pressure rises in inverse proportion to the volume. (ii)

Charles's law: heating a gas increases the kinetic energy and speed of its particles,

so at constant pressure they push the walls further out and the volume grows in

proportion to the absolute temperature. (iii) Avogadro's law: at the same

temperature and pressure, equal volumes contain equal numbers of particles,

because the pressure depends only on the number of particles and their kinetic

energy, not on their chemical identity. (iv) Graham's law: at the same temperature

all gases have the same average kinetic energy (1/2 m v^2), so lighter particles

move faster: v is proportional to 1/sqrt(m), and the rate of diffusion is proportional

to the molecular speed.

Q13(a). Gases show non-ideal behaviour at low temperature and high pressure.

Explain this with the help of a graph.

At low temperature the kinetic energy of the molecules is small, so intermolecular

attractions can hold molecules together and reduce the pressure below the ideal

value; at high pressure the molecules are crowded together, so their own finite

volume becomes a significant part of the container volume and the free volume is

less than V. On a PV-versus-P plot an ideal gas gives a horizontal line (PV = nRT

constant), but a real gas curve dips below it at moderate pressures (attractions

dominate) and rises above it at high pressures (molecular volume dominates).

Q13(b). Do you think that some of the postulates of kinetic molecular theory of gases

are faulty? Point out these postulates.

Yes, two postulates are faulty for real gases: (1) that the volume of the gas

molecules themselves is negligible - at high pressure it is a significant fraction of

the container volume; and (2) that there are no intermolecular attractions - at low

temperature attractions are significant and reduce the pressure. The other

postulates (random motion, elastic collisions, pressure from wall collisions, kinetic

energy proportional to temperature) remain good approximations.

Q13(c). Hydrogen and helium are ideal at room temperature, but SO2 and Cl2 are

non-ideal. How will you explain this?

Hydrogen and helium are very small, light, non-polar molecules with extremely

weak intermolecular attractions, so both faulty postulates are nearly true for them

even at room temperature: their molecular volume is tiny and their attractions are

negligible. SO2 and Cl2 are larger molecules with stronger attractions (SO2 is polar,

Cl2 is large and easily polarised), so their attractions and molecular volumes are

significant and they deviate noticeably from ideal behaviour.

Q14(a). Derive van der Waals equation for real gases.

The ideal equation PV = nRT is corrected in two ways. (1) The molecules themselves

occupy volume nb, so the free volume is (V - nb). (2) Attractions between molecules

reduce the pressure by a term proportional to the square of the concentration, a

n^2/V^2, so the observed pressure P must be increased by that amount. Hence (P

+ a n^2/V^2)(V - nb) = nRT, the van der Waals equation for n moles (for 1 mol: (P

+ a/V^2)(V - b) = RT).

Q14(b). What is the physical significance of van der Waals constants, 'a' and 'b'?
Give

their units.

'a' measures the strength of the intermolecular attractions: larger 'a' means

stronger attractions and a larger pressure reduction. Its units are atm dm6 mol-2

(pressure x volume^2 / moles^2). 'b' measures the volume actually occupied by

one mole of molecules (the excluded volume): larger 'b' means larger molecules. Its

units are dm3 mol-1.

Q15. Explain: (i) The plot of PV versus P is a straight line at constant temperature and

with a fixed number of moles of an ideal gas. (ii) The straight line in (a) is parallel to

pressure-axis and goes away from the pressure axis at higher pressures for many

gases. (iii) Pressure of NH3 gas at given conditions (say 20 atm pressure and room

temperature) is less as calculated by van der Waals equation than that calculated

by general gas equation. (iv) Water vapours do not behave ideally at 273 K. (v) SO2

is comparatively non-ideal at 273 K but behaves ideally at 327 degrees C.

(i) For an ideal gas at constant temperature, PV = nRT is constant, so a plot of PV

against P is a horizontal straight line. (ii) For many real gases the line is horizontal

only at low pressure; at higher pressures it moves away from the pressure axis

(rises), because the finite molecular volume makes PV larger than nRT. (iii) NH3 has

strong intermolecular attractions (hydrogen bonding, polar), so the attraction term

lowers its pressure below the ideal value, as van der Waals equation predicts. (iv) At

273 K water vapour is close to its condensation point, so attractions between

molecules are strong and it behaves non-ideally. (v) SO2 is fairly easily liquefied and

its attractions are significant at 273 K, but at 327 degrees C (600 K) the kinetic

energy is so large that attractions become negligible and it behaves almost ideally.

Q16. Helium gas in a 100 cm3 container at a pressure of 500 torr is transferred to a

container with a volume of 250 cm3. What will be the new pressure (a) if no change

in temperature occurs (b) if its temperature changes from 20 degrees C to 15

degrees C?

Step 1 (a) - Boyle's law at constant temperature: P1V1 = P2V2, so P2 = P1 x (V1/V2)

= 500 torr x (100/250).

Step 2 (a) - P2 = 200 torr.

Step 3 (b) - Combined gas law: P2 = P1 x (V1/V2) x (T2/T1). T1 = 20 + 273 = 293 K,

T2 = 15 + 273 = 288 K.

Step 4 (b) - P2 = 500 x (100/250) x (288/293) = 500 x 0.4 x 0.9829 = 196.6 torr.

Answer: (a) 200 torr (b) 196.56 torr (matches the book's printed answers).

Q17. (a) What are the densities in kg/m3 of the following gases at STP (P = 101325 N

m-2, T = 273 K, molecular masses are in kg mol-1): (i) methane, (ii) oxygen, (iii)

hydrogen. (b) Compare the values of densities in proportion to their mole masses.

(c) How do you justify that increase of volume up to 100 dm3 at 27 degrees C of 2

moles of NH3 will allow the gas behave ideally, as compared to S.T.P. conditions?

Step 1 (a) - At STP one mole occupies 22.414 dm3 = 0.022414 m3. Density = molar

mass / molar volume.

Step 2 - Methane: 0.016 kg mol-1 / 0.022414 m3 mol-1 = 0.714 kg m-3. Oxygen:

0.032/0.022414 = 1.428 kg m-3. Hydrogen: 0.002/0.022414 = 0.089 kg m-3.

Step 3 - These are the same numbers as 0.714, 1.428 and 0.089 g dm-3; the book's

printed values (0.714, 1.428, 0.089) are in kg m-3, i.e. g dm-3, not kg dm-3 as the

question's wording states - flagged.

Step 4 (b) - The densities are in the ratio 0.714 : 1.428 : 0.089, which is the same as

the molar-mass ratio 16 : 32 : 2, because at the same temperature and pressure all

gases have the same molar volume.

Step 5 (c) - At STP, 2 mol of NH3 occupy only 44.8 dm3, so the molecules are close

together and attractions (and the molecular volume) matter. Expanded to 100 dm3

at 27 degrees C, the pressure falls and the molecules are much further apart, so

attractions become negligible and the free volume is essentially the whole volume:

the gas behaves ideally.

Answer: (a) CH4 = 0.714 kg m-3, O2 = 1.428 kg m-3, H2 = 0.089 kg m-3 (matches

the book's printed answers, with the unit note in Step 3).

Q18. A sample of krypton with a volume of 6.25 dm3, a pressure of 765 torr and a

temperature of 20 degrees C is expanded to a volume of 9.55 dm3 and a pressure

of 375 torr. What will be its final temperature in degrees C?

Step 1 - Combined gas law: T2 = T1 x (P2/P1) x (V2/V1). T1 = 20 + 273 = 293 K.

Step 2 - P2/P1 = 375/765 = 0.4902. V2/V1 = 9.55/6.25 = 1.528.

Step 3 - T2 = 293 x 0.4902 x 1.528 = 219.5 K.

Step 4 - In Celsius: 219.5 - 273 = -53.5 degrees C.

Answer: T = -53.6 degrees C (matches the book's printed answer; the 0.1 degree

difference is rounding).

Q19. Working at a vacuum line, a chemist isolated a gas in a weighing bulb with a

volume of 255 cm3, at a temperature of 25 degrees C and under a pressure in the

bulb of 10.0 torr. The gas weighed 12.1 mg. What is the molecular mass of this gas?

Step 1 - Convert: V = 255 cm3 = 0.255 dm3; T = 25 + 273 = 298 K; P = 10.0/760 =

0.01316 atm.

Step 2 - Moles from PV = nRT: n = PV/RT = (0.01316 x 0.255) / (0.0821 x 298) =

0.003356 / 24.466 = 1.372 x 10^-4 mol.

Step 3 - Molar mass = mass / moles = 0.0121 g / 1.372 x 10^-4 mol = 88.2 g mol-1.

Answer: About 88 g mol-1 (book prints 87.93 g mol-1; the small difference is

rounding of R and the pressure conversion).

Q20. What pressure is exerted by a mixture of 2.00 g of H2 and 8.00 g of N2 at 273 K

in a 10 dm3 vessel?

Step 1 - Moles of H2 = 2.00/2 = 1.00 mol. Moles of N2 = 8.00/28 = 0.2857 mol.

Step 2 - Total moles = 1.00 + 0.2857 = 1.2857 mol.

Step 3 - From PV = nRT: P = nRT/V = (1.2857 x 0.0821 x 273) / 10.

Step 4 - P = 28.82 / 10 = 2.88 atm.

Answer: P = 2.88 atm (matches the book's printed answer).

Q21. (a) The relative densities of two gases A and B are 1:1.5. Find out the volume of

B which will diffuse in the same time in which 150 dm3 of A will diffuse. (b)

Hydrogen (H2) diffuses through a porous plate at a rate of 500 cm3 per minute at 0

degrees C. What is the rate of diffusion of oxygen through the same porous plate at

0 degrees C? (c) The rate of effusion of an unknown gas A through a pinhole is

found to be 0.279 times the rate of effusion of H2 gas through the same pinhole.

Calculate the molecular mass of the unknown gas at STP.

Step 1 (a) - By Graham's law, volumes diffused in the same time are in the ratio of

the rates: VB/VA = sqrt(dA/dB) = sqrt(1/1.5) = 0.8165.

Step 2 (a) - VB = 150 x 0.8165 = 122.47 dm3.

Step 3 (b) - Rate of O2 / rate of H2 = sqrt(M_H2 / M_O2) = sqrt(2/32) = sqrt(1/16) =

0.25. Rate of O2 = 500 x 0.25 = 125 cm3 per minute.

Step 4 (c) - Rate ratio = sqrt(M_H2 / M_A) = 0.279. Squaring: M_H2 / M_A = 0.279^2

= 0.07784.

Step 5 (c) - M_A = 2 / 0.07784 = 25.7 g mol-1.

Answer: (a) 122.47 dm3 (b) 125 cm3 per minute (c) 25.7 g mol-1. All match the

book's printed answers.

Q22. Calculate the number of molecules and the number of atoms in the given

amounts of each gas: (a) 20 cm3 of CH4 at 0 degrees C and pressure of 700 mm of

mercury. (b) 1 cm3 of NH3 at 100 degrees C and pressure of 1.5 atm.

Step 1 (a) - Convert: P = 700/760 = 0.921 atm; V = 20 cm3 = 0.020 dm3; T = 273

K.

Step 2 (a) - Moles = PV/RT = (0.921 x 0.020) / (0.0821 x 273) = 0.01842 / 22.413 =

8.22 x 10^-4 mol.

Step 3 (a) - Molecules = 8.22 x 10^-4 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 4.95 x 10^20. Each CH4

molecule has 5 atoms, so atoms = 5 x 4.95 x 10^20 = 24.7 x 10^20.

Step 4 (b) - Convert: V = 1 cm3 = 0.001 dm3; T = 100 + 273 = 373 K; P = 1.5 atm.

Step 5 (b) - Moles = (1.5 x 0.001) / (0.0821 x 373) = 0.0015 / 30.62 = 4.90 x 10^-5

mol.

Step 6 (b) - Molecules = 4.90 x 10^-5 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 2.94 x 10^19. Each NH3

molecule has 4 atoms, so atoms = 4 x 2.94 x 10^19 = 1.177 x 10^20.

Answer: (a) 4.936 x 10^20 molecules, 24.7 x 10^20 atoms (b) 2.94 x 10^19

molecules, 1.177 x 10^20 atoms. Matches the book's printed answers.

Q23. Calculate the masses of 10^20 molecules of each of H2, O2 and CO2 at STP.

What will happen to the masses of these gases, when the temperature of these

gases are increased by 100 degrees C and the pressure is decreased by 100 torr?

Step 1 - Moles in 10^20 molecules = 10^20 / 6.02 x 10^23 = 1.661 x 10^-4 mol.

Step 2 - Mass of H2 = 1.661 x 10^-4 x 2 = 3.3 x 10^-4 g. Mass of O2 = 1.661 x

10^-4 x 32 = 5.31 x 10^-3 g. Mass of CO2 = 1.661 x 10^-4 x 44 = 7.30 x 10^-3 g.

Step 3 - The mass of a given number of molecules is fixed by the count and the

molar mass (mass = n x M). Changing the temperature or the pressure changes the

volume the gas occupies, not the mass of those molecules, so the masses do not

change.

Answer: H2 = 3.3 x 10^-4 g, O2 = 5.31 x 10^-3 g, CO2 = 7.30 x 10^-3 g; the

masses are unchanged by the temperature rise and pressure fall (matches the

book's printed answers).

Q24. (a) Two moles of NH3 are enclosed in a 5 dm3 flask at 27 degrees C. Calculate

the pressure exerted by the gas assuming that (i) it behaves like an ideal gas (ii) it

behaves like a real gas (a = 4.17 atm dm6 mol-2, b = 0.0371 dm3 mol-1). (b) Also

calculate the amount of pressure lessened due to forces of attraction at these

conditions of volume and temperature. (c) Do you expect the same decrease in the

pressure of two moles of NH3 having a volume of 40 dm3 and at temperature of 27

degrees C?

Step 1 (a)(i) - Ideal gas: P = nRT/V = (2 x 0.0821 x 300) / 5 = 49.26 / 5 = 9.85 atm.

Step 2 (a)(ii) - Van der Waals: P = nRT/(V - nb) - a n^2/V^2. V - nb = 5 - (2 x 0.0371)

= 4.9258 dm3. nRT/(V - nb) = 49.26/4.9258 = 10.00 atm. Attraction term = 4.17 x 4

/ 25 = 0.667 atm. Hence P = 10.00 - 0.667 = 9.33 atm.

Step 3 (b) - The net pressure lessening against the ideal value is 9.85 - 9.33 = 0.52

atm (book prints 0.51 atm; the difference is rounding). The attraction term alone is

0.667 atm, partly offset by the volume correction, which raises the pressure.

Step 4 (c) - No. At 40 dm3 the attraction term is 4.17 x 4 / 1600 = 0.0104 atm,

about sixty times smaller, and the volume correction is also negligible, so the gas is

almost ideal and the pressure decrease is only about 0.01 atm, not 0.51 atm.

Answer: (a)(i) 9.85 atm (ii) 9.33 atm (b) about 0.51 atm lessened (c) No, the

decrease is negligible at 40 dm3.

mcqs.q: Boyle's law states that at constant temperature, for a fixed mass of gas:
options: Volume is inversely proportional to pressure, PV = constant
Volume is directly proportional to pressure
Pressure is directly proportional to temperature
Volume is directly proportional to temperature
mcqs.why: The notes define Boyle's law as volume inversely proportional to pressure at constant temperature, written as PV = constant.

mcqs.q: Carbon monoxide occupies 150.0 mL at 25.0 degrees C and is cooled at constant pressure to 100.0 mL. Its new temperature is about:
mcqs.why: Charles's law: T1 = 25 + 273 = 298 K and T2 = 298 * (100 / 150) = 198.7 K, matching the worked answer in the notes.

mcqs.q: Helium in a 100 cm3 container at 500 torr is transferred to a 250 cm3 container at constant temperature. The new pressure is:
mcqs.why: Boyle's law: P2 = 500 * (100 / 250) = 500 * 0.4 = 200 torr, exactly as calculated in the notes.

mcqs.q: In the helium transfer above, if the temperature also falls from 20 degrees C to 15 degrees C, the new pressure is about:
Krypton at 6.25 dm3, 765 torr and 20 degrees C expands to 9.55 dm3 and 375 torr. Its final temperature is about:
What pressure is exerted by 2.00 g H2 and 8.00 g N2 at 273 K in a 10 dm3 vessel?
Hydrogen diffuses at 500 cm3 per minute at 0 degrees C. The rate of diffusion of oxygen through the same plate is:
mcqs.why: Graham's law: rate ratio = sqrt(2 / 32) = sqrt(0.0625) = 0.25, so the oxygen rate = 500 * 0.25 = 125 cm3 per minute.

mcqs.q: A gas effuses at 0.279 times the rate of H2 through the same pinhole. Its molecular mass is about:
mcqs.why: Rate ratio squared gives 0.279 * 0.279 = 0.07784, so M = 2 / 0.07784 = 25.7 g/mol, as worked out in the notes.

mcqs.q: Two moles of NH3 in a 5 dm3 flask at 27 degrees C behave ideally. The pressure is:
mcqs.why: Ideal gas: T = 300 K, so P = 2 * 0.0821 * 300 / 5 = 49.26 / 5 = 9.85 atm, matching the notes.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • The polarizability of noble gases increases down the group and results in the increase in their boiling points.
  • is developed in acetone and chloroform when they are mixed together.
  • Exceptionally weak acidity of HF is due to strong hydrogen bonding present in it.
  • The concept of dynamic equilibrium is the ultimate state of all reversible systems.
  • The enthalpy of vaporisation of C6H14 should be greater than that of C2H6, because the larger molecule has stronger London dispersion forces and more surface area, so more energy is needed to separate its molecules.
  • During the formation of ice from liquid water there is a 9 percent % increase in volume.
  • The rate of increase of vapour pressure of water increases at high temperatures.
  • A layer of ice on the surface of water insulates the water underneath for further heat loss.

mcqs.q: How does the polarizability of noble gases change down the group?
options: It stays constant down the group
It first decreases then becomes zero

lessons.title: Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
QLiquids 4(a). What type of intermolecular forces will dominate in the following

liquids: (i) Ammonia, NH3 (ii) Octane, C8H18 (iii) Argon, Ar (iv) Propanone,

CH3COCH3 (v) Methanol, CH3OH.

(i) Ammonia, NH3: hydrogen bonding dominates (N-H with a lone pair on nitrogen).

(ii) Octane, C8H18: London dispersion forces only (non-polar hydrocarbon). (iii)

Argon, Ar: London dispersion forces only (single non-polar atom). (iv) Propanone,

CH3COCH3: dipole-dipole forces dominate (polar C=O, no O-H hydrogen bonding).

(v) Methanol, CH3OH: hydrogen bonding dominates (O-H group).

QLiquids 4(b). Propanone, propanol and butane have very similar relative molecular

masses. List them in the expected increasing boiling points. Explain your answer.

Increasing order of boiling points: butane < propanone < propanol. Butane is

non-polar, held only by weak London forces, so it boils lowest. Propanone is polar,

held by dipole-dipole forces, so it boils higher. Propanol can form hydrogen bonds

through its O-H group, the strongest of the three, so it boils highest, even though all

three have similar molar masses.

QLiquids 5. Explain with reasons: (i) In the hydrogen bonded structure of HF, which is

the stronger bond: the shorter covalent bond or the longer hydrogen bond between

different molecules? (ii) In a very cold winter the fish in garden ponds owe their lives

to hydrogen bonding? (iii) Water and ethanol can mix easily and in all proportions.

(iv) The origin of the intermolecular forces in water.

(i) The covalent H-F bond inside one HF molecule is much stronger (and shorter)

than the hydrogen bond between two HF molecules: the covalent bond is a full

shared-electron bond, while the hydrogen bond is only a weak electrostatic

attraction between molecules. (ii) In a very cold winter the surface water of a pond

freezes to ice, which floats and insulates the water below, so the water under the

ice stays liquid (near 4 degrees C) and the fish survive; this floating ice is a

consequence of hydrogen bonding in water. (iii) Water and ethanol both form

hydrogen bonds, and their molecules can hydrogen-bond to each other, so they mix

in all proportions. (iv) The intermolecular forces in water are hydrogen bonding

(dominant), dipole-dipole forces (water is polar) and London dispersion forces

(present in all molecules).

QLiquids 6(a). Briefly consider some of the effects on our lives if water has only a very

weak hydrogen bonding present among its molecules. (b) All gases have a

characteristic critical temperature. Above the critical temperature it is impossible to

liquefy a gas. The critical temperatures of carbon dioxide and methane are 31.14

degrees C and -81.9 degrees C, respectively. Which gas has the stronger

intermolecular forces? Briefly explain your choice.

(a) If water had only very weak hydrogen bonding, it would be a gas at room

temperature (like H2S), ice would not float, the oceans would freeze solid from the

bottom up, and life as we know it could not exist; the high boiling point, high heat

capacity and solvent power of water all depend on its strong hydrogen bonding. (b)

Carbon dioxide has the stronger intermolecular forces: its critical temperature

(31.14 degrees C) is far higher than methane's (-81.9 degrees C). A higher critical

temperature means stronger attractions must be overcome, and CO2 is larger and

more polarizable (with a quadrupole moment) than the small, symmetrical CH4

molecule.

QLiquids 7. Three liquids have the properties: Water: H2O, molar mass 18, enthalpy of

vaporisation 41.1 kJ mol-1, boiling point 100 degrees C. Propanone: C3H6O, molar

mass 58, enthalpy of vaporisation 31.9 kJ mol-1, boiling point 56 degrees C.

Pentane: C5H12, molar mass 72, enthalpy of vaporisation 27.7 kJ mol-1, boiling

point 36 degrees C. (a) What type of intermolecular force predominates in each

liquid? (b) What do you deduce about the relative strength of these forces? Justify.

(c) If the liquids are shaken together in pairs: (i) Which pair would be unlikely to

mix? (ii) Explain this immiscibility in terms of the forces between the molecules. (iii)

Choose one of the pairs that mix and say whether the enthalpy change on mixing

would be positive or negative.

(a) Water: hydrogen bonding predominates. Propanone: dipole-dipole forces

predominate. Pentane: London dispersion forces predominate. (b) Relative strength:

water > propanone > pentane. Justification: water has the highest enthalpy of

vaporisation (41.1 kJ mol-1) and the highest boiling point (100 degrees C) although

it has the lowest molar mass (18), which is only possible if its intermolecular forces

are the strongest. Propanone is next (31.9 kJ mol-1, 56 degrees C) and pentane is

weakest (27.7 kJ mol-1, 36 degrees C) although it has the highest molar mass (72),

showing its forces are the weakest. (c) (i) The water-pentane pair is unlikely to mix:

water is polar and hydrogen-bonded, pentane is non-polar, and mixing would break

strong water-water hydrogen bonds without replacing them. (ii) This immiscibility is

explained by the forces: like dissolves like; water-water and pentane-pentane

attractions are each stronger than water-pentane attractions. (iii) For a pair that

does mix, for example water-propanone, the enthalpy change on mixing is negative

(heat is given out), because new hydrogen bonds and dipole attractions form

between the different molecules.

QLiquids 8. Describe the various forces responsible for keeping the particles together

in the following elements and compounds and their effects on physical properties,

from the data: Neon (Ne, molar mass 20, M.P. -248 degrees C); Argon (Ar, 40, -189

degrees C); Water (H2O, 18, 0 degrees C); Sodium fluoride (NaF, 42, 993 degrees

C); Diamond (C, 12, 3350 degrees C).

Neon and argon are held together only by very weak London forces between small

atoms, so their melting points are extremely low (-248 and -189 degrees C). Water,

although its molar mass is only 18, melts at 0 degrees C because its molecules are

held by strong hydrogen bonds. Sodium fluoride is ionic, held by strong electrostatic

forces between Na+ and F- ions, so it melts at 993 degrees C. Diamond is a

covalent network solid with strong covalent bonds throughout the crystal, so it

melts at 3350 degrees C. The melting points therefore follow the strength of the

bonding: London < hydrogen bonding < ionic < covalent network.

QLiquids 9. The boiling points and molar masses of hydrides of some first row

elements are: CH4 109 K, 16 g mol-1; NH3 240 K, 17 g mol-1; H2O 373 K, 18 g

mol-1. Suggest reasons for the difference in their boiling points in terms of the type

of molecules involved and the nature of the forces present between them.

Although the molar masses are similar (16, 17, 18), the boiling points rise sharply:

CH4 109 K, NH3 240 K, H2O 373 K. Methane is non-polar, held only by weak London

forces, so it boils lowest. Ammonia is polar and forms hydrogen bonds, so it boils

much higher. Water forms the most extensive hydrogen bonding (each molecule can

form up to four hydrogen bonds in a network) and is the most polar, so it boils

highest. The differences are therefore due to the type and strength of the

intermolecular forces, not the molar masses.

QLiquids 10. Explain the term saturated vapour pressure. Arrange in order of

increasing vapour pressure: 1 dm3 water, 1 dm3 ethanol, 50 cm3 water, 50 cm3

ethanol and 50 cm3 of ether.

Saturated vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapour of a liquid when it

is in dynamic equilibrium with the liquid in a closed container at a given

temperature. It depends only on the liquid and the temperature, not on the amount

of liquid or the volume of the container. Increasing order of vapour pressure: the two

water samples are equal and lowest, the two ethanol samples are equal and next,

and ether is highest. So: 1 dm3 water = 50 cm3 water < 1 dm3 ethanol = 50 cm3

ethanol < 50 cm3 ether.

QLiquids 11. While a volatile liquid standing in a beaker evaporates, the temperature

of the liquid remains the same as that of its surrounding. If the same liquid is

allowed to vaporize into atmosphere in an insulated vessel, its temperature falls

below that of its surrounding. Explain the difference in behaviour.

In the open beaker, heat is continuously supplied from the surroundings to replace

the heat used in evaporation, so the liquid stays at the surrounding temperature. In

the insulated vessel no heat can enter from outside, so the heat needed for

evaporation is taken from the liquid itself: the fastest molecules escape, the

average kinetic energy of the remaining liquid falls, and its temperature drops

below that of the surroundings.

QLiquids 12. How does hydrogen bonding explain: (i) Structure of DNA (ii) Hydrogen

bonding in proteins (iii) Formation of ice and its lesser density than liquid water (iv)

Solubilities of compounds.

(i) Structure of DNA: the two strands of the double helix are held together by

hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs (A-T with two hydrogen bonds,

G-C with three). (ii) Hydrogen bonding in proteins: hydrogen bonds between the

C=O and N-H groups of the peptide chain hold the alpha-helix and beta-sheet

secondary structures. (iii) Formation of ice and its lesser density than liquid water:

in ice each water molecule is hydrogen-bonded to four neighbours in an open,

cage-like structure with empty spaces, so ice occupies more volume and is less

dense than liquid water, and floats. (iv) Solubilities: a substance dissolves in water if

it can form hydrogen bonds with water (or ion-dipole attractions), which is why

alcohols, sugars and many polar compounds are soluble, while non-polar

hydrocarbons are not.

QLiquids 13. What are liquid crystals?
Give their uses in daily life.

Liquid crystals are substances that flow like liquids but keep some of the ordered

molecular arrangement of a crystal: they are an intermediate state between a solid

crystal and an ordinary liquid. Uses in daily life: liquid crystal displays (LCDs) in

watches, calculators, mobile phones and televisions; liquid crystal thermometers

(temperature strips); and optical shutters and display panels.

QLiquids 14. Explain with reasons: (i) Evaporation causes cooling. (ii) Evaporation

takes place at all temperatures. (iii) Boiling needs a constant supply of heat. (iv)

Earthenware vessels keep water cool. (v) One feels sense of cooling under the fan

after bath. (vi) Dynamic equilibrium is established during evaporation of a liquid in a

closed vessel at constant temperature. (vii) The boiling point of water is different at

Murree hills and at Mount Everest. (viii) Vacuum distillation can be used to avoid

decomposition of a sensitive liquid. (ix) Heat of sublimation of a substance is

greater than that of heat of vaporization. (x) Heat of sublimation of iodine is very

high.

(i) Evaporation causes cooling because only the molecules with the highest kinetic

energy can escape from the surface; their departure lowers the average kinetic

energy (temperature) of the remaining liquid. (ii) Evaporation takes place at all

temperatures because at any temperature some surface molecules have enough

energy to overcome the intermolecular forces, even though the number increases

rapidly with temperature. (iii) Boiling needs a constant supply of heat because the

heat is used to break the intermolecular forces and separate the molecules, while

the temperature stays constant at the boiling point. (iv) Earthenware vessels keep

water cool because water seeps through the porous walls and evaporates from the

outer surface; the evaporation takes heat from the vessel and the water inside. (v)

One feels cooling under a fan after a bath because the moving air removes the

vapour and speeds up the evaporation of water from the skin, taking heat from the

body. (vi) Dynamic equilibrium is established during evaporation of a liquid in a

closed vessel at constant temperature: the rate of evaporation becomes equal to

the rate of condensation, so the vapour pressure stays constant. (vii) The boiling

point of water is different at Murree hills and at Mount Everest because the

atmospheric pressure is lower at higher altitude: water boils when its vapour

pressure equals the external pressure, so at lower pressure it boils at a lower

temperature. (viii) Vacuum distillation can be used to avoid decomposition of a

sensitive liquid because lowering the pressure lowers its boiling point, so it can be

distilled at a temperature below its decomposition temperature. (ix) Heat of

sublimation of a substance is greater than its heat of vaporization because

sublimation includes both melting (fusion) and vaporisation: solid to liquid to gas

needs more energy than liquid to gas alone. (x) Heat of sublimation of iodine is very

high because I2 molecules are large and highly polarizable, so the London forces

between them are strong and much energy is needed to separate them.

QSolids 4. What are solids? Give general properties of solids. How do you differentiate

between crystalline solids and amorphous solids?

Solids are substances with a definite shape and a definite volume, whose particles

are held in fixed positions by strong forces. General properties: definite shape and

volume, high density, incompressibility, slow diffusion, and a sharp (crystalline) or

gradual (amorphous) melting point. Crystalline solids have a regular, repeating

arrangement of particles, sharp melting points, flat faces and clean cleavage;

amorphous solids have no regular arrangement, soften over a range of

temperature, and break with irregular fracture (for example glass, plastic, rubber).

QSolids 5(a). Explain the following properties of crystalline solids, giving three

examples in each case: (i) Anisotropy (ii) Cleavage (iii) Habit of a crystal (iv)

Isomorphism (v) Polymorphism (vi) Transition temperature (vii) Symmetry (viii)

Growing of a crystal. (b) How polymorphism and allotropy are related to each other?

Give examples.

Crystalline solids show: (i) Anisotropy: properties differ in different directions (for

example cleavage and conductivity). (ii) Cleavage: they split along definite planes.

(iii) Habit of a crystal: the characteristic external shape of the crystal. (iv)

Isomorphism: different substances with similar formulae crystallise in the same form

(for example NaNO3 and CaCO3). (v) Polymorphism: the same substance exists in

more than one crystalline form (for example CaCO3 as calcite and aragonite). (vi)

Transition temperature: the temperature at which one crystalline form changes into

another. (vii) Symmetry: the crystal looks the same after certain rotations or

reflections. (viii) Growing of a crystal: crystals grow by adding particles layer by

layer from a saturated solution or melt. (b) Polymorphism and allotropy are related:

allotropy is polymorphism in elements (the same element in different forms, for

example carbon as diamond and graphite, sulphur as rhombic and monoclinic);

polymorphism is the general term, used for compounds as well as elements.

QSolids 6(a). Define unit cell. What are unit cell dimensions?
How the idea of crystal

lattice is developed from the concept of unit cell? (b) Explain seven crystal systems

and draw the shapes of their unit cells.

A unit cell is the smallest repeating unit of a crystal lattice which, when repeated in

three dimensions, builds the whole crystal. Unit cell dimensions are its edge lengths

(a, b, c) and the angles between them (alpha, beta, gamma): six parameters in all.

The crystal lattice is developed by repeating the unit cell in all three directions, so

that the pattern of points (lattice points) extends through the whole crystal. (b) The

seven crystal systems are: cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, hexagonal,

rhombohedral (trigonal), monoclinic and triclinic, distinguished by their edge

lengths and angles; their unit-cell shapes are drawn as boxes with the

corresponding equalities of edges and angles (for example cubic: a = b = c, all

angles 90 degrees; hexagonal: a = b, not equal to c, gamma = 120 degrees). This is

a drawing task: sketch each of the seven unit cells with its edges and angles

labelled.

QSolids 7(a). What are ionic solids?
Give their properties. Explain the structure of

NaCl. Sketch a model to justify that unit cell of NaCl has four formula units in it. (b)

What are covalent solids? Give their properties. Explain the structure of diamond.

(c) What are molecular crystals? Give their properties. Justify that molecular crystals

are softer than ionic crystals.

Ionic solids consist of positive and negative ions held by strong electrostatic forces.

Properties: high melting and boiling points, hard and brittle, soluble in polar

solvents, non-conductors in the solid state but conductors in the molten state and in

solution. NaCl structure: a face-centred cubic arrangement in which each Na+ is

surrounded by 6 Cl- ions and each Cl- by 6 Na+ ions; the unit cell contains 4 Na+

and 4 Cl- ions, that is, 4 formula units of NaCl (corner and face-centre counting: 8

corners x 1/8 + 6 faces x 1/2 = 4). (b) Covalent solids consist of atoms joined by

covalent bonds in a network: hard, very high melting points, poor conductors (for

example diamond, in which each carbon is tetrahedrally bonded to four others). (c)

Molecular crystals consist of molecules held by weak intermolecular forces: soft, low

melting points, poor conductors. Molecular crystals are softer than ionic crystals

because their molecules are held only by weak van der Waals or hydrogen-bond

forces, whereas ionic crystals are held by strong electrostatic forces between ions.

QSolids 8(a). Give different theories of a metallic bond. How does electron sea theory

justify the electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity and shining surfaces of

metals? (b) Explain with the help of a diagram: (i) Cubic close packing in the

structure of metals (ii) Hexagonal close packing in the structure of metals.

Theories of metallic bond: (1) Electron sea theory: metal atoms release their

valence electrons into a common sea of mobile electrons in which positive metal

ions (kernels) are immersed. (2) Band theory: the atomic orbitals overlap to form

energy bands, and the partly filled conduction band allows electrons to move.

Electron sea theory explains: electrical conductivity (the mobile electrons carry

current), thermal conductivity (the mobile electrons carry heat energy), and shining

surfaces/lustre (the mobile electrons absorb and re-emit light). (b) Cubic close

packing: layers of spheres in ABCABC stacking, giving a face-centred cubic

arrangement with 74% space occupied. Hexagonal close packing: layers in ABAB

stacking, giving a hexagonal arrangement, also 74% occupied. These are drawing

tasks: sketch the layer stacking for each case.

QSolids 9. Crystals of salts fracture easily, but metals are deformed under stress

without fracturing. Explain the difference.

In an ionic crystal, if one layer of ions is shifted by stress, ions of like charge come

to face each other and repel strongly, so the crystal cleaves (fractures) along the

plane. In a metal, the layers of positive ions can slide over each other without

changing the nature of the bonding, because the mobile electron sea adjusts to the

new positions; the metal therefore deforms (is malleable and ductile) instead of

fracturing.

QSolids 10. What is the coordination number of an ion?
What is the coordination

number of the cation in (a) NaCl structure and (b) CsCl structure? Explain the reason

for this difference.

Coordination number is the number of nearest neighbours (opposite ions)

surrounding an ion in the crystal. (a) In NaCl structure the cation (Na+) is

surrounded by 6 Cl- ions, so its coordination number is 6. (b) In CsCl structure the

cation (Cs+) is surrounded by 8 Cl- ions, so its coordination number is 8. The

difference is due to the radius ratio: the larger Cs+ ion can accommodate 8 large Cl-

ions around it, while the smaller Na+ ion can accommodate only 6.

QSolids 11. Give examples of ionic solids, molecular solids and covalent

macromolecular solids. What are the factors which determine whether each of these

types of solid will dissolve in water or not?

Examples: ionic solids: NaCl, KCl, CaF2; molecular solids: dry ice (CO2), ice, iodine;

covalent macromolecular solids: diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide (quartz).

Whether a solid dissolves in water depends on: whether water can break its bonding

(ion-dipole attractions for ionic solids, hydrogen bonding for molecular solids that

can hydrogen-bond), the lattice energy (high lattice energy resists dissolution), and

the hydration energy of the ions (high hydration energy favours dissolution); a solid

dissolves when the hydration energy can overcome the lattice energy.

QSolids 12. Explain with reasons: (i) Sodium is softer than copper, but both are very

good electrical conductors. (ii) Diamond is hard and an electrical insulator. (iii)

Sodium chloride and caesium chloride have different structures. (iv) Iodine dissolves

readily in tetrachloromethane.

(i) Sodium is softer than copper, but both are very good electrical conductors: both

have a sea of mobile electrons (hence conductivity), but sodium has only one

valence electron per atom and weaker metallic bonding than copper, so its lattice is

softer. (ii) Diamond is hard because every carbon atom is joined by strong covalent

bonds to four neighbours in a rigid network; it is an electrical insulator because all

its valence electrons are used in those bonds and none are free to move. (iii)

Sodium chloride and caesium chloride have different structures because of their

different radius ratios: Na+ is small enough for 6-coordination (NaCl structure),

while the larger Cs+ allows 8-coordination (CsCl structure). (iv) Iodine dissolves

readily in tetrachloromethane because both are non-polar: iodine molecules are

held by London forces, which are similar to the forces in CCl4, so like dissolves like.

mcqs.q: What type of intermolecular force dominates in liquid ammonia, NH3?
options: Dipole-dipole forces only with no hydrogen bonding
mcqs.why: The notes state that in ammonia hydrogen bonding dominates, because of the N-H bonds and the lone pair present on nitrogen.

mcqs.q: What type of intermolecular force dominates in octane, C8H18?
mcqs.why: The notes state that octane, a non-polar hydrocarbon, is held together by London dispersion forces only.

mcqs.q: What type of intermolecular force dominates in propanone, CH3COCH3?
options: Hydrogen bonding through an O-H group
mcqs.why: The notes state propanone is polar through its C=O group, so dipole-dipole forces dominate and there is no O-H hydrogen bonding.

mcqs.q: Propanone, propanol and butane have similar molar masses. Their increasing order of boiling points is:
mcqs.why: Butane has only weak London forces, propanone has dipole-dipole forces, and propanol forms hydrogen bonds, so boiling points rise in the order given in the notes.

mcqs.q: In hydrogen-bonded HF, which bond is stronger?
options: The longer hydrogen bond between different molecules
The shorter covalent H-F bond inside the molecule
Both are exactly equal in strength
mcqs.why: The notes explain the covalent H-F bond is a full shared-electron bond and is much stronger and shorter than the weak hydrogen bond between molecules.

mcqs.q: Critical temperatures: CO2 = 31.14 degrees C, CH4 = -81.9 degrees C. Which gas has stronger intermolecular forces?
mcqs.why: A higher critical temperature means stronger attractions: 31.14 is far higher than -81.9, and 31.14 - (-81.9) = 113.04 degrees difference, so CO2 has the stronger forces.

mcqs.q: Water (enthalpy of vaporisation 41.1 kJ/mol, molar mass 18), propanone (31.9, mass 58) and pentane (27.7, mass 72): the strongest intermolecular forces are in:
options: Pentane, because it has the largest molar mass
Propanone, because it is in the middle
mcqs.why: Water has the highest enthalpy of vaporisation, 41.1 kJ/mol, and the highest boiling point although it has the lowest molar mass, 18, proving its forces are strongest.

mcqs.q: Which pair of liquids would be unlikely to mix when shaken together?
options: Propanone and pentane in every proportion as stated
mcqs.why: The notes state the water-pentane pair is unlikely to mix because water is polar and hydrogen-bonded while pentane is non-polar, so like does not dissolve unlike here.

mcqs.q: Saturated vapour pressure of a liquid at a given temperature depends on:
options: The volume of liquid taken, 1 dm3 giving more than 50 cm3
The size of the container only
Only the liquid and the temperature, not the amount of liquid
The amount of vapour already removed
mcqs.why: The notes define saturated vapour pressure as depending only on the liquid and temperature, so 1 dm3 of water and 50 cm3 of water have equal vapour pressures.

mcqs.q: How many formula units of NaCl are in its unit cell?
mcqs.why: Corner and face counting gives 8 * (1/8) = 1 plus 6 * (1/2) = 3, and 1 + 3 = 4, so the NaCl unit cell contains 4 formula units as shown in the notes.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • Beta-particles are nothing but electrons moving with a very high speed.
  • The charge on one mole of electrons is 96500 coulombs.
  • The mass of hydrogen atom is 1.67 x 10^-24 grams.
  • The mass of one mole of electrons is 0.55 mg.
  • Energy is emitted when electron jumps from higher to a lower orbit.
  • The ionization energy of hydrogen atom can be calculated from Bohr model of atom.
  • For d-subshell, the azimuthal quantum number has value of 2.
  • The number of electrons in a given subshell is given by formula 2(2l + 1).

mcqs.q: What are beta-particles?
options: Electrons moving with a very high speed
Protons moving with a very high speed
Neutrons moving with a very high speed
Alpha-particles moving with a very high speed
mcqs.why: The key facts state directly that beta-particles are nothing but electrons moving with a very high speed.

mcqs.q: What is the charge on one mole of electrons?
mcqs.why: The notes give the charge on one mole of electrons as 96500 coulombs, a standard value listed in the key facts.

mcqs.q: What is the mass of a hydrogen atom?
mcqs.why: The key facts list the mass of the hydrogen atom as 1.67 x 10^-24 grams, much larger than the mass of a single electron.

mcqs.q: What is the mass of one mole of electrons?
mcqs.why: The notes state that the mass of one mole of electrons is only 0.55 mg, showing how light electrons are.

mcqs.q: When is energy emitted by an electron in an atom?
options: When the electron jumps from a lower orbit to a higher orbit
When the electron jumps from a higher orbit to a lower orbit
When the electron stays in the same orbit
When the electron leaves the atom completely
mcqs.why: The key facts state that energy is emitted when an electron jumps from a higher orbit to a lower orbit; the reverse jump absorbs energy.

mcqs.q: From which model can the ionization energy of the hydrogen atom be calculated?
options: The Rutherford model of the atom
The Bohr model of the atom
The Dalton model of the atom
mcqs.why: The notes state that the ionization energy of the hydrogen atom can be calculated from the Bohr model of the atom.

mcqs.q: What is the value of the azimuthal quantum number l for the d-subshell?
mcqs.why: The key facts give l = 2 for the d-subshell; by comparison s has l = 0, p has l = 1 and f has l = 3.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the number of electrons in a given subshell?
mcqs.why: The notes give the number of electrons in a subshell as 2(2l + 1), where l is the azimuthal quantum number of that subshell.

mcqs.q: Using 2(2l + 1), how many electrons can the d-subshell (l = 2) hold?
mcqs.why: Working: 2 * (2 * 2 + 1) = 2 * 5 = 10, so the d-subshell with l = 2 holds a maximum of 10 electrons.

mcqs.q: Using 2(2l + 1), how many electrons can the p-subshell (l = 1) hold?
mcqs.why: Working: 2 * (2 * 1 + 1) = 2 * 3 = 6, so the p-subshell with l = 1 holds a maximum of 6 electrons.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q1(i). The nature of the positive rays depend on
A. the nature of the electrode
B. the nature of the discharge tube
✓ C. the nature of the residual gas
D. all of the above

Q1(ii). The velocity of photon is
✓ A. independent of its wavelength
B. depends on its wavelength
C. equal to square of its amplitude
D. depends on its source

Q1(iii). The wave number of the light emitted by a certain source is 2 x 10^6 m^-1.
The wavelength of this light will be
✓ A. 500 nm
B. 500 m
C. 200 nm
D. 5 x 10^7 m

Q1(iv). Rutherford's model of atom failed because
A. the atom did not have a nucleus and electrons
B. it did not account for the attraction between protons and neutrons
✓ C. it did not account for the stability of the atom
D. there is actually no space between the nucleus and the electrons

Q1(v). Bohr model of atom is contradicted by
A. Planck's quantum theory
B. dual nature of matter
✓ C. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle
D. all of the above

Q1(vi). Splitting of spectral lines when atoms are subjected to strong electric field is
called
A. Zeeman effect
✓ B. Stark effect
C. Photoelectric effect
D. Compton effect

Q1(vii). In the ground state of an atom, the electron is present
A. in the nucleus
B. in the second shell
✓ C. nearest to the nucleus
D. farthest from the nucleus

Q1(viii). Quantum number values for 2p orbitals are
✓ A. n = 2, l = 1
B. n = 1, l = 2
C. n = 1, l = 0
D. n = 2, l = 0

Q1(ix). Orbitals having same energy are called
A. hybrid orbitals
B. valence orbitals
✓ C. degenerate orbitals
D. d-orbitals

Q1(x). When 6d orbital is complete, the entering electron goes into
A. 7f
B. 7s
✓ C. 7p
D. 7d

mcqs.q: On what does the nature of the positive rays depend?
options: The nature of the residual gas in the discharge tube
The nature of the discharge tube
The colour of the discharge tube
mcqs.why: Positive rays are ions of the gas left in the tube, so their nature depends on the nature of the residual gas, unlike cathode rays.

mcqs.q: The velocity of a photon is:
options: Equal to the square of its amplitude
mcqs.why: All photons travel at the speed of light in vacuum, so the velocity of a photon is independent of its wavelength.

mcqs.q: The wave number of light from a source is 2 x 10^6 m^-1. What is its wavelength?
mcqs.why: Working: wavelength = 1 / wave number = 1 / (2 * 10^6) = 5 * 10^-7 m = 500 * 10^-9 m = 500 nm.

mcqs.q: Why did Rutherford's model of the atom fail?
options: It did not have a nucleus and electrons
It did not account for the attraction between protons and neutrons
It said there is no space between the nucleus and the electrons
It did not account for the stability of the atom
mcqs.why: Rutherford's model could not explain why electrons circling the nucleus do not radiate energy and fall in, so it did not account for atomic stability.

mcqs.q: The Bohr model of the atom is contradicted by:
mcqs.why: Bohr fixed the electron in an exact orbit, but Heisenberg's uncertainty principle says position and momentum cannot both be known exactly, contradicting Bohr.

mcqs.q: The splitting of spectral lines when atoms are placed in a strong electric field is called:
mcqs.why: Splitting of spectral lines in a strong electric field is the Stark effect; splitting in a magnetic field is the Zeeman effect.

mcqs.q: In the ground state of an atom, the electron is present:
mcqs.why: In the ground state the electron occupies the lowest energy level, which is the level nearest to the nucleus.

mcqs.q: What are the quantum number values for 2p orbitals?
mcqs.why: For a 2p orbital the principal quantum number is n = 2 and a p-subshell always has azimuthal quantum number l = 1.

mcqs.q: Orbitals having the same energy are called:
mcqs.why: Orbitals of equal energy, such as the three 2p orbitals in an isolated atom, are called degenerate orbitals.

mcqs.q: When the 6d orbital is complete, the entering electron goes into:
mcqs.why: Following the filling order, once the 6d orbital is complete the next entering electron goes into the 7p orbital.

lessons.title: Fill in the Blanks
lessons.notes_html:
2(i). Beta-particles are nothing but electrons moving with a very high speed.

2(ii). The charge on one mole of electrons is 96500 coulombs.

2(iii). The mass of hydrogen atom is 1.67 x 10^-24 grams.

2(iv). The mass of one mole of electrons is 0.55 mg.

2(v). Energy is emitted when electron jumps from higher to a lower orbit.

2(vi). The ionization energy of hydrogen atom can be calculated from Bohr model of atom.

2(vii). For d-subshell, the azimuthal quantum number has value of 2.

2(viii). The number of electrons in a given subshell is given by formula 2(2l + 1).

2(ix). The electronic configuration of H is 1s^1.

mcqs.q: Beta-particles are electrons moving with:
mcqs.why: The fill-in facts state that beta-particles are nothing but electrons moving with a very high speed.

mcqs.q: The charge on one mole of electrons is _____ coulombs.
mcqs.why: The notes fill this blank with 96500 coulombs, the charge carried by one mole of electrons (the Faraday).

mcqs.q: The mass of the hydrogen atom is _____ grams.
mcqs.why: The blank is filled with 1.67 x 10^-24 grams, the mass of one hydrogen atom as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: The mass of one mole of electrons is _____ mg.
mcqs.why: The notes give the mass of one mole of electrons as 0.55 mg, an extremely small mass for a mole of particles.

mcqs.q: Energy is _____ when an electron jumps from a higher orbit to a lower orbit.
mcqs.why: The blank is filled with emitted: an electron falling from a higher to a lower orbit gives out the energy difference as radiation.

mcqs.q: The ionization energy of the hydrogen atom can be calculated from the _____ model of the atom.
mcqs.why: The notes name the Bohr model, whose energy equation E depends on 1/n^2, as the model used to calculate hydrogen's ionization energy.

mcqs.q: For the d-subshell, the azimuthal quantum number has the value:
mcqs.why: The fill-in answer is 2: the azimuthal quantum number l takes the value 2 for every d-subshell.

mcqs.q: The number of electrons in a given subshell is given by the formula:
mcqs.why: The notes give the subshell capacity formula as 2(2l + 1); the factor (2l + 1) counts orbitals and the 2 allows two electrons per orbital.

mcqs.q: What is the electronic configuration of hydrogen?
mcqs.why: Hydrogen has a single electron, which occupies the lowest orbital, so its electronic configuration is written as 1s^1.

mcqs.q: Applying the formula 2(2l + 1) with l = 3, the f-subshell can hold:
mcqs.why: Working: 2 * (2 * 3 + 1) = 2 * 7 = 14, so the f-subshell with l = 3 holds a maximum of 14 electrons.

lessons.title: True or False
lessons.notes_html:
3(i). A neutron is slightly lighter particle than a proton. False

3(ii). A photon is the massless bundle of energy but has momentum. True

3(iii). The unit of Rydberg constant is the reciprocal of unit of length. True

3(iv). The actual isotopic mass is a whole number. False

3(v). Heisenberg's uncertainty principle is applicable to macroscopic bodies. False

3(vi). The nodal plane in an orbital is the plane of zero electron density. True

3(vii). The number of orbitals present in a sublevel is given by the formula (2l + 1). True

3(viii). The magnetic quantum number was introduced to explain Zeeman and Stark effect. True

3(ix). Spin quantum number tells us the direction of spin of electron around the nucleus. False

mcqs.q: The statement 'a neutron is slightly lighter than a proton' is:
options: False - the neutron is not lighter than the proton
True - the neutron is much lighter
True - they have exactly equal mass
False - the neutron has a negative charge
mcqs.why: The true/false answer is False: the neutron is slightly heavier than the proton, not lighter, so the statement as written is wrong.

mcqs.q: A photon is a massless bundle of energy but it has momentum. This statement is:
options: False - a photon has mass but no momentum
False - a photon has neither energy nor momentum
False - a photon has mass and momentum
mcqs.why: The answer given is True: a photon has zero rest mass, yet as a bundle of moving energy it still carries momentum.

mcqs.q: The unit of the Rydberg constant is:
options: The reciprocal of the unit of length (m^-1)
mcqs.why: The statement is marked True: since the Rydberg constant multiplies dimensionless terms to give wave number, its unit is reciprocal length, m^-1.

mcqs.q: The actual isotopic mass of an element is a whole number. This statement is:
mcqs.why: The answer is False: actual isotopic masses are close to, but not exactly, whole numbers; only the mass number is a whole number.

mcqs.q: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle is applicable to macroscopic bodies. This statement is:
options: True - it applies equally at all sizes
False - it matters only for microscopic particles
True - it was made for macroscopic bodies
False - it applies to no bodies at all
mcqs.why: The answer is False: the uncertainty principle has a noticeable effect only for microscopic particles like electrons, not for macroscopic bodies.

mcqs.q: The nodal plane in an orbital is the plane of:
mcqs.why: The statement is True: a nodal plane is a plane passing through the orbital where the probability of finding the electron is zero.

mcqs.q: The number of orbitals present in a sublevel is given by the formula:
mcqs.why: The statement is True: a sublevel contains (2l + 1) orbitals; for example l = 1 gives 2 * 1 + 1 = 3 p-orbitals.

mcqs.q: The magnetic quantum number was introduced to explain:
mcqs.why: The statement is True: the splitting of spectral lines in magnetic and electric fields (Zeeman and Stark effects) led to the magnetic quantum number.

mcqs.q: The spin quantum number tells us the direction of spin of the electron around the nucleus. This statement is:
options: True - spin is motion around the nucleus
True - spin gives the orbit radius
False - it gives the spin of the electron about its own axis
False - spin has only one value
mcqs.why: The answer is False: the spin quantum number (+1/2 or -1/2) describes the electron spinning about its own axis, not its motion around the nucleus.

mcqs.q: For l = 2, the number of orbitals in the sublevel is:
mcqs.why: Working: number of orbitals = 2 * 2 + 1 = 5, so the d-sublevel (l = 2) contains five orbitals, matching the (2l + 1) rule.

lessons.title: Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Note on True/False 3(ix) - Spin quantum number tells us the direction of spin of

electron around the nucleus.

Marked False. The spin quantum number (+1/2 or -1/2) gives the direction of the

electron's spin about its OWN axis (clockwise or anticlockwise). Motion around the

nucleus is described by the orbital quantum numbers, so the statement as printed,

with 'around the nucleus', is False.

Q4(a). Keeping in mind the discharge tube experiment, why is it necessary to

decrease the pressure in the discharge tube to get the cathode rays?

At low pressure there are few gas molecules in the tube, so the cathode rays can

travel a long distance without colliding with gas molecules, and a clear beam

reaches the anode. At ordinary pressure the rays are scattered by collisions and no

beam is seen.

Q4(b). Whichever gas is used in the discharge tube, the nature of the cathode rays

remains the same. Why?

Cathode rays are streams of electrons knocked out of the atoms of the cathode

material itself. Whatever gas is present, the particles emitted are the same

electrons, so their nature does not depend on the gas in the tube.

Q4(c). Why is the e/m value of the cathode rays just equal to that of electron?

The measured e/m of cathode rays is 1.7588 x 10^11 C kg^-1, exactly the e/m of

an electron. Since every cathode-ray particle has this same charge-to-mass ratio,

the rays consist of electrons.

Q4(d). How does the bending of the cathode rays in the electric and magnetic fields

show that they are negatively charged?

In an electric field the rays bend towards the positive plate, and in a magnetic field

they bend in the direction expected for a negatively charged particle. Only a

negative charge bends in these directions, so the rays are negatively charged.

Q4(e). Why are the positive rays also called canal rays?

Positive rays pass through holes (canals) drilled in the cathode and travel in the

opposite direction to the cathode rays. Because they stream through these canals,

they are called canal rays.

Q4(f). The e/m values of positive rays for different gases are different, but those for

cathode rays are the same. Justify it.

Positive rays are the positive ions left when gas atoms lose electrons, so their mass

is the mass of the gas atom (or ion). Different gases give ions of different mass, so

e/m differs from gas to gas. Cathode rays are always electrons, whose mass is the

same, so their e/m is always the same.

Q4(g). The e/m value for positive rays obtained from hydrogen gas is 1836 times less

than that of cathode rays. Justify it.

For hydrogen the positive ray is the proton, mass 1.6726 x 10^-27 kg, while the

electron mass is 9.109 x 10^-31 kg. The ratio is about 1836, so the e/m of the

proton is 1836 times smaller than the e/m of the electron, the charge being the

same in both cases.
