Q5(a). Explain Millikan's oil drop experiment to determine the charge of an electron.

Millikan sprayed fine oil drops between two charged plates. By adjusting the voltage

he balanced a drop so that the electric force on it exactly cancelled its weight. From

the balancing voltage, the drop's radius (from its rate of fall) and the density of oil,

he found the charge on the drop. Repeating for many drops, every charge was a

whole-number multiple of 1.602 x 10^-19 C, the charge of one electron.

Q5(b). What is J.J. Thomson's experiment for determining e/m value of electron?

J.J. Thomson passed cathode rays through crossed electric and magnetic fields and

adjusted them until the beam was undeflected. From the balancing fields he found

the velocity of the rays, and from the deflection in the magnetic field alone he found

e/m = 1.7588 x 10^11 C kg^-1 for the electron.

Q5(c). Evaluate mass of electron from the above two experiments.

Mass of electron = charge / (charge/mass) = 1.602 x 10^-19 C / 1.7588 x 10^11 C

kg^-1 = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg. This is the mass of the electron.

Q6(a). Discuss Chadwick's experiment for the discovery of neutron. Compare the

properties of electron, proton and neutron.

Chadwick bombarded beryllium with alpha-particles. The radiation given out

knocked protons out of paraffin wax, and from the energies of those protons he

showed the radiation consisted of neutral particles of about the mass of a proton:

the neutron. Electron: charge -1.602 x 10^-19 C, mass 9.109 x 10^-31 kg. Proton:

charge +1.602 x 10^-19 C, mass 1.6726 x 10^-27 kg. Neutron: charge 0, mass

1.6749 x 10^-27 kg. All three are the fundamental particles of the atom.

Q6(b). Rutherford's atomic model is based on the scattering of alpha-particles from a

thin gold foil. Discuss it and explain the conclusions.

Rutherford fired alpha-particles at a very thin gold foil. Most passed straight

through, some were deflected through small angles, and a very few bounced almost

straight back. Conclusions: (i) most of the atom is empty space, since most particles

pass through; (ii) the positive charge and almost all the mass are concentrated in a

tiny central nucleus, which repels the few particles that come close; (iii) electrons

occupy the large empty space around the nucleus.

Q7(a). Give the postulates of Bohr's atomic model. Which postulate tells us that orbits

are stationary and energy is quantized?

Postulates: (i) the electron revolves around the nucleus in certain permitted circular

orbits of fixed energy, without radiating energy; (ii) the angular momentum of the

electron is quantized, mvr = nh/2pi; (iii) energy is absorbed or emitted only when

the electron jumps from one permitted orbit to another, as a photon of energy delta

E = h x nu. The postulate that tells us orbits are stationary and energy is quantized

is the quantized-angular-momentum postulate, mvr = nh/2pi.

Q7(b). Derive the equation for the radius of nth orbit of hydrogen atom using Bohr's

model.

Centripetal force = electrostatic attraction: mv^2/r = (1/4pi epsilon0) x (Ze^2/r^2).

With mvr = nh/2pi, eliminating v gives r = (epsilon0 h^2 n^2)/(pi m Z e^2). For

hydrogen Z = 1, r_n = 0.529 x n^2 angstrom.

Q7(c)(i). How does the radius equation tell you that radius is directly proportional to

the square of the number of orbit?

r_n = 0.529 x n^2 angstrom, so r is proportional to n^2. Doubling n multiplies the

radius by four, so the radius is directly proportional to the square of the number of

the orbit.

Q7(c)(ii). How does the radius equation tell you that radius is inversely proportional to

the number of protons in the nucleus?

For hydrogen r_n = 0.529 x n^2 / Z angstrom with Z = 1, and in general r_n is

proportional to n^2/Z. The radius is therefore inversely proportional to the number

of protons in the nucleus (the atomic number Z): a larger nuclear charge pulls the

electron into a smaller orbit.

Q7(d). How do you come to know that the velocities of electrons in higher orbits are

less than those in lower orbits of hydrogen atom?

Bohr's velocity equation is v = (Z e^2)/(2 epsilon0 h n), so v is proportional to 1/n.

As n increases the velocity falls, so electrons in higher orbits move more slowly than

those in lower orbits.

Q7(e). Justify that the distance gaps between different orbits go on increasing from

the lower to the higher orbits.

r_n = 0.529 x n^2 angstrom, so successive radii are 0.529, 2.116, 4.761, 8.464

angstrom. The gaps are 1.587, 2.645, 3.703 angstrom, growing by 2 x 0.529

angstrom each time, so the distance gaps between orbits increase from lower to

higher orbits.

Q8(a). Derive the formula for calculating the energy of an electron in nth orbit using

Bohr's model.

Total energy = kinetic energy + potential energy = (1/2)mv^2 - (1/4pi

epsilon0)(Ze^2/r). Substituting Bohr's r_n and v gives E_n = -(m Z^2 e^4)/(8

epsilon0^2 h^2 n^2). For hydrogen Z = 1, E_n = -2.18 x 10^-18 / n^2 joule.

Q8(b). The potential energy of the bounded electron is negative.

The potential energy of the electron is -(1/4pi epsilon0)(Ze^2/r), negative because

the zero of potential energy is taken at infinite separation, where electron and

nucleus no longer attract. Bringing them together from infinity releases energy, so

at any finite distance the potential energy is below zero.

Q8(c). Total energy of the bounded electron is also negative.

The total energy is negative because the electron is bound: energy must be

supplied to remove it to infinity (zero energy). A negative total energy is the sign of

a bound system; a free electron has zero or positive energy.

Q8(d). Energy of an electron is inversely proportional to n^2, but energy of higher

orbits are always greater than those of the lower orbits.

E_n = -2.18 x 10^-18 / n^2 joule, so E is inversely proportional to n^2 in

magnitude, but the values are -2.18, -0.545, -0.242 x 10^-18 J for n = 1, 2, 3. The

magnitude falls, so the energy itself (a negative number) increases towards zero:

higher orbits have greater (less negative) energy than lower orbits.

Q9(a). Derive the equations for hydrogen atom related to (i) energy difference

between two levels n1 and n2, (ii) frequency of photon emitted when an electron

jumps from n2 to n1, (iii) wave number of the photon when the electron jumps from

n2 to n1.

(i) Energy difference: delta E = 2.18 x 10^-18 x (1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2) joule, for a jump

from n2 down to n1. (ii) Frequency: nu = delta E / h. (iii) Wave number: wavenumber

= (1/lambda) = delta E/(h c) = R x (1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2), with R = 1.097 x 10^7 m^-1.

Q9(b). Justify that Bohr's equation for the wave number can explain the spectral lines

of Lyman, Balmer and Paschen series.

Wavenumber = R x (1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2). With n1 = 1 the lines are the Lyman series

(ultraviolet), with n1 = 2 the Balmer series (visible), and with n1 = 3 the Paschen

series (infrared). One formula, with n1 = 1, 2, 3, reproduces all three series, which is

the success of Bohr's equation.

Q10(a). What is spectrum? Differentiate between continuous spectrum and line

spectrum.

A spectrum is the pattern of radiation obtained when light is dispersed by

wavelength, for example by a prism. A continuous spectrum shows all wavelengths

without gaps, as from a hot solid. A line spectrum shows only certain sharp

wavelengths, as from excited atoms, each line being one permitted electron jump.

Q10(b). Compare line emission and line absorption spectra.

In a line emission spectrum the excited atom emits photons and gives bright lines

on a dark background. In a line absorption spectrum white light passing through a

gas loses exactly those wavelengths, giving dark lines on a bright continuous

background. The two sets of lines occur at the same wavelengths.

Q10(c). What is the origin of line spectrum?

Line spectra arise because an atom's electron can occupy only certain energy

levels. When it jumps from a higher to a lower level it emits a photon of one fixed

energy, hence one fixed wavelength; each permitted jump gives one line. No other

wavelengths can be emitted, so the spectrum is a set of lines, not continuous.

Q11(a). Hydrogen atom and He+ are mono-electronic systems, but the size of He+ is

much smaller than H, why?

Both are one-electron systems, but He+ has nuclear charge Z = 2 while H has Z =

1. Bohr's radius r = 0.529 x n^2 / Z angstrom, so for n = 1 the He+ radius is

0.529/2 = 0.265 angstrom, half the hydrogen radius. The stronger nuclear pull

shrinks the He+ atom.

Q11(b). Do you think that the size of Li2+ is even smaller than He+?
Justify with

calculations.

For Li2+, Z = 3, so r1 = 0.529/3 = 0.176 angstrom, smaller than He+ (0.265

angstrom) and smaller than H (0.529 angstrom). Yes, Li2+ is even smaller, because

the radius is inversely proportional to Z.

Q12(a). What are X-rays? What is their origin?
How was the idea of atomic number

derived from the discovery of X-rays?

X-rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiations of very short wavelength,

produced when fast electrons strike a heavy metal target and knock out inner-shell

electrons; outer electrons falling into the vacancies emit X-rays. Moseley found that

the square root of the X-ray frequency is proportional to (Z - b), where Z is the

atomic number. This regular dependence on Z, not on atomic mass, showed that the

atomic number, the number of protons, is the fundamental identity of an element.

Q12(b). How does Bohr's model justify Moseley's equation?

Moseley's law, sqrt(nu) = a(Z - b), follows from Bohr's model because the X-ray

frequency depends on the effective nuclear charge felt by the inner electron, which

grows with Z. Bohr's energy levels, E proportional to Z^2, give frequencies that

increase regularly with Z, exactly as Moseley observed.

Q13. Point out the defects of Bohr's model. How are these defects partially covered by

dual nature of electron and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle?

Defects of Bohr's model: (i) it keeps electrons in fixed orbits, contradicting

Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and the dual nature of the electron, which forbid

an exact path; (ii) it works only for one-electron systems (H, He+, Li2+), not for

multi-electron atoms; (iii) it cannot explain the fine splitting of spectral lines, nor the

Zeeman and Stark effects. The dual nature and the uncertainty principle replace

fixed orbits by probability distributions (orbitals), which is the wave-mechanical

model.

Q14(a). Briefly discuss the wave mechanical model of atom. How has it given the idea

of orbital? Compare orbit and orbital.

In the wave-mechanical model the electron is not on a fixed path; Schrodinger's

wave equation gives a wave function whose square is the probability of finding the

electron in a region. That region of high probability is an orbital. An orbit is a fixed

circular path of definite radius (Bohr); an orbital is a three-dimensional region where

the electron is most likely to be found, with no definite path.

Q14(b). What are quantum numbers?
Discuss their significance.

Quantum numbers: principal (n) gives the shell and the energy/size; azimuthal (l)

gives the subshell and the shape (l = 0 s, 1 p, 2 d, 3 f); magnetic (m) gives the

orientation of the orbital in space; spin (s) gives the direction of the electron's own

spin (+1/2 or -1/2). Together they completely specify an electron in an atom.

Q14(c). When azimuthal quantum number has a value 3, then there are seven values

of magnetic quantum number. Give reasons.

For l = 3, m runs from -3 to +3, giving -3, -2, -1, 0, +1, +2, +3: seven values. Each

value is one orientation of the f-subshell, so there are seven f-orbitals.

Q15(a). Discuss rules for the distribution of electrons in energy subshells and in

orbitals.

Distribution rules: (i) Aufbau: electrons fill subshells in order of increasing (n + l)

energy; (ii) Pauli's exclusion principle: no two electrons in an atom have all four

quantum numbers the same, so an orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite

spin; (iii) Hund's rule: in degenerate orbitals electrons occupy separate orbitals

singly first, with parallel spins, before pairing.

Q15(b). What is (n + l) rule? Arrange the orbitals according to this rule. Do you think

that this rule is applicable to degenerate orbitals?

The (n + l) rule: a subshell of lower (n + l) is filled first; if two subshells have the

same (n + l), the one with lower n is filled first, e.g. 4s (4 + 0 = 4) before 3d (3 + 2

= 5). Degenerate orbitals (same n and l, e.g. the three 2p orbitals) have the same

(n + l) and the same energy, so the rule orders subshells, not orbitals within a

degenerate set; within the set Hund's rule applies.

Q15(c). Distribute electrons in orbitals of 57La, 29Cu, 79Au, 24Cr, 53I, 86Rn.

57La: [Xe] 6s^2 5d^1. 29Cu: [Ar] 3d^10 4s^1 (the 4s electron moves into 3d to

complete the d-subshell). 79Au: [Xe] 4f^14 5d^10 6s^1 (same reason as copper).

24Cr: [Ar] 3d^5 4s^1 (half-filled d-subshell is extra stable). 53I: [Kr] 4d^10 5s^2

5p^5. 86Rn: [Xe] 4f^14 5d^10 6s^2 6p^6.

Q16. Draw the shapes of s, p and d-orbitals. Justify these by keeping in view the

azimuthal and magnetic quantum numbers.

Labelled drawing instruction: draw an s-orbital as a sphere, centred on the nucleus.

Draw each p-orbital as a dumb-bell along one axis: px along x, py along y, pz along

z, with two lobes and a node at the nucleus. Draw d-orbitals as four-lobed clover

leaves (dxy, dxz, dyz, dx^2-y^2), except dz^2, which is a dumb-bell along z with a

doughnut-shaped ring around its middle. Justification: l = 0 (s) has no angular node,

so it is spherical; l = 1 (p) has one angular node, giving two lobes; l = 2 (d) has two

angular nodes, giving four lobes (dz^2 is the exception). The magnetic quantum

number m gives the orientations: one s, three p, five d orbitals.

mcqs.q: Why must the pressure inside a discharge tube be decreased to obtain cathode rays?
options: At low pressure there are few gas molecules, so the rays travel far without collisions and a clear beam forms
Low pressure increases the charge on the cathode
Low pressure converts the gas into electrons
At low pressure the anode attracts the gas molecules
mcqs.why: With few gas molecules in the tube the cathode rays travel a long distance without colliding and reach the anode as a clear beam; at ordinary pressure collisions scatter them.

mcqs.q: Why does the nature of cathode rays stay the same whichever gas is used in the tube?
options: All gases contain the same positive ions
Cathode rays are electrons knocked out of the cathode material itself, the same for every gas
The gas changes into the same plasma
Cathode rays are made of the glass of the tube
mcqs.why: Cathode rays are streams of electrons emitted from the cathode material, so whatever gas is present the particles are the same electrons and their nature is unchanged.

mcqs.q: What is the measured e/m value of cathode rays, equal to that of the electron?
mcqs.why: The e/m of cathode rays was measured as 1.7588 x 10^11 C kg^-1, exactly the charge-to-mass ratio of an electron, showing the rays consist of electrons.

mcqs.q: How does the bending of cathode rays in electric and magnetic fields show they are negatively charged?
options: They bend towards the negative plate in an electric field
They are not deflected by either field
They bend only when the fields are switched off
They bend towards the positive plate in an electric field, the direction expected for a negative charge
mcqs.why: In an electric field the rays bend towards the positive plate, and in a magnetic field they bend as a negative particle should; only a negative charge behaves this way.

mcqs.q: Why are positive rays also called canal rays?
options: They are produced inside metal canals
They pass through holes (canals) drilled in the cathode
They flow like water in a canal
They were discovered near a canal
mcqs.why: Positive rays stream through the canals (holes) drilled in the cathode and travel opposite to the cathode rays, which is why they are called canal rays.

mcqs.q: In Millikan's oil drop experiment, every measured charge on the drops was a whole-number multiple of:
options: 96500 C, the charge of a mole of electrons
1.602 x 10^-19 C, the charge of one electron
mcqs.why: Millikan balanced oil drops against their weight and found every charge was a whole-number multiple of 1.602 x 10^-19 C, identifying it as the charge of a single electron.

mcqs.q: Calculate the mass of the electron from e = 1.602 x 10^-19 C and e/m = 1.7588 x 10^11 C kg^-1.
mcqs.why: Working: mass = charge / (charge/mass) = 1.602 * 10^-19 / (1.7588 * 10^11) = 9.11 * 10^-31 kg, the mass of the electron.

mcqs.q: In Chadwick's experiment, the neutron was discovered by bombarding which element with alpha-particles?
mcqs.why: Chadwick bombarded beryllium with alpha-particles; the neutral radiation given out knocked protons from paraffin wax, proving it consisted of neutrons of about proton mass.

mcqs.q: According to Bohr's model, the angular momentum of the electron is quantized as:
mcqs.why: Bohr's postulate sets the angular momentum mvr = nh/2pi, where n is the orbit number; this postulate makes the orbits stationary and the energy quantized.

mcqs.q: Using r = 0.529 x n^2 / Z angstrom, what is the radius of the first orbit of He+ (Z = 2)?
mcqs.why: Working: r = 0.529 * 1 * 1 / 2 = 0.529 / 2 = 0.265 angstrom, half the hydrogen radius because the stronger nuclear charge of He+ pulls the electron in.

lessons.title: Numerical Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q17(a). A photon of light with energy 10^-19 J is emitted by a source of light. Convert

this energy into the wavelength, frequency and wave number of the photon in terms

of meters, hertz and m^-1, respectively.

Step 1 - Write the given data: E = 10^-19 J, h = 6.626 x 10^-34 J s, c = 3 x 10^8 m

s^-1.

Step 2 - Frequency from Planck's equation E = h x nu: nu = E/h = 10^-19 / 6.626 x

10^-34 = 1.51 x 10^14 s^-1 (hertz).

Step 3 - Wavelength from c = nu x lambda: lambda = c/nu = 3 x 10^8 / 1.51 x

10^14 = 1.98 x 10^-6 m.

Step 4 - Wave number = 1/lambda = 1 / 1.98 x 10^-6 = 5.0 x 10^5 m^-1.

Answer: frequency 1.51 x 10^14 Hz; wavelength 1.98 x 10^-6 m; wave number 5 x

10^5 m^-1. (Note: the book prints the wavelength as 1.98 x 10^6 m, but the minus

sign is required: 1.98 x 10^-6 m is the value consistent with the book's own part (b)

answer of 1.98 x 10^4 cm.)

Q17(b). Convert this energy of the photon into ergs and calculate the wavelength in

cm, frequency in Hz and wave number in cm^-1. [h = 6.626 x 10^-34 J s or 6.625 x

10^-27 erg s, c = 3 x 10^8 m s^-1 or 3 x 10^10 cm s^-1]

Step 1 - Convert energy to ergs: 1 J = 10^7 erg, so E = 10^-19 x 10^7 = 10^-12

erg.

Step 2 - Frequency: nu = E/h = 10^-12 / 6.625 x 10^-27 = 1.51 x 10^14 s^-1

(hertz). The frequency is unchanged by the change of units.

Step 3 - Wavelength in cm: lambda = c/nu = 3 x 10^10 / 1.51 x 10^14 = 1.98 x

10^-4 cm.

Step 4 - Wave number in cm^-1: 1/lambda = 1 / 1.98 x 10^-4 = 5 x 10^3 cm^-1.

Answer: frequency 1.51 x 10^14 Hz; wavelength 1.98 x 10^-4 cm; wave number 5

x 10^3 cm^-1 (matches the book's printed answers).

Q18. The formula for calculating the energy of an electron in hydrogen atom given by

Bohr's model is E_n = -(m e^4)/(8 epsilon0^2 h^2 n^2). Calculate the energy of

the electron in first orbit of hydrogen atom. The values of various parameters are

same as provided in Q19.

Step 1 - For the first orbit n = 1, so E_1 = -(m e^4)/(8 epsilon0^2 h^2).

Step 2 - Substituting m = 9.108 x 10^-31 kg, e = 1.602 x 10^-19 C, epsilon0 =

8.85 x 10^-12 C^2 J^-1 m^-1 and h = 6.624 x 10^-34 J s gives E_1 = -2.18 x

10^-18 J.

Answer: -2.18 x 10^-18 J (matches the book's printed answer).

Q19(a). Bohr's equation for the radius of nth orbit of electron in hydrogen atom is r_n

= (epsilon0 h^2 n^2)/(pi e^2 m). When the electron moves from n = 1 to n = 2,

how much does the radius of the orbit increase?

Step 1 - Radius of first orbit: r_1 = 0.529 x 1^2 = 0.529 angstrom.

Step 2 - Radius of second orbit: r_2 = 0.529 x 2^2 = 0.529 x 4 = 2.116 angstrom.

Step 3 - Increase in radius = r_2 - r_1 = 2.116 - 0.529 = 1.587 angstrom.

Answer: 1.587 angstrom (matches the book's printed answer).

Q19(b). What is the distance travelled by the electron when it goes from n = 2 to n =

3 and n = 9 to n = 10? [epsilon0 = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2 J^-1 m^-1, h = 6.624 x

10^-34 J s, pi = 3.14, m = 9.108 x 10^-31 kg, e = 1.602 x 10^-19 C]

Step 1 - Use r_n = 0.529 x n^2 angstrom. Radii: r_2 = 2.116 angstrom, r_3 = 4.761

angstrom, r_9 = 42.849 angstrom, r_10 = 52.9 angstrom.

Step 2 - Distance from n = 2 to n = 3 = r_3 - r_2 = 4.761 - 2.116 = 2.645 angstrom,

about 2.65 angstrom.

Step 3 - Distance from n = 9 to n = 10 = r_10 - r_9 = 52.9 - 42.849 = 10.051

angstrom, about 10.05 angstrom.

Answer: 2.65 angstrom and 10.05 angstrom (matches the book's printed answers).

Note: the 'distance travelled' here is the increase in orbital radius between the two

orbits.

Q20(a). Calculate the energy of first five orbits of hydrogen atom and determine the

energy differences between them.

Step 1 - Use E_n = -2.18 x 10^-18 / n^2 J. E_1 = -2.18 x 10^-18 J; E_2 = -2.18/4 =

-0.545 x 10^-18 J; E_3 = -2.18/9 = -0.242 x 10^-18 J; E_4 = -2.18/16 = -0.136 x

10^-18 J; E_5 = -2.18/25 = -0.087 x 10^-18 J.

Step 2 - Differences: E_2 - E_1 = 1.635 x 10^-18 J; E_3 - E_2 = 0.303 x 10^-18 J;

E_4 - E_3 = 0.106 x 10^-18 J; E_5 - E_4 = 0.049 x 10^-18 J.

Answer: energies -2.18, -0.545, -0.242, -0.136, -0.087 (all x 10^-18 J) for n = 1 to 5;

the gaps shrink rapidly as n increases.

Q20(b). Justify that energy difference between second and third orbits is

approximately five times smaller than that between first and second orbits.

Step 1 - Difference between first and second orbits = 1.635 x 10^-18 J (from

Q20(a)).

Step 2 - Difference between second and third orbits = 0.303 x 10^-18 J.

Step 3 - Ratio = 1.635 / 0.303 = 5.4, approximately 5.

Answer: the second-to-third gap is about five times smaller than the first-to-second

gap, as stated.

Q20(c). Calculate the energy of electron in He+ in first five orbits and justify that the

energy differences are different from those of hydrogen atom.

Step 1 - For He+, Z = 2, so E_n = -2.18 x Z^2 / n^2 x 10^-18 = -8.72 / n^2 x

10^-18 J. E_1 = -8.72, E_2 = -2.18, E_3 = -0.969, E_4 = -0.545, E_5 = -0.349 (all x

10^-18 J).

Step 2 - Differences: E_2 - E_1 = 6.54 x 10^-18 J; E_3 - E_2 = 1.211 x 10^-18 J, and

so on.

Step 3 - Every He+ energy and every gap is exactly Z^2 = 4 times the

corresponding hydrogen value.

Answer: the He+ energies differ from hydrogen's by the factor Z^2 = 4, because

the energy is proportional to the square of the nuclear charge.

Q20(d). Do you think that groups of the spectral lines of He+ are at different places

than those for hydrogen atom? Give reasons.

Step 1 - Spectral line positions are set by energy differences, delta E = h x nu.

Step 2 - For He+ every energy difference is 4 times the hydrogen difference

(Q20(c)).

Step 3 - Hence every He+ line has 4 times the frequency (one quarter the

wavelength) of the corresponding hydrogen line.

Answer: yes, the He+ line groups lie at different places, shifted to higher frequency

and shorter wavelength by the factor 4.

Q21. Calculate the value of principal quantum number if an electron in hydrogen atom

revolves in an orbit of energy -0.242 x 10^-18 J.

Step 1 - Use E_n = -2.18 x 10^-18 / n^2 J, with E_n = -0.242 x 10^-18 J.

Step 2 - So 0.242 = 2.18 / n^2, giving n^2 = 2.18 / 0.242 = 9.0.

Step 3 - n = 3.

Answer: n = 3 (matches the book's printed answer).

Q22(a). Bohr's formula for the energy levels of hydrogen atom for any system H, He+,

Li2+, etc. is E_n = -(Z^2 e^4 m)/(8 epsilon0^2 h^2 n^2) or E_n = -K [Z^2/n^2].

For hydrogen Z = 1 and for He+ Z = 2. Draw an energy level diagram for hydrogen

atom and He+.

Step 1 - Labelled drawing instruction: draw a vertical energy axis with zero at the

top (free electron) and negative energies below.

Step 2 - For hydrogen mark levels at -2.18 (n = 1), -0.545 (n = 2), -0.242 (n = 3),

-0.136 (n = 4), -0.087 (n = 5), all x 10^-18 J, the gaps shrinking upwards.

Step 3 - For He+ mark levels at -8.72 (n = 1), -2.18 (n = 2), -0.969 (n = 3), -0.545 (n

= 4), -0.349 (n = 5), all x 10^-18 J, on the same scale, so the He+ ladder is

stretched four times deeper than hydrogen's.

Answer: see the drawing instruction above; the two ladders differ by the factor Z^2

= 4.

Q22(b). Thinking that K = 2.18 x 10^-18 J, calculate the energy needed to remove the

electron from hydrogen atom and from He+.

Step 1 - Ionization energy = energy to take the electron from n = 1 to infinity (E =

0). For hydrogen: 0 - (-2.18 x 10^-18) = 2.18 x 10^-18 J.

Step 2 - For He+: E_1 = -K x Z^2 = -2.18 x 4 = -8.72 x 10^-18 J, so the energy

needed = 8.72 x 10^-18 J.

Answer: 2.18 x 10^-18 J for H and 8.72 x 10^-18 J for He+ (matches the book's

printed answers).

Q22(c). How do you justify that the energies calculated in (b) are the ionization

energies of H and He+?

Step 1 - Ionization energy is defined as the energy needed to remove the electron

completely from the atom, i.e. to take it from its ground state to infinity.

Step 2 - At infinity the electron is free and its energy is defined as zero.

Step 3 - The energy supplied must therefore equal 0 - E_1, which is exactly what

was calculated in (b).

Answer: the calculated values are ionization energies because they are the

ground-state-to-infinity energy differences.

Q22(d). Use Avogadro's number to convert ionization energy values in kJ mol^-1 for H

and He+.

Step 1 - Multiply the per-atom energy by Avogadro's number, 6.022 x 10^23

mol^-1. For H: 2.18 x 10^-18 x 6.022 x 10^23 = 1.313 x 10^6 J mol^-1 = 1313 kJ

mol^-1.

Step 2 - For He+: 8.72 x 10^-18 x 6.022 x 10^23 = 5.251 x 10^6 J mol^-1 = 5251

kJ mol^-1.

Answer: about 1313.3 kJ mol^-1 for H and 5249.4 kJ mol^-1 for He+ as printed in

the book (the small differences are rounding of K and Avogadro's number).

Q22(e). The experimental values of ionization energy of H and He+ are 1331 kJ

mol^-1 and 5250 kJ mol^-1, respectively. How do you compare your values with

experimental values?

Step 1 - Calculated: about 1313 kJ mol^-1 (H) and 5249 kJ mol^-1 (He+).

Experimental: 1331 and 5250 kJ mol^-1.

Step 2 - The He+ values agree closely (5249 vs 5250). The hydrogen value is about

1.3% low (1313 vs 1331), the difference coming from the rounded constants used in

the book's calculation.

Answer: the calculated values agree well with experiment; the hydrogen value is

slightly low because of rounding in the constants (the book prints 5249 kJ mol^-1

for He+ in this comparison).

Q23. Calculate the wave number of the photon when the electron jumps from (i) n = 5

to n = 2, (ii) n = 5 to n = 1. In which series of spectral lines and spectral regions

these photons will appear?

Step 1 - Use wavenumber = R x (1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2) with R = 1.097 x 10^7 m^-1.

Step 2 - (i) n = 5 to n = 2: 1/4 - 1/25 = 0.21, so wavenumber = 1.097 x 10^7 x 0.21

= 2.3 x 10^6 m^-1. The lower level is n = 2, so this is the Balmer series, in the

visible region.

Step 3 - (ii) n = 5 to n = 1: 1 - 1/25 = 0.96, so wavenumber = 1.097 x 10^7 x 0.96

= 1.05 x 10^7 m^-1. The lower level is n = 1, so this is the Lyman series, in the

ultraviolet region.

Answer: (i) 2.3 x 10^6 m^-1, Balmer series, visible; (ii) 1.05 x 10^7 m^-1, Lyman

series, ultraviolet (matches the book's printed answers).

Q24(a). A photon of a wave number 102.70 x 10^5 m^-1 is emitted when electron

jumps from higher to n = 1. Determine the number of that orbit from where the

electron falls.

Step 1 - Wavenumber = 102.70 x 10^5 = 1.027 x 10^7 m^-1. Use wavenumber =

R x (1 - 1/n^2) with R = 1.097 x 10^7 m^-1, since the lower level is n = 1.

Step 2 - 1 - 1/n^2 = 1.027 x 10^7 / 1.097 x 10^7 = 0.936.

Step 3 - 1/n^2 = 0.064, so n^2 = 15.6, about 16, giving n = 4.

Answer: n = 4 (matches the book's printed answer).

Q24(b). Indicate the name of the series to which this photon belongs.

Step 1 - The electron falls to n = 1.

Step 2 - All lines ending at n = 1 form the Lyman series.

Answer: Lyman series (matches the book's printed answer).

Q24(c). If the electron will fall from higher orbit to n = 2, then calculate the wave

number of the photon emitted. Why is this energy difference so small as compared

to that in part (a)?

Step 1 - From part (a) the higher orbit is n = 4. Falling to n = 2: wavenumber = R x

(1/4 - 1/16) = 1.097 x 10^7 x 0.1875 = 2.06 x 10^6 m^-1 = 20.6 x 10^5 m^-1,

about 20.5 x 10^5 m^-1 as printed.

Step 2 - The energy difference is smaller because the energy levels get closer

together as n increases (E proportional to -1/n^2): the gap between n = 4 and n = 2

is much smaller than the gap between n = 4 and n = 1.

Answer: about 20.5 x 10^5 m^-1; the gap is smaller because higher levels are

crowded together near zero energy.

Q25(a). What is de-Broglie's wavelength of an electron in meters travelling at half a

speed of light? [m = 9.109 x 10^-31 kg, c = 3 x 10^8 m s^-1]

Step 1 - Velocity v = c/2 = 3 x 10^8 / 2 = 1.5 x 10^8 m s^-1.

Step 2 - de Broglie wavelength lambda = h/(m v) = 6.626 x 10^-34 / (9.109 x

10^-31 x 1.5 x 10^8).

Step 3 - Denominator = 1.366 x 10^-22, so lambda = 4.85 x 10^-12 m.

Answer: 4.85 x 10^-12 m = 0.048 angstrom, about 0.048 angstrom as printed in

the book.

Q25(b). Convert the mass of electron into grams and velocity of light into cm s^-1 and

then calculate the wavelength of an electron in cm.

Step 1 - Mass in grams: 9.109 x 10^-31 kg = 9.109 x 10^-28 g. Velocity of light in

cm s^-1: 3 x 10^10 cm s^-1, so half the speed of light = 1.5 x 10^10 cm s^-1.

Step 2 - Planck's constant in cgs: h = 6.626 x 10^-27 erg s. lambda = h/(m v) =

6.626 x 10^-27 / (9.109 x 10^-28 x 1.5 x 10^10).

Step 3 - Denominator = 1.366 x 10^-17, so lambda = 4.85 x 10^-10 cm = 0.048 x

10^-8 cm.

Answer: 0.048 x 10^-8 cm (matches the book's printed answer).

Q25(c). Convert the wavelength of electron from meters to (i) nm, (ii) angstrom, (iii)

pm.

Step 1 - From part (a), lambda = 4.85 x 10^-12 m.

Step 2 - (i) In nm: 1 nm = 10^-9 m, so lambda = 4.85 x 10^-12 / 10^-9 = 0.00485

nm, about 0.0048 nm.

Step 3 - (ii) In angstrom: 1 angstrom = 10^-10 m, so lambda = 0.0485 angstrom,

about 0.048 angstrom. (iii) In pm: 1 pm = 10^-12 m, so lambda = 4.85 pm.

Answer: 0.0048 nm; 0.048 angstrom; 4.85 pm (matches the book's printed

answers).

mcqs.q: A photon has energy 10^-19 J. Using E = h x nu with h = 6.626 x 10^-34 J s, its frequency is:
For the same photon, with frequency 1.51 x 10^14 Hz and c = 3 x 10^8 m s^-1, the wavelength is:
mcqs.why: Working: lambda = c / nu = 3 * 10^8 / (1.51 * 10^14) = 1.98 * 10^-6 m, using the relation c = nu x lambda.

mcqs.q: The wave number of a photon whose wavelength is 1.98 x 10^-6 m is:
mcqs.why: Working: wave number = 1 / lambda = 1 / (1.98 * 10^-6) = 5.05 * 10^5 m^-1, the reciprocal of the wavelength in metres, which the book rounds to 5 x 10^5 m^-1.

mcqs.q: Using Bohr's formula, the energy of the electron in the first orbit of hydrogen is:
mcqs.why: Working: E_1 = -2.18 * 10^-18 / 1^2 = -2.18 * 10^-18 / 1 = -2.18 * 10^-18 J; the negative sign shows the electron is bound to the nucleus.

mcqs.q: By how much does the orbit radius increase when the electron moves from n = 1 to n = 2 in hydrogen?
mcqs.why: Working: r_1 = 0.529 * 1 = 0.529 angstrom; r_2 = 0.529 * 4 = 2.116 angstrom; increase = 2.116 - 0.529 = 1.587 angstrom.

mcqs.q: What is the increase in orbital radius when the electron goes from n = 2 to n = 3 in hydrogen?
mcqs.why: Working: r_2 = 0.529 * 4 = 2.116 angstrom; r_3 = 0.529 * 9 = 4.761 angstrom; distance = 4.761 - 2.116 = 2.645 angstrom.

mcqs.q: What is the energy of the electron in the third orbit (n = 3) of hydrogen?
An electron in hydrogen revolves in an orbit of energy -0.242 x 10^-18 J. The principal quantum number is:
mcqs.why: Working: n^2 = 2.18 / 0.242 = 9.0, and 3 * 3 = 9, so n = 3, from rearranging E_n = -2.18 x 10^-18 / n^2.

mcqs.q: Using wave number = R x (1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2) with R = 1.097 x 10^7 m^-1, the wave number for a jump from n = 5 to n = 2 is:
options: 1.05 x 10^7 m^-1, a Lyman series line
2.3 x 10^5 m^-1, a Balmer series line
2.3 x 10^6 m^-1, a Balmer series line
2.06 x 10^6 m^-1, a Paschen series line
mcqs.why: Working: 1 / 4 - 1 / 25 = 0.25 - 0.04 = 0.21; wave number = 1.097 * 10^7 * 0.21 = 2.3 * 10^6 m^-1; the lower level n = 2 makes it a Balmer line.

mcqs.q: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron travelling at half the speed of light (v = 1.5 x 10^8 m s^-1, m = 9.109 x 10^-31 kg)?

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • The tendency of atoms to attain maximum of eight electrons in the valence shell is called completion of octet.
  • The geometrical shape of SiCl4 and PCl3 can be explained on the basis of sp3 and sp3 hybridizations.
  • The VSEPR theory stands for Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion.
  • For N2 molecule, the energy of sigma (2p)x orbital is greater than pi (2p)y orbital.
  • The paramagnetic property of O2 is well explained on the basis of MO theory in terms of the presence of two unpaired electrons in two MO orbitals.
  • The values of dipole moment for CS2 is zero while for SO2 is 1.61 D.
  • The bond order of N2 is three while that of Ne2 is zero.

mcqs.q: The tendency of atoms to attain a maximum of eight electrons in the valence shell is called:
mcqs.why: The key facts define the tendency of atoms to attain eight electrons in the valence shell as the completion of octet.

mcqs.q: The geometrical shapes of SiCl4 and PCl3 are explained on the basis of which hybridization?
mcqs.why: The notes state that the shapes of both SiCl4 and PCl3 can be explained on the basis of sp3 hybridization of the central atom.

mcqs.q: VSEPR theory stands for:
mcqs.why: The key facts expand VSEPR as Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion, the theory that electron pairs around a central atom repel and spread apart.

mcqs.q: For the N2 molecule, the energy of the sigma (2p)x orbital is:
options: Less than that of the pi (2p)y orbital
Equal to that of the pi (2p)y orbital
Zero compared with the pi (2p)y orbital
Greater than that of the pi (2p)y orbital
mcqs.why: The notes state that in N2 the sigma (2p)x orbital lies at greater energy than the pi (2p)y orbital, an ordering peculiar to nitrogen.

mcqs.q: The paramagnetic property of O2 is explained by MO theory in terms of:
options: Two paired electrons in one molecular orbital
Two unpaired electrons in two molecular orbitals
A triple bond between the oxygen atoms
The lone pairs on the oxygen atoms
mcqs.why: MO theory places two unpaired electrons in two separate molecular orbitals of O2, which explains why oxygen is paramagnetic.

mcqs.q: The dipole moment of CS2 is:
mcqs.why: The key facts give the dipole moment of CS2 as zero because the linear molecule is symmetrical, while bent SO2 has a dipole moment of 1.61 D.

mcqs.q: The dipole moment of SO2 is:
mcqs.why: The notes give the dipole moment of SO2 as 1.61 D; its bent shape stops the bond dipoles cancelling, unlike linear CS2 whose value is zero.

mcqs.q: The bond order of N2 is:
mcqs.why: The key facts state the bond order of N2 is three, matching its triple bond, whereas the bond order of Ne2 is zero.

mcqs.q: The bond order of Ne2 is:
mcqs.why: The notes give the bond order of Ne2 as zero, which means no net bonding, in contrast to N2 whose bond order is three.

mcqs.q: In the formation of NaCl as shown in the notes, the ionic bond forms because:
options: Sodium and chlorine share a pair of electrons equally
Chlorine loses an electron to sodium
Both atoms gain electrons from each other
Sodium (11 electrons) loses an electron to chlorine (17 electrons), forming Na+ and Cl- ions
mcqs.why: The diagram shows Na with 11 electrons losing one electron and Cl with 17 electrons gaining it, giving Na+ and Cl- held together by an ionic bond.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q1(i). An ionic compound A+ B- is most likely to be formed when
A. the ionization energy of A is high and electron affinity of B is low
✓ B. the ionization energy of A is low and electron affinity of B is high
C. both the ionization energy of A and electron affinity of B are high
D. both the ionization energy of A and electron affinity of B are low

Q1(ii). The number of bonds in nitrogen molecule is
A. one sigma and one pi
✓ B. one sigma and two pi
C. three sigma only
D. two sigma and one pi

Q1(iii). Which of the following statements is not correct regarding bonding molecular
orbitals?
A. Bonding molecular orbitals possess less energy than atomic orbitals from which
they are formed.
✓ B. Bonding molecular orbitals have low electron density between the two nuclei.
C. Every electron in the bonding molecular orbitals contributes to the attraction
between atoms.
D. Bonding molecular orbitals are formed when the electron waves undergo
constructive interference.

Q1(iv). Which of the following molecules has zero dipole moment?
A. NH3
B. CHCl3
C. H2O
✓ D. BF3

Q1(v). Which of the hydrogen halides has the highest percentage of ionic character?
A. HCl
B. HBr
✓ C. HF
D. HI

Q1(vi). Which of the following species has unpaired electrons in antibonding molecular
orbitals?
A. O2^2+
✓ B. N2^2-
C. B2
D. F2

mcqs.q: An ionic compound A+ B- is most likely to be formed when:
options: The ionization energy of A is low and the electron affinity of B is high
The ionization energy of A is high and the electron affinity of B is low
Both the ionization energy of A and the electron affinity of B are high
Both the ionization energy of A and the electron affinity of B are low
mcqs.why: A loses an electron easily when its ionization energy is low, and B gains it readily when its electron affinity is high, so ions A+ and B- form most readily then.

mcqs.q: The bonds in the nitrogen molecule consist of:
options: One sigma and one pi bond
One sigma and two pi bonds
Two sigma and one pi bond
mcqs.why: The triple bond of N2 is made of one sigma bond formed head-on and two pi bonds formed by sideways overlap of p-orbitals.

mcqs.q: Which statement about bonding molecular orbitals is NOT correct?
options: Bonding molecular orbitals possess less energy than the atomic orbitals they form from
Every electron in a bonding molecular orbital contributes to the attraction between atoms
Bonding molecular orbitals have low electron density between the two nuclei
Bonding molecular orbitals form when electron waves undergo constructive interference
mcqs.why: Bonding molecular orbitals actually concentrate electron density between the two nuclei; low density between the nuclei describes an antibonding orbital, so that statement is not correct.

mcqs.q: Which of the following molecules has zero dipole moment?
mcqs.why: BF3 is trigonal planar and symmetrical, so its three bond dipoles cancel and the molecule has zero dipole moment, unlike pyramidal NH3 or bent H2O.

mcqs.q: Which hydrogen halide has the highest percentage of ionic character?
mcqs.why: Fluorine is the most electronegative halogen, so the H-F bond has the largest electronegativity difference and the highest percentage of ionic character among the hydrogen halides.

mcqs.q: Which of the following species has unpaired electrons in antibonding molecular orbitals?
mcqs.why: In N2^2- the two extra electrons enter the pi antibonding orbitals singly, leaving unpaired electrons in antibonding molecular orbitals; in B2 the unpaired electrons are in bonding orbitals.

mcqs.q: Bonding molecular orbitals possess, compared with the atomic orbitals they form from:
mcqs.why: One of the correct statements in the lesson is that bonding molecular orbitals possess less energy than the atomic orbitals from which they are formed, which is why they stabilize the molecule.

mcqs.q: Bonding molecular orbitals are formed when the electron waves undergo:
mcqs.why: The lesson states that bonding molecular orbitals are formed when the electron waves of the two atoms undergo constructive interference, building up density between the nuclei.

mcqs.q: In a bonding molecular orbital, the electron density between the two nuclei is:
mcqs.why: Since the statement that bonding orbitals have low density between the nuclei is the incorrect one, bonding orbitals must have high electron density there, and every such electron contributes to the attraction.

mcqs.q: How many bonds in total does the nitrogen molecule contain?
options: Two bonds (one sigma and one pi)
Four bonds (two sigma and two pi)
Three bonds (one sigma and two pi)
mcqs.why: Working: total bonds = 1 + 2 = 3; the N2 molecule has one sigma bond plus two pi bonds, giving three bonds in total, a triple bond.

lessons.title: Fill in the Blanks
lessons.notes_html:
2(i). The tendency of atoms to attain maximum of eight electrons in the valence shell is called completion of octet.

2(ii). The geometrical shape of SiCl4 and PCl3 can be explained on the basis of sp3 and sp3 hybridizations.

2(iii). The VSEPR theory stands for Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion.

2(iv). For N2 molecule, the energy of sigma (2p)x orbital is greater than pi (2p)y orbital.

2(v). The paramagnetic property of O2 is well explained on the basis of MO theory in terms of the presence of two unpaired electrons in two MO orbitals.

2(vi). The values of dipole moment for CS2 is zero while for SO2 is 1.61 D.

2(vii). The bond order of N2 is three while that of Ne2 is zero.

mcqs.q: The tendency of atoms to attain a maximum of eight electrons in the valence shell is called completion of:
mcqs.why: The blank is filled with octet: atoms tend to attain a maximum of eight electrons in the valence shell, the completion of octet.

mcqs.q: The geometrical shape of SiCl4 can be explained on the basis of _____ hybridization.
mcqs.why: The notes fill this blank with sp3: silicon in SiCl4 uses four sp3 hybrid orbitals directed tetrahedrally to the four chlorine atoms.

mcqs.q: The geometrical shape of PCl3 can be explained on the basis of _____ hybridization.
mcqs.why: The blank for PCl3 is also sp3: phosphorus uses sp3 hybrid orbitals, three forming bonds and one holding the lone pair, giving a pyramidal shape.

mcqs.q: VSEPR stands for Valence Shell _____ Pair Repulsion.
mcqs.why: The missing word is Electron: VSEPR is the Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory used to predict molecular shapes.

mcqs.q: For the N2 molecule, the energy of sigma (2p)x is _____ than pi (2p)y.
mcqs.why: The blank is filled with greater: in N2 the sigma (2p)x orbital has greater energy than the pi (2p)y orbital.

mcqs.q: The paramagnetic property of O2 is explained by MO theory through the presence of _____ unpaired electrons.
mcqs.why: The notes state that O2 has two unpaired electrons in two molecular orbitals, and unpaired electrons are what make a substance paramagnetic.

mcqs.q: The value of the dipole moment for CS2 is:
mcqs.why: The fill-in answer for CS2 is zero dipole moment, because the molecule is linear and symmetrical, so its bond dipoles cancel.

mcqs.q: The value of the dipole moment for SO2 is _____ D.
mcqs.why: The blank is filled with 1.61 D for SO2, whose bent shape prevents cancellation of the bond dipoles, unlike CS2 with zero moment.

mcqs.q: The bond order of N2 is:
mcqs.why: The notes fill this blank with three: nitrogen's bond order is three, corresponding to its triple bond, while Ne2 has bond order zero.

mcqs.q: The bond order of Ne2 is:
mcqs.why: The blank is filled with zero for Ne2: equal bonding and antibonding electrons give no net bond, in contrast to the bond order three of N2.

lessons.title: True or False
lessons.notes_html:
3(i). The core of an atom is the atom minus its valence shell. True

3(ii). The molecules of nitrogen (N triple bond N) and acetylene (HC triple bond CH) are not isoelectronic. False

3(iii). There are four coordinate covalent bonds in NH4+ ion. False

3(iv). A sigma-bond is stronger than a pi-bond and the electrons of sigma-bond are more diffused than pi-bond. False

3(v). The bond energy of heteroatomic diatomic molecules increases with the decrease in the electronegativities of the bonded atoms. False

3(vi). With increase in bond order, bond length decreases and bond strength increases. True

3(vii). The first ionization energies of the elements rise steadily with the increasing atomic number from top to bottom in a group. False

3(viii). A double bond is stronger than a single bond and a triple bond is weaker than a double bond. False

3(ix). The bonds formed between the elements having electronegativity difference more than 1.7 are said to be covalent in nature. False

3(x). The repulsive force between the two bonding pairs is less than that between the two lone pairs. True

3(xi). The number of covalent bonds an atom can form is related to the number of unpaired electrons it has. True

3(xii). The rules which govern the filling of electrons into the atomic orbitals also govern filling of electrons into the molecular orbitals. True

mcqs.q: The core of an atom is the atom minus its valence shell. This statement is:
options: False - the core includes the valence shell
False - the core is only the electrons
False - the core is only the neutrons
mcqs.why: The answer given is True: the core consists of the nucleus plus the inner shells, which is exactly the atom with its valence shell removed.

mcqs.q: N2 and acetylene (C2H2) are isoelectronic. Judged against the printed claim that they are NOT isoelectronic, the correct position is:
options: The printed claim is True - they are not isoelectronic
The printed claim is False - they are isoelectronic
They have different numbers of atoms and electrons
mcqs.why: Working: N2 has 7 + 7 = 14 electrons and C2H2 has 12 + 2 = 14 electrons, so they are isoelectronic and the printed claim that they are not is False.

mcqs.q: The claim that there are four coordinate covalent bonds in the NH4+ ion is:
options: True for NH3 but not NH4+
mcqs.why: The statement is marked False: NH4+ does not contain four coordinate covalent bonds, so the claim as printed is incorrect.

mcqs.q: With an increase in bond order, bond length decreases and bond strength increases. This statement is:
options: False - both length and strength increase
False - length increases and strength decreases
False - neither changes with bond order
mcqs.why: The answer is True: more shared electron pairs pull the nuclei closer together, so higher bond order means a shorter and stronger bond.

mcqs.q: The first ionization energies of the elements rise steadily with increasing atomic number from top to bottom in a group. This statement is:
options: True for the first two groups only
True when read bottom to top
mcqs.why: The statement is marked False: first ionization energy does not rise steadily down a group, so the claim as written is incorrect.

mcqs.q: A double bond is stronger than a single bond, and a triple bond is:
options: Equal in strength to a single bond
Stronger than a double bond, not weaker
mcqs.why: The printed claim that a triple bond is weaker than a double bond is False; bond strength increases with bond order, so triple is stronger than double, which is stronger than single.

mcqs.q: Bonds formed between elements having an electronegativity difference of more than 1.7 are said to be:
mcqs.why: The statement calling such bonds covalent is marked False: an electronegativity difference greater than about 1.7 makes a bond predominantly ionic.

mcqs.q: The repulsive force between two bonding pairs is less than that between two lone pairs. This statement is:
options: False - bonding pairs repel the most
False - lone pairs do not repel
mcqs.why: The answer is True: the repulsion order is lone pair-lone pair greater than lone pair-bonding pair greater than bonding pair-bonding pair, the basis of VSEPR shapes.

mcqs.q: The number of covalent bonds an atom can form is related to the number of unpaired electrons it has. This statement is:
options: False - it depends only on atomic mass
False - it depends only on the lone pairs
False - it is the same for every atom
mcqs.why: The answer is True: each unpaired electron can pair with an electron from another atom to form one covalent bond, so bond count follows unpaired electron count.

mcqs.q: The rules which govern the filling of electrons into atomic orbitals also govern the filling of electrons into molecular orbitals. This statement is:
options: False - molecular orbitals have no filling rules
False - only the Pauli principle applies
False - Hund's rule never applies to molecules
mcqs.why: The answer is True: molecular orbitals are filled using the same Aufbau order, Pauli exclusion principle and Hund's rule as atomic orbitals.

lessons.title: Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q3(i). reason - The core of an atom is the atom minus its valence shell.

True. The core is the inner, non-valence part of the atom: the nucleus plus all inner

shells. Removing the valence shell leaves exactly the core.

Q3(ii). reason - The molecules of nitrogen and acetylene are not isoelectronic.

False. N2 has 7 + 7 = 14 electrons and acetylene C2H2 has 12 + 2 = 14 electrons,

with the same number of atoms in the same connectivity pattern, so the two

molecules ARE isoelectronic. The statement that they are not isoelectronic is false.

Q3(iii). reason - There are four coordinate covalent bonds in NH4+ ion.

False. In NH4+ the nitrogen forms three ordinary covalent bonds with three

hydrogens and only ONE coordinate covalent bond, with the fourth hydrogen (the

H+ that accepts the lone pair). So there is one coordinate bond, not four.

Q3(iv). reason - A sigma-bond is stronger than a pi-bond and the electrons of

sigma-bond are more diffused than pi-bond.

False, as a whole. A sigma-bond IS stronger than a pi-bond, but sigma electrons are

concentrated on the line between the nuclei, while pi electrons are spread above

and below it. So sigma electrons are LESS diffused than pi electrons, not more.

Q3(v). reason - The bond energy of heteroatomic diatomic molecules increases with

the decrease in the electronegativities of the bonded atoms.

False. The bond energy of a heteroatomic molecule increases as the

electronegativity difference of the bonded atoms INCREASES, because the bond

gains partial ionic character, which strengthens it. Decreasing the difference

weakens this effect.

Q3(vi). reason - With increase in bond order, bond length decreases and bond strength

increases.

True. Higher bond order means more shared electron pairs pulling the nuclei

together, so the bond is shorter and stronger: single < double < triple in strength,

and the reverse in length.

Q3(vii). reason - The first ionization energies of the elements rise steadily from top to

bottom in a group.

False. First ionization energy DECREASES down a group, because the outer electron

is farther from the nucleus and better shielded by inner shells, so it is held less

tightly. It generally increases across a period, not down a group.

Q3(viii). reason - A double bond is stronger than a single bond and a triple bond is

weaker than a double bond.

False. A double bond is stronger than a single bond, and a triple bond is stronger

than a double bond: bond strength increases with bond order.

Q3(ix). reason - Bonds with electronegativity difference more than 1.7 are covalent in

nature.

False. On Pauling's scale, an electronegativity difference greater than about 1.7

marks a bond as predominantly IONIC, not covalent. Smaller differences give

covalent (or polar covalent) bonds.

Q3(x). reason - The repulsive force between the two bonding pairs is less than that

between the two lone pairs.

True. The repulsion order is lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bonding pair > bonding

pair-bonding pair, so two bonding pairs repel each other less than two lone pairs do.

This is the basis of VSEPR shapes.

Q3(xi). reason - The number of covalent bonds an atom can form is related to the

number of unpaired electrons it has.

True. Each unpaired electron can pair with an electron from another atom to form

one covalent bond, so the number of bonds an atom normally forms equals its

number of unpaired electrons (before hybridization or promotion).

Q3(xii). reason - The rules for filling atomic orbitals also govern filling of molecular

orbitals.

True. Molecular orbitals are filled by the Aufbau order, Pauli's exclusion principle (at

most two electrons of opposite spin per orbital) and Hund's rule, exactly as for

atomic orbitals.

Q4. What is a chemical bond?
Discuss the formation of ionic and covalent bonds. How

does the electronegativity difference differentiate between ionic and covalent bond?

A chemical bond is the force that holds two or more atoms or ions together in a

molecule or crystal, formed because the combined system has lower energy than

the separate atoms. An ionic bond forms by complete transfer of electrons from a

metal (low ionization energy) to a non-metal (high electron affinity), giving

oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction, e.g. Na+ Cl-. A covalent

bond forms by mutual sharing of electron pairs between atoms, e.g. H2, Cl2.

Electronegativity difference decides the type: a difference near zero gives a

non-polar covalent bond; a moderate difference gives a polar covalent bond; a

difference above about 1.7 gives a predominantly ionic bond.

Q5(a). Define ionization energy and electron affinity. How do these quantities change

in the periodic table? What factors are responsible for their variation?

Ionization energy is the minimum energy needed to remove the most loosely held

electron from an isolated gaseous atom. Electron affinity is the energy released

when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom. Both generally increase

across a period (greater nuclear charge, smaller size) and decrease down a group

(larger size, more shielding). Factors responsible: nuclear charge, atomic size,

shielding effect of inner electrons, and the stability of half-filled or completely filled

subshells.

Q5(b). Explain what you understand by the term electronegativity. Discuss its

variations in the periodic table. How does it affect the bond strengths?

Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared pair

of electrons towards itself. It increases across a period and decreases down a group;

fluorine (4.0) is the most electronegative element. Greater electronegativity

difference makes a bond more polar and, up to a point, stronger, because partial

ionic character adds electrostatic attraction to the covalent sharing; when the

difference exceeds about 1.7 the bond becomes predominantly ionic.

Q6. Write the Lewis structures for the following compounds: (i) HCN (ii) CCl4 (iii) CS2

(iv) H3N->AlF3 (v) NH4OH (vi) H2SO4 (vii) H3PO4 (viii) K2Cr2O7 (ix) N2O5 (x)

Ag(NH3)2NO3. (Note: the book's printed numbering of (vi)/(vii) is unclear under

show-through; the ten compounds are given here in the printed order.)

Labelled drawing instructions (draw dots for valence electrons, lines for shared

pairs, and show charges where present): (i) HCN: H-C triple bond N, with one lone

pair on N. (ii) CCl4: central C singly bonded to four Cl atoms, each Cl with three lone

pairs. (iii) CS2: S double bond C double bond S, each S with two lone pairs. (iv)

H3N->AlF3: NH3 donating its lone pair to AlF3, shown by an arrow from N to Al; Al

bonded to three F atoms, each F with three lone pairs. (v) NH4OH: [NH4]+ with N

bonded to four H atoms (one bond shown as the coordinate bond) and OH- with O

bonded to H and three lone pairs on O. (vi) H2SO4: central S double bonded to two

O atoms and singly bonded to two OH groups, each O with lone pairs as required.

(vii) H3PO4: central P double bonded to one O and singly bonded to three OH

groups. (viii) K2Cr2O7: two K+ ions with the dichromate ion Cr2O7^2-, two CrO4

tetrahedra sharing one oxygen. (ix) N2O5: O2N-O-NO2, each N bonded to three O

atoms (one bridging). (x) Ag(NH3)2NO3: [Ag(NH3)2]+ with Ag bonded to two NH3

molecules by coordinate bonds, and NO3- as a separate ion with N bonded to three

O atoms.

Q7(a). Explain qualitatively the valence bond theory. How does it differ from molecular

orbital theory?

Valence bond theory: a covalent bond forms when two half-filled atomic orbitals, one

from each atom, overlap, and the two electrons of opposite spin pair in the overlap

region. Greater overlap gives a stronger bond; head-on overlap gives a sigma bond,

sideways overlap gives a pi bond. Difference from molecular orbital theory: valence

bond theory keeps the electrons in localized bonds between two atoms and retains

atomic-orbital character, while molecular orbital theory combines atomic orbitals

into new orbitals spread over the whole molecule, with bonding and antibonding

levels, and explains bond order and paramagnetism (e.g. of O2) that valence bond

theory cannot.

Q7(b). How can the bonding in Cl2, O2, N2, HF, H2S be explained with respect to

valence bond theory?

Cl2: overlap of two half-filled 3p orbitals head-on gives one sigma bond. O2: one

sigma bond from head-on 2p overlap plus one pi bond from sideways 2p overlap, a

double bond. N2: one sigma plus two pi bonds from 2p overlaps, a triple bond. HF:

overlap of the H 1s orbital with a half-filled F 2p orbital gives one sigma bond. H2S:

overlap of two H 1s orbitals with two half-filled S 3p orbitals gives two sigma bonds,

with two lone pairs left on sulphur.

Q8. Explain VSEPR theory. Discuss the structures of CH4, NH3, H2O, BeCl2, BF3, SO2,

SO3 with reference to this theory.

VSEPR theory: electron pairs around a central atom (bonding pairs and lone pairs)

repel each other and take up positions as far apart as possible, giving the molecule

its shape; lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs. CH4: four bonding

pairs, tetrahedral, 109.5 degrees. NH3: three bonding pairs and one lone pair,

pyramidal, 107.5 degrees. H2O: two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, bent, 104.5

degrees. BeCl2: two bonding pairs, linear, 180 degrees. BF3: three bonding pairs,

trigonal planar, 120 degrees. SO2: two bonding pairs and one lone pair on sulphur,

bent. SO3: three bonding pairs, trigonal planar, 120 degrees.

Q9. The molecules NF3 and BF3 both have molecular formulae of the type XF3, but

they have different structural formulas. Keeping in view VSEPR theory, sketch the

shape of each molecule and explain the origin of differing in shapes.

Both are XF3, but NF3 has a lone pair on nitrogen while BF3 has none. NF3: three

bonding pairs plus one lone pair on N, so the electron geometry is tetrahedral but

the shape is pyramidal, and the molecule is polar. BF3: three bonding pairs and no

lone pair on B, so the shape is trigonal planar with 120 degree angles, and the three

equal bond dipoles cancel, so it is non-polar. The lone pair on nitrogen is the origin

of the difference in shape.

Q10. The species NH2-, NH3, NH4+ have bond angles of 105 degrees, 107.5 degrees

and 109.5 degrees respectively. Justify these values by drawing their structures.

Labelled drawing instructions: draw NH2- as a bent (angular) ion with two N-H

bonds and two lone pairs on N; draw NH3 as a pyramid with three N-H bonds and

one lone pair on N; draw NH4+ as a regular tetrahedron with four N-H bonds and no

lone pair on N. Justification: lone pair-bonding pair repulsion is stronger than

bonding pair-bonding pair repulsion, so each lone pair squeezes the H-N-H angle

below the tetrahedral 109.5 degrees. NH4+ has no lone pair, so it keeps 109.5

degrees; NH3 with one lone pair is squeezed to 107.5 degrees; NH2- with two lone

pairs is squeezed most, to 105 degrees.

Q11(a). Explain atomic orbital hybridization with reference to sp3, sp2 and sp modes

of hybridization for PH3, C2H4 and C2H2. Discuss geometries of CCl4, PCl3 and H2S

by hybridization of central atoms.

Hybridization is the mixing of atomic orbitals of an atom to form an equal number of

new hybrid orbitals of the same energy, which then form bonds. sp3: one s and

three p orbitals mix to give four sp3 orbitals pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron

(109.5 degrees), e.g. PH3 (pyramidal, one orbital holding a lone pair) and CCl4

(tetrahedral). sp2: one s and two p orbitals mix to give three sp2 orbitals in a plane

(120 degrees) plus one unhybridized p orbital, e.g. C2H4 (planar, with a pi bond

from the p orbitals). sp: one s and one p orbital mix to give two sp orbitals in a line

(180 degrees) plus two unhybridized p orbitals, e.g. C2H2 (linear, with two pi

bonds). PCl3: central P is sp3 hybridized, pyramidal (one lone pair). H2S: central S is

sp3 hybridized, bent (two lone pairs).

Q11(b). The linear geometry of BeCl2 suggests that central Be atom is sp-hybridized.

What type of hybridization does a central atom undergo when the atoms bonded to

it are located at the corners of (a) an equilateral triangle (b) a regular tetrahedron

(c) a trigonal bipyramid?

(a) Atoms at the corners of an equilateral triangle: the central atom is sp2

hybridized (three hybrid orbitals in a plane, 120 degrees apart). (b) Atoms at the

corners of a regular tetrahedron: the central atom is sp3 hybridized (four hybrid

orbitals, 109.5 degrees apart). (c) Atoms at the corners of a trigonal bipyramid: the

central atom is sp3d hybridized (five hybrid orbitals). BeCl2 is linear because Be is

sp hybridized, with two hybrid orbitals at 180 degrees.

Q12(a). Give the basis of the molecular orbital theory and discuss the molecular

orbital configurations of (i) He2 (ii) N2 (iii) O2 (iv) O2^2+ (v) O2^2-.

Molecular orbital theory: atomic orbitals combine to form molecular orbitals spread

over the whole molecule; n atomic orbitals give n molecular orbitals, half bonding

(lower energy) and half antibonding (higher energy). Bond order = (bonding

electrons - antibonding electrons)/2. (i) He2: (sigma 1s)^2 (sigma* 1s)^2, bond

order 0, so He2 does not exist. (ii) N2: (sigma 2s)^2 (sigma* 2s)^2 (pi 2p)^4 (sigma

2p)^2, bond order 3. (iii) O2: (sigma 2s)^2 (sigma* 2s)^2 (sigma 2p)^2 (pi 2p)^4

(pi* 2p)^2, bond order 2, with two unpaired electrons in the pi* orbitals. (iv)

O2^2+: as O2 but with the pi* orbitals empty, bond order 3. (v) O2^2-: as O2 but

with the pi* orbitals full (four electrons), bond order 1.

Q12(b). How does molecular orbital theory explain the paramagnetic character of O2,

O2+ and O2^2- species?

O2 has two unpaired electrons in its pi* antibonding orbitals, so it is paramagnetic.

O2+ has lost one pi* electron, leaving one unpaired pi* electron, so it is also

paramagnetic (less strongly). O2^2- has a full pi* set (four electrons, all paired), so

it has no unpaired electrons and is diamagnetic. Molecular orbital theory explains

this directly from the pi* occupancy, which valence bond theory cannot.

Q13(a). Sketch the molecular orbital pictures of (i) pi (2p)x and pi* (2p)x (ii) O2, O2+,

O2- (iii) He2 and Ne2.

Labelled drawing instructions: (i) pi (2p)x bonding orbital: draw two p orbitals

overlapping sideways, with electron density above and below the line joining the

nuclei and no node between the nuclei. pi* (2p)x antibonding orbital: draw the same

two p orbitals with opposite phases, with a node (zero electron density) between the

nuclei and density pushed to the outer sides. (ii) O2, O2+, O2-: draw energy-level

diagrams with the pi* level holding two, one and four electrons respectively (see

Q12). (iii) He2 and Ne2: draw energy-level diagrams in which bonding and

antibonding levels hold equal numbers of electrons, giving bond order zero, so

neither molecule exists as a stable species.

Q13(b). Sketch the hybrid orbitals of the species PCl3, SiCl4 and NH4+.

Labelled drawing instructions: draw PCl3 with P at the apex of a pyramid, three Cl

atoms at the base, and one lone pair on P (sp3, tetrahedral electron geometry,

pyramidal shape). Draw SiCl4 with Si at the centre of a tetrahedron and four Cl

atoms at the corners (sp3, tetrahedral). Draw NH4+ with N at the centre of a

tetrahedron and four H atoms at the corners, with a + charge on the ion (sp3,

tetrahedral). In each case the central atom uses four sp3 hybrid orbitals; the shapes

differ only because PCl3 has one lone pair while SiCl4 and NH4+ have none.

Q14(a). Define bond energy. Explain the various parameters which determine its

strength.

Bond energy is the average energy required to break one mole of a particular type

of bond in a gaseous molecule, a measure of bond strength. Parameters that

determine it: bond length (shorter bonds are stronger), bond order (higher order is

stronger), electronegativity difference (greater difference adds ionic character and

strength), atomic size and orbital overlap (better overlap gives a stronger bond),

and lone-pair repulsions.

Q14(b). How do you compare the bond strengths of (i) polar and non-polar molecules

(ii) sigma- and pi-bonds?

(i) Polar vs non-polar: a polar bond, with partial ionic character from an

electronegativity difference, is stronger than a comparable non-polar bond, because

electrostatic attraction adds to the covalent sharing. (ii) Sigma vs pi: a sigma bond

is stronger than a pi bond, because head-on overlap puts electron density directly

between the nuclei, while sideways pi overlap is less effective.

Q14(c). Calculate the bond energy of H-Br. The bond energy of H-H is 436 kJ mol^-1

and that of Br-Br is 193 kJ mol^-1.

Step 1 - Use the mean of the two homonuclear bond energies: E(H-Br) = (E(H-H) +

E(Br-Br)) / 2.

Step 2 - Substitute: E(H-Br) = (436 + 193) / 2 = 629 / 2 = 314.5 kJ mol^-1.

Answer: 314.5 kJ mol^-1 (matches the book's printed answer).

Q15(a). Define dipole moment. Give its various units. Find relationship between Debye

and C m. How does it help to find out the shapes of molecules?

Dipole moment is the product of the charge (q) at either end of a polar bond and

the distance (r) between the two oppositely charged centres: mu = q x r. It is a

vector quantity, measured in Debye (D) or in coulomb-metre (C m). 1 D = 3.336 x

10^-30 C m. A molecule's shape follows from its dipole moment: if the individual

bond moments cancel (zero resultant), the molecule is symmetrical (linear, trigonal

planar, tetrahedral); if they do not cancel, the molecule is unsymmetrical (bent,

pyramidal) and polar.

Q15(b). The bond length of H-Br is 1.4 x 10^-10 m. Its observed dipole moment is

0.79 D. Find the percentage ionic character of the bond. Unit positive charge =

1.6022 x 10^-19 C and 1 D = 3.336 x 10^-30 C m.

Step 1 - Dipole moment if the bond were 100% ionic: mu(ionic) = q x r = 1.6022 x

10^-19 C x 1.4 x 10^-10 m = 2.243 x 10^-29 C m.

Step 2 - Convert to Debye: mu(ionic) = 2.243 x 10^-29 / 3.336 x 10^-30 = 6.72 D.

Step 3 - Percentage ionic character = (mu(observed) / mu(ionic)) x 100 = (0.79 /

6.72) x 100 = 11.7%.

Answer: 11.7% (matches the book's printed answer).

Q16. PF3 is a polar molecule with dipole moment 1.02 D and thus the P-F bond is

polar. Si is in the proximity of P in the periodic table. It is expected that Si-F bond

would also be polar, but SiF4 has no dipole moment. Explain it.

PF3 is pyramidal (three P-F bonds plus one lone pair on P), so its three bond dipoles

do not cancel and the molecule has a dipole moment of 1.02 D: the P-F bond is

polar. SiF4 is tetrahedral and perfectly symmetrical, so its four equal Si-F bond

dipoles cancel exactly, giving zero resultant dipole moment, even though each Si-F

bond is polar. Symmetry, not bond polarity alone, decides whether a molecule is

polar.

Q17. Which of the following molecules will be polar or non-polar?
Sketch the

structures and justify your answer: (i) CCl4 (ii) SO3 (iii) NF3 (iv) SO2.

Labelled drawing instructions: (i) CCl4: draw C at the centre of a tetrahedron with

four Cl atoms at the corners; the four equal bond dipoles cancel, so CCl4 is

non-polar. (ii) SO3: draw S at the centre of a triangle with three O atoms at the

corners in one plane; the three bond dipoles cancel, so SO3 is non-polar. (iii) NF3:

draw N at the apex of a pyramid with three F atoms at the base and one lone pair

on N; the dipoles do not cancel, so NF3 is polar. (iv) SO2: draw S with two O atoms

at an angle (bent shape) and one lone pair on S; the dipoles do not cancel, so SO2 is

polar (1.61 D).

Q18. Explain the following with reasons (as printed, the list runs (i), (ii), (iii), (vi), (v),

(vi), (vii): the (iv) entry is missing and (vi) appears twice in print; the items are

answered here in printed order).

(i) Bond distance is the distance at which the attraction between the nuclei and the

shared electrons exactly balances the repulsion between the nuclei and between

the electrons: the energy minimum. If the atoms come closer, repulsion rises

steeply; if they move apart, attraction is lost. The observed bond length is this

compromise distance. (ii) After a coordinate bond forms, the donated pair becomes

indistinguishable from any other shared pair in the molecule, so in NH4+, H3O+ and

CH3NH3+ no experiment can tell which bond was the coordinate one: the

distinction vanishes. (iii) H2O and NH3 are sp3 hybridized like CH4, but their lone

pairs repel bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other,

squeezing the angles from 109.5 degrees to 104.5 degrees (two lone pairs) and

107.5 degrees (one lone pair). (iv) [printed as (vi)] Pi-bonds are formed by sideways

overlap, so their electron density lies above and below the bond axis and is spread

over a larger region: pi-bonds are more diffused than sigma-bonds, whose density is

concentrated on the axis. (v) In HI the iodine atom is much larger and its orbitals

more diffused than in HCl, so the H-I bond is longer and weaker and the abnormality

of bond length and strength (compared with the trend) is less prominent than in

HCl. (vi) CO2 and CS2 are linear and symmetrical, so their equal and opposite bond

dipoles cancel and the dipole moment is zero; SO2 is bent, so its bond dipoles add

to 1.61 D. (vii) Electrovalent (ionic) compounds are held in a crystal lattice by strong

electrostatic forces between ions, so much more energy is needed to melt, boil,

vaporize or sublime them than for covalent compounds, which are held only by

weak intermolecular forces.

mcqs.q: How does electronegativity difference differentiate ionic and covalent bonds?
options: A difference above about 1.7 gives a predominantly ionic bond, a moderate difference gives polar covalent, and near zero gives non-polar covalent
A difference above 1.7 gives a non-polar covalent bond
Electronegativity difference has no effect on bond type
A difference near zero gives an ionic bond
mcqs.why: The notes explain that electronegativity difference decides bond type: near zero is non-polar covalent, moderate is polar covalent, and above about 1.7 the bond is predominantly ionic.

mcqs.q: According to VSEPR theory, the shape and bond angle of CH4 are:
mcqs.why: CH4 has four bonding pairs and no lone pair on carbon, so VSEPR gives a tetrahedral shape with the full tetrahedral angle of 109.5 degrees.

mcqs.q: Why is the bond angle in NH3 (107.5 degrees) smaller than in NH4+ (109.5 degrees)?
options: NH3 has a larger central atom than NH4+
NH4+ has two lone pairs on nitrogen
NH3 has one lone pair, whose stronger repulsion squeezes the H-N-H angle below 109.5 degrees
The N-H bonds in NH3 are ionic
mcqs.why: Lone pair-bonding pair repulsion is stronger than bonding pair-bonding pair repulsion; the one lone pair in NH3 squeezes the angle to 107.5 degrees, while NH4+ has no lone pair and keeps 109.5 degrees.

mcqs.q: A central atom bonded to atoms at the corners of a regular tetrahedron undergoes which hybridization?
mcqs.why: Four hybrid orbitals pointing to the corners of a regular tetrahedron at 109.5 degrees are formed by sp3 hybridization, one s and three p orbitals mixing.

mcqs.q: Using the N2 configuration (sigma 2s)^2 (sigma* 2s)^2 (pi 2p)^4 (sigma 2p)^2, the bond order of N2 is:
mcqs.why: Working: bonding electrons = 2 + 4 + 2 = 8; antibonding electrons = 2; bond order = (8 - 2) / 2 = 6 / 2 = 3, so N2 has bond order three.

mcqs.q: How does MO theory explain the behaviour of O2^2- compared with O2?
options: O2^2- has more unpaired electrons than O2
O2 has no unpaired electrons at all
O2^2- has a full pi* set with all electrons paired, so it is diamagnetic, while O2 has two unpaired pi* electrons and is paramagnetic
Both have three unpaired pi* electrons
mcqs.why: O2 carries two unpaired electrons in its pi* orbitals and is paramagnetic; adding two more electrons fills the pi* set in O2^2-, leaving no unpaired electrons, so it is diamagnetic.

mcqs.q: Calculate the bond energy of H-Br, given H-H = 436 kJ mol^-1 and Br-Br = 193 kJ mol^-1, using the mean of the two.
mcqs.why: Working: E(H-Br) = (436 + 193) / 2 = 629 / 2 = 314.5 kJ mol^-1, the mean of the two homonuclear bond energies as used in the notes.

mcqs.q: The H-Br bond length is 1.4 x 10^-10 m and its observed dipole moment is 0.79 D. Its percentage ionic character is:
Why does SiF4 have no dipole moment even though each Si-F bond is polar?
options: The Si-F bond is actually non-polar
Silicon has a lone pair that cancels the dipoles
SiF4 is tetrahedral and perfectly symmetrical, so the four equal bond dipoles cancel exactly
mcqs.why: Each Si-F bond is polar, but the tetrahedral symmetry of SiF4 makes the four equal bond dipoles cancel, giving zero resultant dipole moment; symmetry, not bond polarity alone, decides molecular polarity.

mcqs.q: Dipole moment is defined as mu = q x r. One Debye equals:
mcqs.why: The notes define dipole moment as the product of charge and separation distance, mu = q x r, and give the conversion 1 D = 3.336 x 10^-30 C m.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • The substance undergoing a physical or a chemical change forms a chemical system.
  • The change in internal energy can be measured.
  • Solids which have more than one crystalline forms possess different values of heats of formation.
  • A process is called spontaneous if it takes place on its own without any external assistance.
  • A state function is a macroscopic property of a system which is 2(v) Complete: A ___ is a macroscopic property of a system which is ___ of the path adopted to bring about that change. A state function is a macroscopic property of a system which is independent of the path adopted to bring about that change.

mcqs.q: What does the substance undergoing a physical or a chemical change form?
mcqs.why: The notes state directly that the substance undergoing a physical or a chemical change forms a chemical system.

mcqs.q: Which quantity does the lesson say can be measured for a system?
options: The path adopted to bring about a change
The number of crystalline forms of a solid
The external assistance given to a process
mcqs.why: The notes state that the change in internal energy can be measured, which is why internal energy changes are used in thermochemistry.

mcqs.q: Solids which have more than one crystalline form possess different values of which quantity?
mcqs.why: The notes state that solids which have more than one crystalline form possess different values of heats of formation.

mcqs.q: A process is called spontaneous if it:
options: Always needs a continuous supply of energy
Can only take place in a calorimeter
Must involve more than one crystalline form
Takes place on its own without any external assistance
mcqs.why: By definition in the notes, a spontaneous process takes place on its own without any external assistance.

mcqs.q: A state function is a macroscopic property of a system which is:
options: Dependent on the path adopted to bring about that change
Independent of the path adopted to bring about that change
Dependent on the crystalline form of the solid
Measured only during a chemical change
mcqs.why: The notes define a state function as a macroscopic property of a system which is independent of the path adopted to bring about that change.

mcqs.q: Which description fits a state function?
options: A property fixed by the path taken
A property of the surroundings only
A macroscopic property independent of the path taken
A property that changes the internal energy
mcqs.why: A state function is defined in the notes as a macroscopic property of a system which is independent of the path adopted to bring about that change.

mcqs.q: A process that takes place on its own, without any external assistance, is called:
mcqs.why: The notes give exactly this definition: a process is called spontaneous if it takes place on its own without any external assistance.

mcqs.q: Which solids are stated to have different heats of formation?
options: Solids with more than one crystalline form
Solids with only one crystalline form
Solids that form a chemical system
mcqs.why: The notes state that solids which have more than one crystalline form possess different values of heats of formation.

mcqs.q: The substance undergoing a chemical change forms a:
mcqs.why: The lesson states that the substance undergoing a physical or a chemical change forms a chemical system.

mcqs.q: For a state function, the value depends on the present state of the system and NOT on:
options: The macroscopic properties of the system
The internal energy of the system
The path adopted to bring about the change
mcqs.why: The notes define a state function as a macroscopic property which is independent of the path adopted to bring about that change.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q1(i). If an endothermic reaction is allowed to take place very rapidly in the air, the
temperature of the surrounding air
A. remains constant
B. increases
✓ C. decreases
D. remains unchanged

Q1(ii). In endothermic reactions, the heat content of the
✓ A. products is more than that of reactants
B. reactants is more than that of products
C. both (a) and (b)
D. reactants and products are equal

Q1(iii). Calorie is equivalent to
A. 0.4184 J
B. 41.84 J
✓ C. 4.184 J
D. 418.4 J

Q1(iv). The change in heat contents of a chemical reaction at constant temperature
and pressure is called
✓ A. enthalpy change
B. bond energy
C. heat of sublimation
D. internal energy change

Q1(v). Which of the following statements is contrary to the first law of
thermodynamics?
A. Energy can neither be created nor destroyed.
B. One form of energy can be transferred into an equivalent amount of other kinds
of energy.
C. In an adiabatic process, the work done is independent of its path.
✓ D. Continuous production of mechanical work without supplying an equivalent
amount of heat is possible.

Q1(vi). For a given process, the heat changes at constant pressure (qp) and at
constant volume (qv) are related to each other as
A. qp = qv
B. qp < qv
✓ C. qp > qv
D. qp = qv/2

Q1(vii). For the reaction: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O the change in enthalpy is called
A. heat of reaction
B. heat of formation
✓ C. heat of neutralization
D. heat of combustion

Q1(viii). The net heat change in a chemical reaction is same, whether it is brought
about in two or more different ways in one or several steps. It is known as
A. Henry's law
B. Joule's principle
✓ C. Hess's law
D. Law of conservation of energy

Q1(ix). Enthalpy of neutralisation of all the strong acids and strong bases has the
same value because
A. neutralisation leads to the formation of salt and water.
B. strong acids and bases are ionic substances.
C. acids always give rise to H+ ions and bases always furnish OH- ions.
