✓ D. the net chemical change involves the combination of H+ and OH- ions to form
water.

mcqs.q: If an endothermic reaction is allowed to take place very rapidly in the air, the temperature of the surrounding air:
mcqs.why: An endothermic reaction absorbs heat from the surroundings, so the surrounding air loses heat and its temperature decreases.

mcqs.q: In endothermic reactions, the heat content of the:
options: Reactants is more than that of products
Products is more than that of reactants
Products is less than that of reactants
mcqs.why: In an endothermic reaction heat is absorbed and stored in the products, so the heat content of the products is more than that of the reactants.

mcqs.q: One calorie is equivalent to:
mcqs.why: The lesson gives the calorie equivalence as 1 cal = 4.184 J, so one calorie is equivalent to 4.184 joules.

mcqs.q: The change in heat contents of a chemical reaction at constant temperature and pressure is called:
mcqs.why: The heat change of a reaction at constant temperature and pressure is the enthalpy change, as stated in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Which statement is contrary to the first law of thermodynamics?
options: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed
Continuous production of mechanical work without supplying an equivalent amount of heat is possible
One form of energy can be transferred into an equivalent amount of other kinds of energy
Energy is conserved in every process
mcqs.why: The first law says energy can neither be created nor destroyed, so producing work continuously without an equivalent heat supply contradicts it.

mcqs.q: For a given process, the heat changes at constant pressure (qp) and at constant volume (qv) are related as:
mcqs.why: The lesson gives qp greater than qv for a given process, because at constant pressure part of the heat also does expansion work.

mcqs.q: For the reaction NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O, the change in enthalpy is called:
mcqs.why: An acid reacting with a base to form salt and water is neutralization, so its enthalpy change is the heat of neutralization.

mcqs.q: The net heat change in a chemical reaction is the same whether it is brought about in one step or in several steps. This is known as:
mcqs.why: Hess's law of constant heat summation states that the net heat change is the same in one or several steps, as given in the lesson.

mcqs.q: The enthalpy of neutralisation of all strong acids and strong bases has the same value because:
options: Neutralisation leads to the formation of salt and water
Strong acids and bases are ionic substances
The net chemical change involves the combination of H+ and OH- ions to form water
Acids always give rise to H+ ions and bases always furnish OH- ions
mcqs.why: For every strong acid and strong base the only net change is H+ + OH- forming water, so the enthalpy of neutralisation is the same in all cases.

mcqs.q: How many joules are there in 10 calories, given 1 cal = 4.184 J?
mcqs.why: Working: 10 * 4.184 = 41.84, so 10 calories contain 10 * 4.184 = 41.84 joules of energy.

lessons.notes_html:
2(i). The substance undergoing a physical or a chemical change forms a chemical system.

A state function is a macroscopic property of a system which is independent of the path adopted to bring about that change.

mcqs.q: Complete the blank: The substance undergoing a physical or a chemical change forms a chemical ____.
mcqs.why: The fill-in statement in the notes reads: the substance undergoing a physical or a chemical change forms a chemical system.

mcqs.q: Complete the blank: The change in ____ can be measured.
mcqs.why: The notes state as a fill-in fact that the change in internal energy can be measured.

mcqs.q: Complete the blank: Solids which have more than one crystalline form possess different values of ____.
mcqs.why: The notes state that solids with more than one crystalline form possess different values of heats of formation.

mcqs.q: Complete the blank: A process is called spontaneous if it takes place on its own without any ____.
mcqs.why: The definition in the notes is that a spontaneous process takes place on its own without any external assistance.

mcqs.q: Complete the blank: A state function is a macroscopic property of a system which is ____ of the path adopted to bring about that change.
mcqs.why: The completed statement in the notes is that a state function is independent of the path adopted to bring about that change.

mcqs.q: A state function is described in the notes as which kind of property of a system?
options: A property of a crystalline solid
mcqs.why: The notes define a state function as a macroscopic property of a system which is independent of the path adopted.

mcqs.q: Which term is defined as a process that takes place on its own without any external assistance?
mcqs.why: The fill-in section defines a spontaneous process as one that takes place on its own without any external assistance.

mcqs.q: Which term is defined as a macroscopic property independent of the path adopted?
mcqs.why: The notes complete the definition: a state function is a macroscopic property of a system which is independent of the path adopted.

mcqs.q: For a solid with more than one crystalline form, the heats of formation of its forms are:
mcqs.why: The notes state that such solids possess different values of heats of formation, so the values for the different forms are not equal.

mcqs.q: A chemical system is formed by:
options: The surroundings of a reaction vessel
A macroscopic property of a system
The substance undergoing a physical or a chemical change
mcqs.why: The first fill-in statement says the substance undergoing a physical or a chemical change forms a chemical system.

lessons.title: True or False
lessons.notes_html:
3(i). It is necessary that a spontaneous reaction should be exothermic. False

3(ii). Amount of heat absorbed at constant volume is internal energy change. True

3(iii). The work done by the system is given the positive sign. False

3(iv). Enthalpy is a state function but internal energy is not. False

3(v). Total heat content of a system is called enthalpy of the system. True

mcqs.q: Judge the statement: It is necessary that a spontaneous reaction should be exothermic.
mcqs.why: The lesson marks this statement False: a spontaneous reaction does not have to be exothermic to take place on its own.

mcqs.q: Judge the statement: Amount of heat absorbed at constant volume is internal energy change.
mcqs.why: The lesson marks this True: at constant volume the heat absorbed is the internal energy change of the system.

mcqs.why: The lesson marks this statement False, so work done by the system is not given the positive sign in this convention.

lessons.title: Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q3(i). reason - It is necessary that a spontaneous reaction should be exothermic.

False. Spontaneity is decided by the Gibbs energy change, delta G = delta H - T

delta S. An endothermic reaction (positive delta H) can still be spontaneous if the

entropy increase is large enough that T delta S outweighs delta H, e.g. melting of

ice at room temperature.

Q3(ii). reason - Amount of heat absorbed at constant volume is internal energy

change.

True. At constant volume no expansion work is done (w = 0), so by the first law the

heat absorbed equals the change in internal energy: qv = delta E.

Q3(iii). reason - The work done by the system is given the positive sign.

False. In the chemistry sign convention, work done BY the system on the

surroundings is given a NEGATIVE sign (the system loses energy), while work done

ON the system is positive. So delta E = q + w with w negative for expansion work

done by the system.

Q3(iv). reason - Enthalpy is a state function but internal energy is not.

False. Both enthalpy (H = E + PV) and internal energy (E) are state functions: their

values depend only on the present state of the system, not on the path taken to

reach it.

Q3(v). reason - Total heat content of a system is called enthalpy of the system.

True. Enthalpy is defined as H = E + PV and represents the total heat content of a

system at constant pressure; the heat absorbed or evolved at constant pressure

equals the enthalpy change.

Q4. Define the following terms and give three examples of each: (i) System (ii)

Surroundings (iii) State function (iv) Units of energy (v) Exothermic reaction (vi)

Endothermic reaction (vii) Internal energy of the system (viii) Enthalpy of the

system.

System: the part of the universe chosen for study, e.g. the reacting mixture in a

flask; a solution in a calorimeter; a gas in a cylinder. Surroundings: everything

outside the system that can exchange energy or matter with it, e.g. the air around a

flask; the water bath around a calorimeter; the laboratory. State function: a property

whose value depends only on the present state of the system, not on its history,

e.g. temperature; pressure; enthalpy. Units of energy: joule (J); kilojoule (kJ); calorie

(cal, 1 cal = 4.184 J). Exothermic reaction: a reaction that releases heat to the

surroundings, e.g. combustion of methane; neutralization of an acid by a base;

respiration. Endothermic reaction: a reaction that absorbs heat from the

surroundings, e.g. melting of ice; photosynthesis; decomposition of calcium

carbonate. Internal energy of the system: the total energy (kinetic + potential) of all

the particles of the system, e.g. the internal energy of a gas rises when it is heated;

it falls when the gas expands and does work; it is a state function. Enthalpy of the

system: H = E + PV, the total heat content of the system, e.g. the enthalpy of

steam is greater than that of liquid water; the enthalpy change of a reaction at

constant pressure is the heat evolved or absorbed; enthalpy is a state function.

Q5(a). Differentiate between: (i) Internal energy and enthalpy (ii) Internal energy

change and enthalpy change (iii) Exothermic and endothermic reactions.

(i) Internal energy (E) is the total energy of the particles of a system; enthalpy (H =

E + PV) is the total heat content, i.e. internal energy plus the pressure-volume

energy. (ii) Internal energy change (delta E) is the heat change at constant volume

(qv); enthalpy change (delta H) is the heat change at constant pressure (qp); they

differ by the expansion work, delta H = delta E + delta n RT. (iii) Exothermic

reactions release heat (delta H negative, surroundings warm up); endothermic

reactions absorb heat (delta H positive, surroundings cool down).

Q5(b). Define the following enthalpies and give two examples of each: (i) Standard

enthalpy of reaction (ii) Standard enthalpy of combustion (iii) Standard enthalpy of

atomization (iv) Standard enthalpy of solution.

(i) Standard enthalpy of reaction: the enthalpy change when a reaction occurs with

all substances in their standard states (1 atm, 25 degrees C), e.g. H2(g) + 1/2 O2(g)

-> H2O(l), delta H = -285.8 kJ mol^-1; C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), delta H = -393.7 kJ

mol^-1. (ii) Standard enthalpy of combustion: the enthalpy change when one mole

of a substance is completely burnt in excess oxygen in its standard state, e.g.

CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(l), delta H = -890 kJ mol^-1; C2H5OH(l) +

3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(l), delta H = -1367 kJ mol^-1. (iii) Standard enthalpy of

atomization: the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is converted into

gaseous atoms, e.g. Na(s) → Na(g), delta H = +108 kJ mol^-1; 1/2 Cl2(g) → Cl(g),

delta H = +121 kJ mol^-1. (iv) Standard enthalpy of solution: the enthalpy change

when one mole of a solute dissolves in a large excess of solvent, e.g. NH4Cl(s) + aq

-> NH4Cl(aq), endothermic; NaOH(s) + aq → NaOH(aq), exothermic.

Q6(a). What are spontaneous and non-spontaneous processes?
Give examples.

A spontaneous process is one that takes place on its own without external

assistance, e.g. flow of heat from a hot body to a cold one; rusting of iron. A

non-spontaneous process is one that does not take place on its own and needs a

continuous supply of energy, e.g. electrolysis of water; pumping water uphill.

Q6(b). Explain that burning of a candle is a spontaneous process.

Burning a candle is spontaneous because once ignited, the wax burns in air on its

own, releasing heat (exothermic), and the overall Gibbs energy change is negative.

The reaction needs only a small initial push (the match flame) to start; after that it

sustains itself without further help.

Q6(c). Is it true that a non-spontaneous process never happens in the universe?

Explain it.

No, that is not true. A non-spontaneous process can be made to happen by

supplying energy from outside, e.g. water does not split into hydrogen and oxygen

on its own, but electrolysis splits it using electrical energy; a refrigerator pumps

heat from cold to hot using electrical work. Non-spontaneous only means 'not on its

own', not 'never'.

Q7(a). What is the first law of thermodynamics?
How does it explain that (i) qv = delta

E (ii) qp = delta H?

The first law of thermodynamics states that energy can neither be created nor

destroyed, only changed from one form to another: delta E = q + w, where q is heat

absorbed by the system and w is work done on the system. It explains that (i) qv =

delta E: at constant volume no work is done, so all heat goes into internal energy;

(ii) qp = delta H: at constant pressure the heat equals the enthalpy change,

because part of the energy appears as expansion work.

Q7(b). How will you differentiate between delta E and delta H?
Is it true that delta H

and delta E have the same values for the reactions taking place in the solution

state?

Delta E and delta H differ by the expansion work: delta H = delta E + delta n RT,

where delta n is the change in moles of gas. In the solution state there is almost no

volume change (delta n RT is negligible, since liquids and solids hardly expand), so

delta H and delta E have practically the same values for reactions in solution.

Q8(a). What is the difference between heat and temperature?
Write a mathematical

relationship between these two parameters.

Heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference, measured in joules;

temperature is the measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles,

measured in degrees. They are related by q = m x c x delta T, where m is the mass,

c the specific heat capacity, and delta T the temperature change: the same heat

produces a larger temperature rise in a smaller mass or a substance of lower

specific heat.

Q8(b). How do you measure the heat of combustion of a substance by bomb

calorimeter?

A weighed sample is placed in a steel bomb, filled with oxygen at high pressure, and

ignited electrically while the bomb sits in a known mass of water in an insulated

calorimeter. The temperature rise of the water (and calorimeter) is measured. Heat

evolved = (mass of water x specific heat of water + heat capacity of calorimeter) x

temperature rise. Dividing by the moles of sample burnt gives the heat of

combustion (at constant volume, delta E; corrected to delta H if needed).

Q9. Define heat of neutralization. When a dilute solution of a strong acid is neutralized

by a dilute solution of a strong base, the heat of neutralization is found to be nearly

the same in all cases. How do you account for this?

Heat of neutralization is the enthalpy change when one mole of H+ ions from an

acid reacts with one mole of OH- ions from a base to form one mole of water. For a

strong acid and a strong base in dilute solution, the only net reaction is H+ + OH-

-> H2O, whatever the acid and base are, because both are fully ionized and the salt

formed stays in solution. Hence the heat evolved is nearly the same in all cases

(about -57.3 kJ mol^-1).

Q10(a). State the laws of thermochemistry and show how they are based on the first

law of thermodynamics.

Laws of thermochemistry: (i) Lavoisier-Laplace law: the heat change of a reaction in

one direction is equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to that in the reverse

direction. (ii) Hess's law of constant heat summation: the total heat change of a

reaction is the same whether it takes place in one step or in several steps. Both are

based on the first law of thermodynamics: since energy is conserved and enthalpy

is a state function, the total energy change depends only on the initial and final

states, not on the path.

Q10(b). What is a thermochemical equation?
Give three examples. What information

do they convey?

A thermochemical equation is a balanced chemical equation that also states the

enthalpy change and the physical states of all reactants and products, e.g. H2(g) +

1/2 O2(g) → H2O(l), delta H = -285.8 kJ mol^-1; C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), delta H =

-393.7 kJ mol^-1; N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g), delta H = -92.4 kJ mol^-1. It conveys

the reaction, the amounts reacting, the physical states, and whether heat is evolved

(negative delta H) or absorbed (positive delta H).

Q10(c). Why is it necessary to mention the physical states of reactants and products

in a thermochemical reaction? Apply Hess's law to justify your answer.

Physical states must be stated because the enthalpy of a substance depends on its

state: e.g. H2O(l) and H2O(g) have very different enthalpies (the difference is the

heat of vaporization), so a reaction producing liquid water releases more heat than

one producing steam. Hess's law justifies this: the enthalpy change is fixed by the

initial and final states, so unless the states are specified, the initial and final states

are not fully specified and the enthalpy change is not defined.

Q11(a). Define and explain Hess's law of constant heat summation. Explain it with

examples and give its application.

Hess's law of constant heat summation: the enthalpy change of a reaction is the

same whether the reaction takes place in one step or in a series of steps, because

enthalpy is a state function. Example: carbon can burn directly to CO2 (delta H =

-393.7 kJ mol^-1), or first to CO and then to CO2; the sum of the two steps equals

-393.7 kJ mol^-1. Application: it lets us calculate enthalpy changes for reactions

that cannot be carried out directly (e.g. formation of CO from C and O2, heats of

formation, lattice energies) from steps that can be measured.

Q11(b). Hess's law helps us to calculate the heats of those reactions, which cannot be

normally carried out in a laboratory. Explain it.

Many reactions cannot be carried out cleanly in a laboratory, or their heat changes

are too small or too slow to measure, e.g. the formation of methane from its

elements, or the conversion of graphite to diamond. Hess's law lets us build the

impossible reaction out of measurable steps (combustion reactions, solution

reactions) whose enthalpy changes are known, and add them to get the unknown

enthalpy change, since the total depends only on the start and end states.

Q12(a). What is lattice energy?
How does Born-Haber cycle help to calculate the

lattice energy of NaCl?

Lattice energy is the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic crystal is formed

from its gaseous ions, e.g. Na+(g) + Cl-(g) → NaCl(s), delta H = -787 kJ mol^-1

(energy is released). The Born-Haber cycle applies Hess's law to a cycle: elements

-> gaseous atoms (atomization) → gaseous ions (ionization energy, electron

affinity) → crystal (lattice energy), with the direct formation enthalpy measured by

calorimetry. For NaCl: formation enthalpy -411 kJ mol^-1 = atomization of Na

(+108) + ionization of Na (+496) + atomization of Cl (+121) + electron affinity of Cl

(-349) + lattice energy, giving lattice energy = -411 - 376 = -787 kJ mol^-1.

Q12(b). Justify that heat of formation of a compound is the sum of all the other

enthalpies.

By Hess's law, the heat of formation of a compound is the sum of the enthalpy

changes of all the steps that build it from its elements: atomization of the elements,

ionization, electron affinity, and lattice formation. Since enthalpy is a state function,

the sum of the step enthalpies must equal the directly measured formation

enthalpy, whatever route is taken.

Q13. 50 cm^3 of 1.0 M HCl is mixed with 50 cm^3 of 1.00 M NaOH in a glass

calorimeter. The temperature of the resultant mixture increases from 21.0 degrees

C to 27.5 degrees C. Assume that calorimeter losses of heat are negligible.

Calculate the enthalpy change per mole for the reaction. The density of solution is 1

g cm^-3 and specific heat is 4.18 J g^-1 K^-1.

Step 1 - Total volume = 50 + 50 = 100 cm^3, so mass of solution = 100 cm^3 x 1

g cm^-3 = 100 g.

Step 2 - Temperature rise = 27.5 - 21.0 = 6.5 degrees C (= 6.5 K).

Step 3 - Heat evolved = m x c x delta T = 100 g x 4.18 J g^-1 K^-1 x 6.5 K = 2717 J

= 2.717 kJ.

Step 4 - Moles of acid (and base) reacting = 50/1000 dm^3 x 1.0 mol dm^-3 = 0.05

mol.

Step 5 - Enthalpy change per mole = -2.717 kJ / 0.05 mol = -54.3 kJ mol^-1 (heat is

evolved, so the sign is negative).

Answer: about -54 kJ mol^-1 (matches the book's printed answer).

Q14. Hydrazine (N2H4) is a rocket fuel. It burns in O2 to give N2 and H2O: N2H4(l) +

O2(g) → N2(g) + 2H2O(g). 1.00 g of N2H4 is burned in a bomb calorimeter. An

increase of temperature 3.51 degrees C is recorded. The heat capacity of the

calorimeter is 5.5 kJ K^-1. Calculate the quantity of heat evolved. Also, calculate the

heat of combustion of 1 mole of N2H4.

Step 1 - Heat evolved = heat capacity x temperature rise = 5.5 kJ K^-1 x 3.51 K =

19.3 kJ.

Step 2 - Molar mass of N2H4 = 2 x 14 + 4 x 1 = 32 g mol^-1, so 1.00 g = 1.00/32 =

0.03125 mol.

Step 3 - Heat of combustion per mole = -19.3 kJ / 0.03125 mol = -618 kJ mol^-1

(negative because heat is evolved).

Answer: heat evolved 19.3 kJ; heat of combustion -618 kJ mol^-1 (matches the

book's printed answers).

Q15. Octane (C8H18) is a motor fuel. 1.80 g of a sample of octane is burned in a bomb

calorimeter having heat capacity 11.66 kJ K^-1. The temperature of the calorimeter

increases from 21.36 degrees C to 28.78 degrees C. Calculate the heat of

combustion for 1.8 g of octane. Also, calculate the heat for 1 mole of octane.

Step 1 - Temperature rise = 28.78 - 21.36 = 7.42 degrees C.

Step 2 - Heat evolved for 1.80 g = 11.66 kJ K^-1 x 7.42 K = 86.51 kJ.

Step 3 - Molar mass of octane C8H18 = 8 x 12 + 18 x 1 = 114 g mol^-1, so 1.80 g

= 1.80/114 = 0.01579 mol.

Step 4 - Heat of combustion per mole = -86.51 kJ / 0.01579 mol = -5478.8 kJ

mol^-1.

Answer: 86.51 kJ for 1.8 g; -5478.84 kJ mol^-1 for one mole (matches the book's

printed answers).

Q16. By applying Hess's law calculate the enthalpy change for the formation of an

aqueous solution of NH4Cl from NH3 gas and HCl gas. The results for the various

reactions are: (i) NH3(g) + aq → NH3(aq), delta H = -35.16 kJ mol^-1; (ii) HCl(g) +

aq → HCl(aq), delta H = -72.41 kJ mol^-1; (iii) NH3(aq) + HCl(aq) → NH4Cl(aq),

delta H = -51.48 kJ mol^-1.

Step 1 - Add the three steps: NH3(g) + aq → NH3(aq); HCl(g) + aq → HCl(aq);

NH3(aq) + HCl(aq) → NH4Cl(aq).

Step 2 - The aqueous NH3 and HCl cancel, leaving the overall reaction NH3(g) +

HCl(g) + aq → NH4Cl(aq).

Step 3 - By Hess's law, delta H = (-35.16) + (-72.41) + (-51.48) = -159.05 kJ

mol^-1.

Answer: about -159.08 kJ mol^-1 as printed in the book (the 0.03 difference is

rounding).

Q17. Calculate the heat of formation of ethyl alcohol from the following information: (i)

Heat of combustion of ethyl alcohol is -1367 kJ mol^-1; (ii) Heat of formation of

carbon dioxide is -393.7 kJ mol^-1; (iii) Heat of formation of water is -285.8 kJ

mol^-1.

Step 1 - Combustion equation: C2H5OH(l) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(l), delta H

= -1367 kJ mol^-1.

Step 2 - By Hess's law: delta H(combustion) = [2 x delta Hf(CO2) + 3 x delta

Hf(H2O)] - delta Hf(C2H5OH).

Step 3 - So delta Hf(C2H5OH) = [2 x (-393.7) + 3 x (-285.8)] - (-1367) = (-787.4 -

857.4) + 1367 = -277.8 kJ mol^-1.

Answer: about -278 kJ mol^-1. (Note: the book prints -278.4 kcal mol^-1; the value

matches in kJ mol^-1, so the printed unit kcal is an error.)

Q18. If the heats of combustion of C2H4, H2 and C2H6 are -337.2, -68.3 and -372.8

kcal respectively, then calculate the heat of the following reaction: C2H4(g) + H2(g)

-> C2H6(g).

Step 1 - By Hess's law: delta H(reaction) = [delta Hc(C2H4) + delta Hc(H2)] - delta

Hc(C2H6).

Step 2 - Substitute: delta H = (-337.2) + (-68.3) - (-372.8) = -405.5 + 372.8 = -32.7

kcal mol^-1.

Answer: -32.7 kcal mol^-1. (FLAG: the book prints -101 kcal mol^-1, which does not

follow from the printed data; -32.7 kcal mol^-1 is the value the data give, and it is

also the accepted hydrogenation enthalpy of ethene.)

Q19. Graphite and diamond are two forms of carbon. The enthalpy of combustion of

graphite at 25 degrees C is -393.51 kJ mol^-1 and that of diamond is -395.41 kJ

mol^-1. What is the enthalpy change of the process Graphite → Diamond at the

same temperature?

Step 1 - Combustion of graphite: C(graphite) + O2(g) → CO2(g), delta H = -393.51

kJ mol^-1.

Step 2 - Combustion of diamond: C(diamond) + O2(g) → CO2(g), delta H = -395.41

kJ mol^-1.

Step 3 - Graphite → Diamond = (graphite combustion) - (diamond combustion) =

(-393.51) - (-395.41) = +1.90 kJ mol^-1.

Answer: +1.91 kJ mol^-1 as printed in the book (rounding). The process is slightly

endothermic: diamond is higher in enthalpy than graphite.

Q20. What is the meaning of the term enthalpy of ionization?
If the heat of

neutralization of HCl and NaOH is -57.3 kJ mol^-1 and heat of neutralization of

CH3COOH with NaOH is -55.2 kJ mol^-1, calculate the enthalpy of ionization of

CH3COOH.

Step 1 - Enthalpy of ionization is the enthalpy change when one mole of a weak acid

(or base) ionizes in solution, e.g. CH3COOH → CH3COO- + H+.

Step 2 - For the weak acid, neutralization happens in two steps: ionization (delta H

= x) followed by H+ + OH- → H2O (delta H = -57.3 kJ mol^-1).

Step 3 - Total observed = x + (-57.3) = -55.2, so x = -55.2 + 57.3 = +2.1 kJ mol^-1.

Answer: 2.1 kJ mol^-1 (matches the book's printed answer). Ionization absorbs a

little heat, which is why weak-acid neutralization evolves slightly less heat.

Q21(a). Explain what is meant by: (i) Atomization energy (ii) Lattice energy. (b) Draw a

complete, fully labeled Born-Haber cycle for the formation of potassium bromide. (c)

Using the information in the table below, calculate the lattice energy of potassium

bromide: K(s) + 1/2 Br2(l) → KBr(s), -392 kJ mol^-1; K(s) → K(g), +90; K(g) ->

K+(g) + e, +420; 1/2 Br2(l) → Br(g), +112; Br(g) + e → Br-(g), -342 (all kJ mol^-1).

(a) (i) Atomization energy: the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is

converted into gaseous atoms, e.g. Na(s) → Na(g), +108 kJ mol^-1. (ii) Lattice

energy: the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic crystal is formed from its

gaseous ions, e.g. K+(g) + Br-(g) → KBr(s) (negative, energy released). (b) Labelled

drawing instruction: draw the Born-Haber cycle for KBr as a stepwise energy

diagram, labelled at each step: K(s) → K(g) (sublimation/atomization, +90 kJ

mol^-1); K(g) → K+(g) + e- (ionization energy, +420 kJ mol^-1); 1/2 Br2(l) → Br(g)

(atomization, +112 kJ mol^-1); Br(g) + e- → Br-(g) (electron affinity, -342 kJ

mol^-1); K+(g) + Br-(g) → KBr(s) (lattice energy, to be found); and the direct step

K(s) + 1/2 Br2(l) → KBr(s) (heat of formation, -392 kJ mol^-1). (c) By Hess's law:

-392 = 90 + 420 + 112 - 342 + (lattice energy), so lattice energy = -392 - 280 =

-672 kJ mol^-1.

mcqs.q: Using the Born-Haber data for NaCl (formation -411, atomization of Na +108, ionization of Na +496, atomization of Cl +121, electron affinity of Cl -349, all kJ/mol), the lattice energy of NaCl is:
50 cm3 of 1.0 M HCl is mixed with 50 cm3 of 1.0 M NaOH; the temperature rises from 21.0 to 27.5 C, density 1 g/cm3, specific heat 4.18 J/g/K. The enthalpy change per mole is about:
mcqs.why: Working: mass = 100 * 1 = 100 g; rise = 27.5 - 21.0 = 6.5 K; heat = 100 * 4.18 * 6.5 = 2717 J = 2.717 kJ; moles = 0.05; 2.717 / 0.05 = 54.34, and heat is evolved so the value is -54.3 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: 1.00 g of hydrazine is burned in a bomb calorimeter of heat capacity 5.5 kJ/K and the temperature rises by 3.51 K. The heat evolved is:
mcqs.why: Working: heat evolved = heat capacity * temperature rise = 5.5 * 3.51 = 19.305, which rounds to 19.3 kJ.

mcqs.q: For hydrazine, N2H4, 1.00 g burns and evolves 19.3 kJ. The heat of combustion of 1 mole of N2H4 is about:
mcqs.why: Working: molar mass = 2 * 14 + 4 * 1 = 32 g/mol; moles in 1.00 g = 1 / 32 = 0.03125 mol; 19.3 / 0.03125 = 617.6, and heat is evolved so it is about -618 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: 1.80 g of octane is burned in a calorimeter of heat capacity 11.66 kJ/K; the temperature rises from 21.36 to 28.78 C. The heat of combustion of 1 mole of octane (molar mass 114 g/mol) is about:
mcqs.why: Working: rise = 28.78 - 21.36 = 7.42 K; heat for 1.80 g = 11.66 * 7.42 = 86.5172 kJ; moles = 1.8 / 114 = 0.01579 mol; 86.51 / 0.01579 = 5478.8, negative because heat is evolved.

mcqs.q: By Hess's law, the enthalpy change for forming aqueous NH4Cl from NH3(g) and HCl(g), given steps -35.16, -72.41 and -51.48 kJ/mol, is:
mcqs.why: Working: by Hess's law the steps add: -35.16 + -72.41 = -107.57; -107.57 + -51.48 = -159.05 kJ/mol for the overall process.

mcqs.q: The heat of formation of ethyl alcohol, given its heat of combustion -1367 kJ/mol, heat of formation of CO2 -393.7 kJ/mol and of H2O -285.8 kJ/mol, is:
The enthalpy of combustion of graphite is -393.51 kJ/mol and of diamond is -395.41 kJ/mol. The enthalpy change for graphite -> diamond is:
mcqs.why: Working: graphite -> diamond = combustion of graphite minus combustion of diamond = -393.51 - -395.41 = 1.90, so the change is +1.90 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: The heat of neutralization of HCl with NaOH is -57.3 kJ/mol and of CH3COOH with NaOH is -55.2 kJ/mol. The enthalpy of ionization of CH3COOH is:
mcqs.why: Working: ionization + neutralization of the ions = observed value, so x + -57.3 = -55.2; x = -55.2 + 57.3 = 2.1, giving +2.1 kJ/mol.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • Law of mass action states that the rate at which a reaction proceeds, is directly proportional to the product of the active masses of the reactants.
  • In an exothermic reversible reaction, a decrease in temperature will shift the equilibrium towards the forward direction.
  • The equilibrium constant for the reaction 2O3 ⇌ 3O2 is 10^55 at 25 degrees C, it tells that ozone is unstable at room temperature.
  • In a gas phase reaction, if the number of moles of reactants are equal to the number of moles of the products, Kc of the reaction is equal to the Kp.
  • Buffer solution is prepared by mixing together a weak base and its salt with a strong acid or a weak acid and its salt with a strong base.

mcqs.q: The law of mass action states that the rate at which a reaction proceeds is directly proportional to:
options: The product of the active masses of the reactants
The product of the active masses of the products
The sum of the active masses of the reactants
The equilibrium constant of the reaction
mcqs.why: The notes state the law of mass action exactly this way: the rate is directly proportional to the product of the active masses of the reactants.

mcqs.q: In an exothermic reversible reaction, a decrease in temperature will shift the equilibrium towards:
options: The side with more moles of gas
mcqs.why: The notes state that in an exothermic reversible reaction a decrease in temperature shifts the equilibrium towards the forward direction.

mcqs.q: The equilibrium constant for 2O3 <-> 3O2 is 10^55 at 25 C. This tells us that:
options: Ozone is very stable at room temperature
Ozone and oxygen are present in equal amounts
Ozone is unstable at room temperature
The reaction hardly proceeds at all
mcqs.why: The notes link the huge value 10^55 for 2O3 <-> 3O2 directly to ozone being unstable at room temperature.

mcqs.q: In a gas phase reaction, if the number of moles of reactants is equal to the number of moles of products, then:
options: Kc and Kp are both zero
Kc of the reaction is equal to Kp
mcqs.why: The notes state that when the moles of reactants equal the moles of products in a gas phase reaction, Kc is equal to Kp.

mcqs.q: A buffer solution can be prepared by mixing together:
options: A strong acid and its salt with a strong base
A weak acid and its salt with a strong base
A weak acid and a strong base only
A strong acid and a strong base
mcqs.why: The notes give this combination for a buffer: a weak acid and its salt with a strong base, such as an acid with its sodium salt.

mcqs.q: A buffer solution can also be prepared by mixing together:
options: A strong base and its salt with a strong acid
A weak base and a strong acid only
A weak base and its salt with a strong acid
mcqs.why: The notes give the second buffer combination as a weak base and its salt with a strong acid.

mcqs.q: For N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3, at equilibrium:
options: Forward rate is greater than reverse rate
Reverse rate is greater than forward rate
mcqs.why: The notes show the Haber equilibrium with forward and reverse reactions, and at equilibrium the forward rate equals the reverse rate.

mcqs.q: A very large equilibrium constant, such as 10^55 for the ozone reaction, indicates that at equilibrium:
options: The reactants are largely converted to products
The products are largely converted back to reactants
Reactants and products must be equal in amount
mcqs.why: The notes use the 10^55 value to show ozone is unstable at room temperature, meaning the equilibrium lies far towards oxygen, the product.

mcqs.q: Lowering the temperature of an exothermic reversible reaction at equilibrium will:
options: Decrease the amount of products formed
Increase the amount of products formed
mcqs.why: The notes state that a decrease in temperature shifts an exothermic equilibrium in the forward direction, so more products are formed.

mcqs.q: In the law of mass action, the rate of a reaction depends on the active masses of the:
mcqs.why: The law of mass action as stated in the notes makes the rate directly proportional to the product of the active masses of the reactants.

lessons.notes_html:

A. 3.0
✓ B. 2.7
C. 2.0

✓ B. 1.41 x 10^-5 mol dm^-3
C. 1.0 x 10^-10 mol dm^-3

Q1(v). An excess of aqueous silver nitrate is added to aqueous barium chloride and
precipitate is removed by filtration. What are the main ions in the filtrate?
A. Ag+ and NO3- only
✓ B. Ag+ and Ba2+ and NO3-

mcqs.q: For which system does the equilibrium constant Kc have units of (concentration)^-1?
mcqs.why: For 2NO2 <-> N2O4 the change in moles is 1 - 2 = -1, so Kc carries units of (concentration)^-1, as in the lesson question.

mcqs.q: For 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <-> 2SO3(g), delta H = -188.3 kJ/mol, which statement is correct?
options: The value of Kp falls with increasing pressure
The value of Kp falls with a rise in temperature
Adding V2O5 catalyst increases the equilibrium yield of sulphur trioxide
The value of Kp is equal to Kc
mcqs.why: The reaction is exothermic, and the lesson marks as correct that Kp falls with a rise in temperature for this equilibrium.

mcqs.q: The pH of a 10^-3 mol/dm3 aqueous solution of H2SO4 is about:
mcqs.why: Working: sulphuric acid supplies about 2 * 0.001 = 0.002 mol/dm3 of H+ ions; pH = -log(0.002) = 2.70, so the pH is about 2.7.

mcqs.q: The solubility product of AgCl is 2.0 x 10^-10 mol2/dm6. The maximum concentration of Ag+ ions in the solution is:
mcqs.why: Working: [Ag+] = [Cl-], so Ksp = [Ag+] * [Ag+]; 1.41 * 1.41 = 1.9881, about 2.0, so the square root of 2.0 x 10^-10 is 1.41 x 10^-5 mol/dm3.

mcqs.q: An excess of aqueous silver nitrate is added to aqueous barium chloride and the precipitate is removed by filtration. The main ions in the filtrate are:
mcqs.why: Chloride is removed as AgCl precipitate, while the excess Ag+, the Ba2+ and the NO3- ions remain in the filtrate, as in the lesson question.

mcqs.q: For the ammonia equilibrium N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3, the units of Kc are:
mcqs.why: Working: change in moles = 2 - 4 = -2, so Kc for this reaction, listed in the lesson, carries units of (concentration)^-2.

mcqs.q: For H2 + I2 <-> 2HI, listed in the lesson, Kc is unitless because:
options: The moles of gas are the same on both sides, 2 and 2
mcqs.why: Working: change in moles = 2 - 2 = 0, so all concentration units cancel and Kc for H2 + I2 <-> 2HI has no units.

mcqs.q: In the SO2/SO3 equilibrium of the lesson, adding the V2O5 catalyst will:
options: Not increase the equilibrium yield of SO3
Increase the equilibrium yield of SO3
Shift the equilibrium to the right
mcqs.why: The lesson lists increased equilibrium yield from V2O5 as an incorrect statement; a catalyst speeds up reaching equilibrium but does not raise the yield.

mcqs.q: For 2SO2 + O2 <-> 2SO3, Kp is not equal to Kc because:
options: The reaction uses a V2O5 catalyst
The reaction is carried out in the gas phase
The moles of gas change, from 3 moles to 2 moles
SO3 is a product of the reaction
mcqs.why: Working: change in moles = 2 - 3 = -1, which is not zero, so Kp and Kc differ for this equilibrium in the lesson.

mcqs.q: The value delta H = -188.3 kJ/mol for 2SO2 + O2 <-> 2SO3 shows that the forward reaction is:
mcqs.why: A negative enthalpy change means heat is released in the forward direction, so the forward reaction is exothermic, as the lesson data show.

lessons.title: True or False
lessons.notes_html:
3(i). When a reversible reaction attains equilibrium both reactants and products are present in a reaction mixture. True

3(ii). The Kc of the reaction A + B ⇌ C + D is given by Kc = [C][D]/[A][B], therefore it is assumed that [A] = [B] = [C] = [D]. False

3(iii). A catalyst is a compound which increases the speed of the reaction and consequently increases the yield of the product. False

3(iv). Ionic product Kw of pure water at 25 degrees C is 10^-14 mol^2 dm^-6 and is represented by an expression Kw = [H+][OH-] = 10^-14 mol^2 dm^-6. True

mcqs.q: Judge the statement: When a reversible reaction attains equilibrium, both reactants and products are present in the reaction mixture.
mcqs.why: The lesson marks this True: at equilibrium a reversible reaction mixture contains both reactants and products.

mcqs.q: Judge the statement: Kc = [C][D]/[A][B] for A + B <-> C + D, therefore it is assumed that [A] = [B] = [C] = [D].
mcqs.why: The lesson marks this False: writing the Kc ratio does not assume that all four concentrations are equal to each other.

mcqs.q: Judge the statement: A catalyst increases the speed of the reaction and consequently increases the yield of the product.
mcqs.why: The lesson marks this False: although a catalyst increases speed, it does not consequently increase the equilibrium yield.

mcqs.q: Judge the statement: The ionic product Kw of pure water at 25 C is 10^-14 mol2/dm6, given by Kw = [H+][OH-].
mcqs.why: The lesson marks this True and gives the expression Kw = [H+][OH-] = 10^-14 mol2/dm6 at 25 C for pure water.

mcqs.why: The lesson marks this False: AgCl is sparingly soluble, so its solution does not produce an excess of Ag+ and Cl- ions.

mcqs.q: The ionic product of water at 25 C, as given in the lesson, equals:
mcqs.why: Working: in pure water [H+] = [OH-] = 0.0000001 mol/dm3, and 0.0000001 * 0.0000001 = 0.00000000000001 = 1 x 10^-14, matching Kw in the lesson.

lessons.title: Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q3(ii). reason - Kc = [C][D]/[A][B], therefore it is assumed that [A] = [B] = [C] = [D].

False. The Kc expression is a ratio of concentrations; it holds whatever the individual

concentrations are. It never assumes [A] = [B] = [C] = [D]; in general the four

concentrations are all different.

Q3(iii). reason - A catalyst increases the speed of the reaction and consequently

increases the yield of the product.

False. A catalyst increases the speed of both the forward and the reverse reactions

equally, so equilibrium is reached faster, but the equilibrium position and the yield

are unchanged.

Q3(v). reason - AgCl solution produces excess of Ag+ and Cl- ions.

False. AgCl is sparingly soluble, so only a very small, equal amount of Ag+ and Cl-

ions goes into solution (about 1.4 x 10^-5 mol dm^-3). There is no 'excess' of ions;

most of the solid stays undissolved.

Q4(a). Explain the terms 'reversible reaction' and 'state of equilibrium'.

A reversible reaction is one that can proceed in both directions: reactants form

products and products re-form reactants, e.g. N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3. The state of

equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse reactions proceed at the same

rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products stop changing, although both

reactions continue.

Q4(b). Define and explain the Law of mass action and derive the expression for the

equilibrium constant (Kc).

Law of mass action: the rate at which a reaction proceeds is directly proportional to

the product of the active masses (molar concentrations) of the reactants. For aA +

bB ⇌ cC + dD, forward rate = kf [A]^a [B]^b and reverse rate = kr [C]^c [D]^d. At

equilibrium the two rates are equal, so kf/kr = [C]^c [D]^d / [A]^a [B]^b = Kc, the

equilibrium constant.

Q4(c). Write Kc for: (i) Sn2+ + 2Fe3+ ⇌ Sn4+ + 2Fe2+ (ii) Ag+ + Fe2+ ⇌ Fe3+ +

Ag(s) (iii) N2 + O2 ⇌ 2NO (iv) 4NH3 + 5O2 ⇌ 4NO + 6H2O (v) PCl5 ⇌ PCl3 + Cl2.

(i) Sn2+(aq) + 2Fe3+(aq) ⇌ Sn4+(aq) + 2Fe2+(aq): Kc = [Sn4+][Fe2+]^2 /

([Sn2+][Fe3+]^2). (ii) Ag+(aq) + Fe2+(aq) ⇌ Fe3+(aq) + Ag(s): Kc = [Fe3+] /

([Ag+][Fe2+]) (pure solid Ag is omitted). (iii) N2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2NO(g): Kc = [NO]^2

/ ([N2][O2]). (iv) 4NH3(g) + 5O2(g) ⇌ 4NO(g) + 6H2O(g): Kc = [NO]^4 [H2O]^6 /

([NH3]^4 [O2]^5). (v) PCl5(g) ⇌ PCl3(g) + Cl2(g): Kc = [PCl3][Cl2] / [PCl5].

Q5(a). Reversible reactions attain the position of equilibrium which is dynamic in

nature and not static. Explain it.

At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so

molecules keep reacting in both directions while the overall concentrations stay

constant. It is therefore dynamic (reactions still running), not static (reactions

stopped). A static state would mean no reaction at all.

Q5(b). Why do the rates of forward reactions slow down when a reversible reaction

approaches the equilibrium stage?

As the reaction approaches equilibrium, reactants are used up, so their

concentrations fall and the forward rate (which depends on reactant concentrations)

falls. At the same time products build up, so the reverse rate rises. When the two

rates become equal, equilibrium is reached.

Q6. When a graph is plotted between time on x-axis and concentrations of reactants

and products on y-axis for a reversible reaction, the curves become parallel to time

axis at a certain stage. (a) At what stage do the curves become parallel? (b) Before

the curves become parallel, the steepness of curves falls? Give reasons. (c) The rate

of decrease of concentrations of reactants and rate of increase of concentrations of

products may or may not be equal, for various types of reactions, before the

equilibrium time. Explain it.

(a) The curves become parallel at the equilibrium stage, when the concentrations

stop changing. (b) Before equilibrium, the steepness falls because the net rate of

change of concentration falls: as reactants are consumed the forward rate

decreases, and as products accumulate the reverse rate increases, so the net

change per unit time gets smaller until it reaches zero. (c) The rates of decrease of

reactants and increase of products need not be equal before equilibrium, because

they are linked by the stoichiometry: e.g. in N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, hydrogen is

consumed three times as fast as nitrogen. Only the rates divided by their

stoichiometric coefficients are equal.

Q7(a). Write down the relationship of different types of equilibrium constants, i.e. Kc

and Kp, for the general reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD. (b) Decide the comparative

magnitudes of Kc and Kp for: (i) Ammonia synthesis (ii) Dissociation of PCl5.

(a) For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, Kp = Kc (RT)^(delta n), where delta n = (c + d) - (a +

b), R is the gas constant and T the absolute temperature. (b) Ammonia synthesis,

N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3: delta n = 2 - 4 = -2, so Kp = Kc (RT)^-2, and Kp is smaller than

Kc. Dissociation of PCl5, PCl5 ⇌ PCl3 + Cl2: delta n = 2 - 1 = +1, so Kp = Kc (RT),

and Kp is larger than Kc.

Q8(a). Write down Kc for the following reversible reactions, supposing the volume of

reaction mixture in all cases is V dm^3 at equilibrium stage: (i) CH3COOH +

CH3CH2OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O (ii) H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI (iii) 2HI ⇌ H2 + I2 (iv) PCl5 ⇌

PCl3 + Cl2 (v) N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3.

With volume V dm^3 and equilibrium amounts in moles, concentrations are

moles/V. (i) CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O: Kc =

[ester][water]/([acid][alcohol]); the V terms cancel (delta n = 0), so Kc = (moles of

ester x moles of water)/(moles of acid x moles of alcohol). (ii) H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI: Kc =

[HI]^2/([H2][I2]), V cancels. (iii) 2HI ⇌ H2 + I2: Kc = [H2][I2]/[HI]^2, V cancels. (iv)

PCl5 ⇌ PCl3 + Cl2: Kc = [PCl3][Cl2]/[PCl5] = (moles PCl3 x moles Cl2)/(moles PCl5 x

V). (v) N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3: Kc = [NH3]^2/([N2][H2]^3) = (moles NH3)^2 x V^2 /

(moles N2 x (moles H2)^3).

Q8(b). How do you explain that some of the reactions mentioned above are affected

by change of volume at equilibrium stage?

Reactions with delta n = 0 (cases (i), (ii), (iii)) are not affected by a change of

volume, because changing the volume changes all concentrations by the same

factor and the ratio cancels. Reactions with delta n not zero (cases (iv) and (v)) are

affected: increasing the volume (lowering the pressure) shifts equilibrium towards

the side with more moles of gas, and decreasing the volume shifts it towards fewer

moles.

Q9. Explain the following two applications of equilibrium constant. Give examples: (i)

Direction of reaction (ii) Extent of reaction.

(i) Direction of reaction: comparing the reaction quotient Qc with Kc tells which way

the reaction will go: if Qc < Kc the reaction goes forward; if Qc > Kc it goes

backward; if Qc = Kc it is at equilibrium. Example: for the HI equilibrium, adding HI

makes Qc < Kc, so more HI dissociates. (ii) Extent of reaction: the size of Kc tells

how far the reaction goes: a very large Kc (e.g. 10^55 for ozone conversion) means

the reaction goes almost to completion; a very small Kc means it hardly proceeds; a

Kc near 1 means appreciable amounts of reactants and products coexist at

equilibrium.

Q10. Explain with reasons: (a) The change of volume disturbs the equilibrium position

for some gaseous phase reactions but not the equilibrium constant. (b) The change

of temperature disturbs both the equilibrium position and the equilibrium constant

of a reaction. (c) The solubility of glucose in water is increased by increasing the

temperature.

(a) Changing the volume changes the concentrations (and partial pressures), so by

Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium position shifts to counteract the change, but

only for reactions with delta n not zero. The equilibrium constant itself does not

change, because Kc depends only on temperature. (b) Changing the temperature

changes the value of Kc itself (for an exothermic reaction Kc decreases with rising

temperature; for an endothermic reaction it increases), and therefore also shifts the

equilibrium position: temperature is the only factor that changes both. (c) Dissolving

glucose in water is endothermic (heat is absorbed to break the solid lattice), so

raising the temperature supplies that heat and shifts the dissolution equilibrium

forward: solubility increases with temperature.

Q11(a). What is ionic product of water? How does this value vary with temperature?
Is

it true that its value increases 75 times when the temperature of water is increased

from 0 degrees C to 100 degrees C? (b) What is the justification for the increase of

ionic product with temperature? (c) How would you prove that at 25 degrees C, 1

dm^3 of water contains 10^-7 moles of H3O+ and 10^-7 moles of OH-? (Note on

(a): the 75-times figure is answered from the standard Kw values, 0.11 x 10^-14 at

0 degrees C and 51 x 10^-14 at 100 degrees C, which give about a 460-fold rise,

not 75-fold.)

(a) The ionic product of water is Kw = [H+][OH-] = 1.0 x 10^-14 mol^2 dm^-6 at

25 degrees C. It increases with temperature, because the ionization of water is

endothermic, so heating shifts H2O ⇌ H+ + OH- forward. It is not true that it

increases 75 times from 0 to 100 degrees C as a fixed rule: Kw rises from about 0.11

x 10^-14 at 0 degrees C to about 51 x 10^-14 at 100 degrees C, roughly a 460-fold

rise; the '75 times' figure in the question is not the book's value for this range. (b)

Kw increases with temperature because water ionization absorbs heat

(endothermic); by Le Chatelier's principle, heating favours the forward (ionization)

direction, producing more H+ and OH-. (c) In pure water [H+] = [OH-], so Kw =

[H+]^2 = 10^-14, giving [H+] = 10^-7 mol dm^-3. In 1 dm^3 of water there is

therefore 10^-7 mol of H3O+ and 10^-7 mol of OH-.

Q12(a). Define pH and pOH. How are they related with pKw?
(b) What happens to the

acidic and basic properties of aqueous solutions when pH varies from zero to 14? (c)

Is it true that the sum of pKa and pKb is always equal to 14 at all temperatures for

any acid? If not, why? (c) No: pKa + pKb = pKw only for a conjugate acid-base pair,

and pKw itself changes with temperature (14.00 only at 25 degrees C), so the sum

equals 14 only at 25 degrees C; at other temperatures it equals the pKw at that

temperature.

pH = -log [H+], the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration; pOH =

-log [OH-]. Since Kw = [H+][OH-] = 10^-14 at 25 degrees C, taking negative

logarithms gives pH + pOH = pKw = 14 at 25 degrees C. As pH goes from 0 to 14,

the solution goes from strongly acidic (high [H+], e.g. pH 0) through neutral (pH 7,

[H+] = [OH-]) to strongly basic (low [H+], high [OH-], e.g. pH 14): acidity decreases

and basicity increases continuously with pH.

Q13(a). What is Lowry-Bronsted idea of acids and bases?
Explain conjugate acid and

bases.

An acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor (Lowry-Bronsted). A

conjugate acid is formed when a base accepts a proton (e.g. NH3 + H+ → NH4+),

and a conjugate base is formed when an acid loses a proton (e.g. CH3COOH ->

CH3COO- + H+). Every acid has a conjugate base and every base has a conjugate

acid; a strong acid has a weak conjugate base and vice versa.

Q13(b). Acetic acid dissolves in water and gives proton to water, but when dissolved

in H2SO4, it accepts protons. Discuss the role of acetic acid in both cases.

Acetic acid is amphiprotic: in water, which is a stronger base than the acetate ion,

acetic acid donates a proton (CH3COOH + H2O ⇌ CH3COO- + H3O+) and acts as an

acid. In concentrated sulphuric acid, which is a much stronger acid, acetic acid

accepts a proton (CH3COOH + H2SO4 ⇌ CH3COOH2+ + HSO4-) and acts as a base.

Whether it donates or accepts depends on the relative strength of the other

acid-base system present.

Q14. In the equilibrium PCl5(g) ⇌ PCl3(g) + Cl2(g), delta H = 90 kJ mol^-1, what is the

effect on (a) the position of equilibrium (b) equilibrium constant, if (i) temperature is

increased (ii) volume of the container is decreased (iii) catalyst is added (iv) chlorine

is added? Explain your answer.

PCl5(g) ⇌ PCl3(g) + Cl2(g), delta H = +90 kJ mol^-1 (endothermic dissociation). (i)

Temperature increased: equilibrium shifts forward (endothermic direction), so the

position moves right and Kc increases. (ii) Volume decreased (pressure increased):

equilibrium shifts towards fewer moles of gas, i.e. left, towards PCl5; Kc is

unchanged (temperature unchanged). (iii) Catalyst added: no effect on position or

on Kc; equilibrium is reached faster. (iv) Chlorine added: equilibrium shifts left,

towards PCl5, to consume the added Cl2; Kc is unchanged. Summary: position: (i)

right, (ii) left, (iii) no change, (iv) left; Kc: (i) increases, (ii)-(iv) unchanged.

Q15. Synthesis of ammonia by Haber's process is an exothermic reaction: N2(g) +

3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), delta H = -92.46 kJ. (a) What should be the possible effect of

change of temperature at equilibrium stage? (b) How does the change of pressure

or volume shift the equilibrium position of this reaction? (c) What is the role of the

catalyst in this reaction? (d) What happens to equilibrium position if NH3 is removed

from the reaction vessel from time to time?

(a) Temperature: the reaction is exothermic, so raising the temperature shifts

equilibrium left (towards N2 and H2) and lowers the yield of ammonia; lowering the

temperature raises the yield but slows the reaction. (b) Pressure/volume: the

reaction goes from 4 moles of gas to 2, so increasing the pressure (decreasing the

volume) shifts equilibrium right and increases the ammonia yield; decreasing the

pressure shifts it left. (c) Catalyst: iron catalyst speeds up both directions equally, so

it does not change the yield, but it lets equilibrium be reached in a practical time.

(d) Removing NH3: the equilibrium shifts right to replace the ammonia removed, so

more ammonia is formed; removing product continuously drives the reaction

forward.

Q16. Sulphuric acid is produced by the burning of SO2 to SO3 through an exothermic

reversible process. (a) Write the balanced reversible reaction. (b) What is the effect

of pressure change on this reaction? (c) Reaction is exothermic but still the

temperature of 400-500 degrees C is required to increase the yield of SO3. Give

reasons.

(a) Balanced reversible reaction: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g). (b) Pressure: the

reaction goes from 3 moles of gas to 2, so increasing the pressure shifts equilibrium

right, increasing the SO3 yield; decreasing the pressure shifts it left. (c) Although

the reaction is exothermic and low temperature would favour SO3, at low

temperature the reaction is too slow to be useful. A temperature of 400-500

degrees C is a compromise: high enough for a practical rate (with the V2O5

catalyst) while still giving a good yield. Lower temperature would give higher

equilibrium yield but an uneconomically slow reaction.

Q17(a). What are buffer solutions? Why do we need them in daily life?
(b) How does

the mixture of sodium acetate and acetic acid give us the acidic buffer? (c) Explain

that a mixture of NH4OH and NH4Cl gives us the basic buffer. (d) How do you justify

that the greater quantity of CH3COONa in acetic acid decreases the dissociating

power of acetic acid and so the pH increases? (e) Explain the term buffer capacity.

(a) Buffer solutions resist changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are

added. We need them in daily life because many processes need a steady pH: blood

stays near pH 7.4; medicines, foods, and laboratory reactions are kept at a fixed pH.

(b) Acidic buffer: acetic acid (weak acid) with sodium acetate (its salt) gives an

acidic buffer: added H+ is removed by acetate ions (CH3COO- + H+ → CH3COOH)

and added OH- is removed by the acid (CH3COOH + OH- → CH3COO- + H2O), so

the pH stays near the pKa of acetic acid (4.74). (c) Basic buffer: ammonium

hydroxide (weak base) with ammonium chloride (its salt) gives a basic buffer: added

H+ is removed by NH4OH (NH4OH + H+ → NH4+ + H2O) and added OH- is

removed by NH4+ (NH4+ + OH- → NH4OH + H2O), so the pH stays near 9.25. (d)

Adding more sodium acetate (common ion CH3COO-) suppresses the dissociation of

acetic acid by the common ion effect, so less H+ is produced and the pH rises. (e)

Buffer capacity is the amount of acid or base a buffer can absorb without a large

change in pH; it is greatest when the buffer components are concentrated and

present in roughly equal amounts.

Q18(a). What is the solubility product?
Derive the solubility product expression for

sparingly soluble compounds AgCl, Ag2CrO4 and PbCl2. (b) How do you determine

the solubility product of a substance when its solubility is provided in grams/100 g

of water? (c) How do you calculate the solubility of a substance from the value of

solubility product?

(a) Solubility product, Ksp, is the product of the ion concentrations in a saturated

solution of a sparingly soluble salt, each raised to its stoichiometric power. AgCl(s) ⇌

Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq): Ksp = [Ag+][Cl-]. Ag2CrO4(s) ⇌ 2Ag+(aq) + CrO4^2-(aq): Ksp =

[Ag+]^2 [CrO4^2-]. PbCl2(s) ⇌ Pb2+(aq) + 2Cl-(aq): Ksp = [Pb2+][Cl-]^2. (b) If

solubility is given in grams per 100 g of water, convert to moles per dm^3: moles =

(grams per 100 g water x 10) / molar mass, giving grams per dm^3 (taking 100 g

water as about 100 cm^3, i.e. 1 dm^3 holds 10 x 100 g), then divide by the molar

mass to get mol dm^-3. (c) From Ksp, find the molar solubility S from the Ksp

expression: for a 1:1 salt Ksp = S^2, so S = sqrt(Ksp); for Ag2CrO4, Ksp = 4S^3, so

S = (Ksp/4)^(1/3); for PbCl2, Ksp = 4S^3 likewise.

mcqs.q: Write Kc for PCl5(g) <-> PCl3(g) + Cl2(g):
mcqs.why: The notes give Kc for the PCl5 dissociation as the product concentrations over the reactant concentration: [PCl3][Cl2]/[PCl5].

mcqs.q: Write Kc for Ag+(aq) + Fe2+(aq) <-> Fe3+(aq) + Ag(s):
mcqs.why: The notes omit the pure solid Ag from the expression, giving Kc = [Fe3+]/([Ag+][Fe2+]) for this equilibrium.

mcqs.q: For ammonia synthesis, N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3, how do Kc and Kp compare?
mcqs.why: Working: delta n = 2 - 4 = -2, so Kp = Kc(RT)^-2 with a negative power, which makes Kp smaller than Kc, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: For the dissociation of PCl5, PCl5 <-> PCl3 + Cl2, how do Kc and Kp compare?
mcqs.why: Working: delta n = 2 - 1 = 1, so Kp = Kc(RT)^1 with a positive power, which makes Kp larger than Kc, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: If the reaction quotient Qc is less than Kc for a reaction, the reaction will proceed:
options: In neither direction, it is at equilibrium
Only if a catalyst is added
mcqs.why: The notes state that comparing Qc with Kc gives the direction: if Qc < Kc the reaction goes forward towards equilibrium.

mcqs.q: Which factor changes BOTH the equilibrium position and the equilibrium constant of a reaction?
mcqs.why: The notes explain that temperature is the factor that changes the value of Kc itself and therefore also shifts the equilibrium position.

mcqs.q: A solution has pH = 5 at 25 C. Its pOH is:
mcqs.why: Working: at 25 C, pH + pOH = pKw = 14, so pOH = 14 - 5 = 9, using the relation pH + pOH = 14 from the notes.

mcqs.q: In the acidic buffer of acetic acid and sodium acetate, added H+ ions are removed mainly by:
mcqs.why: The notes give the buffer action as CH3COO- + H+ -> CH3COOH, so acetate ions remove the added H+ and the pH stays nearly steady.

mcqs.q: The solubility product expression for Ag2CrO4(s) <-> 2Ag+(aq) + CrO4^2-(aq) is:
mcqs.why: The notes derive Ksp = [Ag+]^2 [CrO4^2-] because two Ag+ ions are produced for each CrO4^2- ion in the dissociation.

mcqs.q: In Haber's process, N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3, what happens if NH3 is removed from the vessel from time to time?
options: The equilibrium shifts left and less ammonia is formed
The equilibrium shifts right and more ammonia is formed
mcqs.why: The notes state that removing NH3 shifts the equilibrium to the right to replace the ammonia removed, so more ammonia is formed.

lessons.title: Numerical Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q19. Kc value for the following reaction is 0.016 at 520 degrees C: 2HI(g) ⇌ H2(g) +

I2(g). Equilibrium mixture contains [HI] = 0.08 M, [H2] = 0.01 M, [I2] = 0.01 M. To

this mixture more HI is added so that its new concentration is 0.096 M. What will be

the concentration of [HI], [H2] and [I2] when equilibrium is re-established?

Step 1 - Check the first equilibrium: Kc = [H2][I2]/[HI]^2 = (0.01 x 0.01)/(0.08)^2 =

0.0156, about 0.016, as given.

Step 2 - After adding HI, [HI] = 0.096 M, [H2] = [I2] = 0.01 M. Let x mol dm^-3 of HI

dissociate to re-establish equilibrium: 2HI → H2 + I2, so [HI] = 0.096 - 2x, [H2] =

[I2] = 0.01 + x.

Step 3 - Kc = (0.01 + x)^2 / (0.096 - 2x)^2 = 0.016. Taking square roots: (0.01 +

x)/(0.096 - 2x) = 0.1265.

Step 4 - Solve: 0.01 + x = 0.01214 - 0.253x, so 1.253x = 0.00214, x = 0.00171 mol

dm^-3.

Step 5 - New concentrations: [HI] = 0.096 - 2(0.00171) = 0.0926 mol dm^-3; [H2] =

[I2] = 0.01 + 0.00171 = 0.01171 mol dm^-3.

Answer: [HI] = 0.0926 mol dm^-3, [H2] = 0.01168 mol dm^-3, [I2] = 0.01168 mol

dm^-3 (matches the book's printed answers).

Q20. The equilibrium constant for the reaction between acetic acid and ethyl alcohol

is 4.0. A mixture of 3 moles of acetic acid and one mole of C2H5OH is allowed to

come to equilibrium. Calculate the amount of ethyl acetate at equilibrium stage in

number of moles and grams. Also calculate the masses of reactants left behind.

Step 1 - Reaction: CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O. Let x moles react:

at equilibrium, acid = 3 - x, alcohol = 1 - x, ester = x, water = x moles.

Step 2 - Kc = x^2 / ((3 - x)(1 - x)) = 4.0, so x^2 = 4(3 - 4x + x^2) = 12 - 16x +

4x^2.

Step 3 - Rearranged: 3x^2 - 16x + 12 = 0. Solving: x = (16 - sqrt(256 - 144))/6 =

(16 - 10.58)/6 = 0.903 mol (the other root, 4.43, is impossible since only 1 mol of

alcohol is present).

Step 4 - Ethyl acetate: 0.903 mol x 88 g mol^-1 = 79.5 g.

Step 5 - Reactants left: acetic acid = 3 - 0.903 = 2.097 mol x 60 g mol^-1 = 126 g;

ethyl alcohol = 1 - 0.903 = 0.097 mol x 46 g mol^-1 = 4.5 g.

Answer: ethyl acetate 0.90 mol, 79.5 g; acetic acid left 126 g; ethyl alcohol left 4.6 g

(matches the book's printed answers).

Q21. Study the equilibrium H2O(g) + CO(g) ⇌ H2(g) + CO2(g). (a) Write an expression

of Kp. (b) When 1.00 mole of steam and 1.00 mole of carbon monoxide are allowed

to reach equilibrium, 33.3% of the equilibrium mixture is hydrogen. Calculate the

value of Kp. State the units of Kp.

Step 1 - Kp = (pH2 x pCO2) / (pH2O x pCO).

Step 2 - Let x moles react: at equilibrium, H2O = 1 - x, CO = 1 - x, H2 = x, CO2 = x.

Total moles = 2 at all stages (2 moles → 2 moles).

Step 3 - Hydrogen is 33.3% of the mixture: x/2 = 0.333, so x = 0.667 mol.

Equilibrium moles: H2O = CO = 0.333, H2 = CO2 = 0.667.

Step 4 - Mole fractions are proportional to partial pressures, so Kp = (0.667 x

0.667)/(0.333 x 0.333) = 4.0.

Answer: Kp = 4, and Kp has no units, because the number of moles of gas is the

same on both sides (delta n = 0), so all pressure units cancel (matches the book's

printed answer).

Q22. Calculate the pH of: (a) 10^-4 mol dm^-3 of HCl (b) 10^-4 mol dm^-3 of

Ba(OH)2 (c) 1.0 mol dm^-3 of H2X, which is only 50% dissociated (d) 1.0 mol

dm^-3 of NH4OH which is 1% dissociated.

Step 1 - (a) HCl is a strong acid: [H+] = 10^-4 mol dm^-3, so pH = -log(10^-4) = 4.

Step 2 - (b) Ba(OH)2 gives two OH- per formula unit: [OH-] = 2 x 10^-4 mol dm^-3.

pOH = -log(2 x 10^-4) = 3.70, so pH = 14 - 3.70 = 10.3.

Step 3 - (c) H2X 50% dissociated (first dissociation counted): [H+] = 0.50 x 1.0 =

0.50 mol dm^-3, so pH = -log(0.50) = 0.30, about zero as printed.

Step 4 - (d) NH4OH 1% dissociated: [OH-] = 0.01 x 1.0 = 0.01 mol dm^-3, so pOH =

2 and pH = 14 - 2 = 12.

Answer: (a) 4 (b) 10.3 (c) zero (d) 12 (matches the book's printed answers).

Q23(a). Benzoic acid, C6H5COOH, is a weak mono-basic acid (Ka = 6.4 x 10^-5 mol

dm^-3). What is the pH of a solution containing 7.2 g of sodium benzoate in one

dm^3 of 0.02 mol dm^-3 benzoic acid?

Step 1 - Molar mass of sodium benzoate C6H5COONa = 144 g mol^-1, so 7.2 g =

7.2/144 = 0.05 mol in 1 dm^3, i.e. [salt] = 0.05 mol dm^-3. [acid] = 0.02 mol

dm^-3.

Step 2 - pKa = -log(6.4 x 10^-5) = 4.19.

Step 3 - Henderson equation: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]) = 4.19 + log(0.05/0.02)

= 4.19 + log(2.5) = 4.19 + 0.40 = 4.59.

Answer: pH = 4.59 (matches the book's printed answer).

Q23(b). A buffer solution has been prepared by mixing 0.2 M CH3COONa and 0.5 M

CH3COOH in 1 dm^3 of solution. Calculate the pH of solution. pKa of acid = 4.74 at

25 degrees C. How will the values of pH change by adding 0.1 mole of NaOH and

0.1 mole of HCl separately?

Step 1 - Initial pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]) = 4.74 + log(0.2/0.5) = 4.74 - 0.40 =

4.34.

Step 2 - Adding 0.1 mol NaOH: it converts 0.1 mol of acid into salt, so [salt] = 0.3 M,

[acid] = 0.4 M. pH = 4.74 + log(0.3/0.4) = 4.74 - 0.12 = 4.62.

Step 3 - Adding 0.1 mol HCl (separately, to a fresh buffer): it converts 0.1 mol of salt

into acid, so [salt] = 0.1 M, [acid] = 0.6 M. pH = 4.74 + log(0.1/0.6) = 4.74 - 0.78 =

3.96.

Answer: initial pH 4.34; after NaOH 4.62; after HCl 3.96 (matches the book's printed

answers).

Q24. The solubility of CaF2 in water at 25 degrees C is found to be 2.05 x 10^-4 mol

dm^-3. What is the value of Ksp at this temperature?

Step 1 - CaF2(s) ⇌ Ca2+(aq) + 2F-(aq). If solubility is S, then [Ca2+] = S and [F-] =

2S.

Step 2 - Ksp = [Ca2+][F-]^2 = S x (2S)^2 = 4S^3.

Step 3 - Ksp = 4 x (2.05 x 10^-4)^3 = 4 x 8.615 x 10^-12 = 3.446 x 10^-11.

Answer: 3.446 x 10^-11 (matches the book's printed answer).

Q25. The solubility product of Ag2CrO4 is 2.6 x 10^-2 at 25 degrees C. Calculate the

solubility of the compound.

Step 1 - Ag2CrO4(s) ⇌ 2Ag+(aq) + CrO4^2-(aq). If solubility is S, then [Ag+] = 2S

and [CrO4^2-] = S.

Step 2 - Ksp = [Ag+]^2 [CrO4^2-] = (2S)^2 x S = 4S^3, so S = (Ksp/4)^(1/3).

Step 3 - S = (2.6 x 10^-2 / 4)^(1/3) = (6.5 x 10^-3)^(1/3) = 0.1866 mol dm^-3.

Answer: 0.1866 mol dm^-3 (matches the book's printed answer, which follows the

printed Ksp value; note that the printed Ksp of 10^-2 is far larger than the usual

literature value of about 10^-12 for Ag2CrO4, so the printed figure itself appears to

be a misprint, but the calculation follows the book's own data).

mcqs.q: For 2HI(g) <-> H2(g) + I2(g) with [HI] = 0.08 M, [H2] = 0.01 M and [I2] = 0.01 M, the value of Kc = [H2][I2]/[HI]^2 is:
In the same HI problem, after HI is raised to 0.096 M, the amount x that dissociates to restore equilibrium (from 1.253x = 0.00214) is:
mcqs.why: Working: x = 0.00214 / 1.253 = 0.001708, which rounds to 0.00171 mol/dm3, the value solved in the notes.

mcqs.q: In the same HI problem, the new equilibrium concentration of HI is:
mcqs.why: Working: [HI] = 0.096 - 2 * 0.00171 = 0.096 - 0.00342 = 0.09258, which rounds to 0.0926 mol/dm3 at the new equilibrium.

mcqs.q: Acetic acid (3 mol) and ethyl alcohol (1 mol) react with Kc = 4.0; solving 3x^2 - 16x + 12 = 0 gives the ethyl acetate formed at equilibrium as:
mcqs.why: Working: x = (16 - 10.58) / 6 = 5.42 / 6 = 0.9033, so 0.903 mol of ethyl acetate forms; the other root 4.43 is impossible with only 1 mol of alcohol.

mcqs.q: The mass of ethyl acetate at equilibrium in that problem (0.903 mol, molar mass 88 g/mol) is:
mcqs.why: Working: mass = moles * molar mass = 0.903 * 88 = 79.464, which rounds to 79.5 g of ethyl acetate at equilibrium.

mcqs.q: The mass of acetic acid left at equilibrium in that problem (3 - 0.903 mol, molar mass 60 g/mol) is about:
mcqs.why: Working: moles left = 3 - 0.903 = 2.097 mol; mass = 2.097 * 60 = 125.82, which is about 126 g of acetic acid left behind.

mcqs.q: For H2O(g) + CO(g) <-> H2(g) + CO2(g), starting with 1 mol each of steam and CO, hydrogen is 33.3% of the equilibrium mixture. The value of Kp is:
The pH of 10^-4 mol/dm3 Ba(OH)2 solution is:
A buffer contains 0.02 M benzoic acid and 7.2 g of sodium benzoate (molar mass 144 g/mol) per dm3, with pKa = 4.19. Its pH is:
mcqs.why: Working: [salt] = 7.2 / 144 = 0.05 M; ratio = 0.05 / 0.02 = 2.5; log(2.5) = 0.40; pH = 4.19 + 0.40 = 4.59 by the Henderson equation.

mcqs.q: The solubility of CaF2 is 2.05 x 10^-4 mol/dm3 and Ksp = 4S^3 for CaF2. The value of Ksp is:

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • Number of molecules of sugar in 1 dm^3 of 1 M sugar solution is 6.02 x 10^23 .
  • 100 g of a 10% aqueous solution of NaOH contains 10 g of NaOH in 90 g of water.
  • When an azeotropic mixture is distilled, its composition remains constant.
  • The molal freezing point constant is also known as cryoscopic constant.
  • The boiling point of an azeotropic solution of two liquids is lower than either of them because the solution shows positive deviation from Raoult's law.
  • Among equimolal aqueous solutions of NaCl, BaCl2 and FeCl3, the maximum depression in freezing point is shown by FeCl3 solution.
  • A solution of ethanol in water shows positive deviations and gives azeotropic solution with lower boiling point than other components.
  • Colligative properties are used to calculate molar mass of a compound.

mcqs.q: How many molecules of sugar are present in 1 dm3 of 1 M sugar solution?
mcqs.why: The notes state that 1 dm3 of 1 M sugar solution contains 6.02 x 10^23 molecules, which is Avogadro's number for one mole.

mcqs.q: 100 g of a 10% aqueous solution of NaOH contains how much NaOH and how much water?
mcqs.why: A 10% solution means 10 g solute in 100 g solution, so the remaining mass is water: 100 - 10 = 90 g of water.

mcqs.q: What happens to the composition of an azeotropic mixture when it is distilled?
mcqs.why: The notes state that when an azeotropic mixture is distilled, its composition remains constant, so it cannot be separated by distillation.

mcqs.q: The molal freezing point constant is also known by which name?
mcqs.why: The notes state directly that the molal freezing point constant is also known as the cryoscopic constant.

mcqs.q: Why is the boiling point of an azeotropic solution of two liquids lower than either of them?
options: The solution shows negative deviation from Raoult's law
The solution shows positive deviation from Raoult's law
mcqs.why: The notes explain that the boiling point is lower than either component because the solution shows positive deviation from Raoult's law.

mcqs.q: Among equimolal aqueous solutions of NaCl, BaCl2 and FeCl3, which shows the maximum depression in freezing point?
mcqs.why: The notes state that among equimolal NaCl, BaCl2 and FeCl3 solutions, the maximum depression in freezing point is shown by FeCl3.

mcqs.q: A solution of ethanol in water shows which type of behaviour?
options: Negative deviation, giving an azeotrope with a higher boiling point
Negative deviation with a lower boiling point
Positive deviation, giving an azeotrope with a lower boiling point
mcqs.why: The notes state that ethanol in water shows positive deviations and gives an azeotropic solution with a lower boiling point than the other components.

mcqs.q: Colligative properties are used to calculate which quantity of a compound?
mcqs.why: The notes state that colligative properties are used to calculate the molar mass of a compound.

mcqs.q: Which solution is an azeotropic mixture according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes give ethanol in water as the solution that shows positive deviation and gives an azeotropic solution with a lower boiling point.

mcqs.q: A 1 M sugar solution has a volume of 1 dm3. How many moles of sugar does it contain?
mcqs.why: Molarity means moles per dm3, so 1 M in 1 dm3 contains 1 * 1 = 1 mole, matching the 6.02 x 10^23 molecules stated in the notes.

Q1(viii). Two solutions of NaCl and KCl are prepared separately by dissolving same

mcqs.q: What is the molarity of pure water?
mcqs.why: One dm3 of water is 1000 g, and moles = 1000 / 18 = 55.56, so the molarity of pure water is about 55.5 mol dm-3.

mcqs.q: 18 g glucose is dissolved in 90 g of water. The relative lowering of vapour pressure is equal to:
mcqs.why: Moles of glucose = 18 / 180 = 0.1 and moles of water = 90 / 18 = 5, so total = 0.1 + 5 = 5.1 and relative lowering = 0.1 / 5.1 = 0.0196, which is 1 / 51.

mcqs.q: A solution of glucose is 10% w/v. In what volume will 1 mole of glucose be dissolved?
mcqs.why: One mole of glucose is 180 g. A 10% w/v solution has 10 g in 100 cm3, so volume = 180 / 10 * 100 = 1800 cm3 = 1.8 dm3.

mcqs.q: An aqueous solution of ethanol in water may have a vapour pressure that is:
options: Equal to that of water only
mcqs.why: The lesson lists that an aqueous solution of ethanol in water may have a vapour pressure more than that of water, due to positive deviation.

mcqs.q: An azeotropic mixture of two liquids boils at a lower temperature than either of them when:
options: It shows negative deviation from Raoult's law
It shows positive deviation from Raoult's law
mcqs.why: The lesson states that a lower boiling azeotrope forms when the mixture shows positive deviation from Raoult's law.

mcqs.q: In an azeotropic mixture showing positive deviation from Raoult's law, the volume of the mixture is:
options: Slightly less than the total volume of the components
Equal to the total volume of the components
Slightly more than the total volume of the components
Half the total volume of the components
mcqs.why: The lesson states that for positive deviation the volume of the mixture is slightly more than the total volume of the components.

mcqs.q: Which of the following solutions has the highest boiling point?
options: All have the same boiling point
mcqs.why: The lesson identifies the 5.85% sodium chloride solution as having the highest boiling point, because NaCl dissociates into more particles.

mcqs.q: The molal boiling point constant is the ratio of the elevation in boiling point to:
mcqs.why: The lesson states that the molal boiling point constant is the ratio of the elevation in boiling point to molality.

mcqs.q: Colligative properties are the properties of:
options: Concentrated solutions which behave as nearly non-ideal solutions
Dilute solutions which behave as nearly ideal solutions
mcqs.why: The lesson defines colligative properties as the properties of dilute solutions which behave as nearly ideal solutions.

mcqs.q: Two solutions are compared in the lesson: NaCl and KCl prepared by dissolving the same amount of solute in water. What does the lesson focus on?
options: Their identical freezing points in all cases
Their different boiling points and vapour pressures
mcqs.why: The lesson's question compares the boiling points and vapour pressures of separately prepared NaCl and KCl solutions, showing they are not identical.

lessons.title: Fill in the Blanks
lessons.notes_html:
2(i). Number of molecules of sugar in 1 dm^3 of 1 M sugar solution is 6.02 x 10^23 .

2(ii). 100 g of a 10% aqueous solution of NaOH contains 10 g of NaOH in 90 g of water.

2(iii). When an azeotropic mixture is distilled, its composition remains constant.

2(vi). Among equimolal aqueous solutions of NaCl, BaCl2 and FeCl3, the maximum depression in freezing point is shown by FeCl3 solution.
