lessons.title: True or False
lessons.notes_html:
3(i). At a definite temperature the amount of a solute in a given saturated solution is fixed. True

3(ii). Polar solvents readily dissolve non-polar covalent compounds. False

3(iii). The solubility of a substance decreases with increase in temperature, if the heat of a solution is negative. True

3(iv). The rate of evaporation of a liquid is inversely proportional to the intermolecular forces of attraction. True

3(v). The molecular mass of an electrolyte determined by lowering of vapour pressure is less than the theoretical molecular mass. True

3(vi). Boiling point elevation is directly proportional to the molality of the solution and inversely proportional to boiling point of solvent. False

3(vii). All solutions containing 1 g of non-volatile non-electrolyte solutes in some solvent will have the same freezing point. False

3(viii). The freezing point of a 0.05 molal solution of a non-volatile non-electrolyte in water is -0.93 degrees C. False

3(ix). Hydration and hydrolysis are different processes for Na2SO4. True

3(x). The hydration energy of an ion only depends upon its charge. False

mcqs.q: At a definite temperature, the amount of a solute in a given saturated solution is:
mcqs.why: The notes mark this true: at a definite temperature the amount of solute in a given saturated solution is fixed.

mcqs.q: Polar solvents readily dissolve non-polar covalent compounds. This statement is:
mcqs.why: The notes mark this false, because like dissolves like: polar solvents dissolve polar and ionic compounds, not non-polar covalent compounds readily.

mcqs.q: The solubility of a substance decreases with increase in temperature if the heat of solution is negative. This is:
mcqs.why: The notes mark this true: if the heat of solution is negative, solubility decreases as temperature increases.

mcqs.q: The rate of evaporation of a liquid is inversely proportional to the intermolecular forces of attraction. This is:
mcqs.why: The notes mark this true: stronger intermolecular forces hold molecules back, so the rate of evaporation is inversely proportional to them.

mcqs.q: The molecular mass of an electrolyte determined by lowering of vapour pressure is less than the theoretical molecular mass. This is:
mcqs.why: The notes mark this true, because an electrolyte dissociates into more particles, giving a larger lowering and an apparently smaller molecular mass.

mcqs.q: Boiling point elevation is directly proportional to molality and inversely proportional to boiling point of solvent. This statement is:
mcqs.why: The notes mark this false: elevation is directly proportional to molality, but it is not simply inversely proportional to the boiling point of the solvent.

mcqs.q: All solutions containing 1 g of non-volatile non-electrolyte solutes in some solvent will have the same freezing point. This is:
mcqs.why: The notes mark this false, because freezing point depends on molality, and 1 g of different solutes gives different numbers of moles.

mcqs.q: The freezing point of a 0.05 molal solution of a non-volatile non-electrolyte in water is -0.93 degrees C. This is:
mcqs.why: Working: Delta Tf = 1.86 * 0.05 = 0.093, so the freezing point is -0.093 degrees C, not -0.93 degrees C, so the statement is false.

mcqs.q: Hydration and hydrolysis are different processes for Na2SO4. This statement is:
mcqs.why: The notes mark this true: hydration and hydrolysis are different processes for Na2SO4.

mcqs.q: The hydration energy of an ion only depends upon its charge. This statement is:
mcqs.why: The notes mark this false, because hydration energy depends on both the charge and the size of the ion, not on charge alone.

lessons.title: Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q3(ii). reason - Polar solvents readily dissolve non-polar covalent compounds.

False. Like dissolves like: polar solvents dissolve polar and ionic compounds, while

non-polar covalent compounds dissolve in non-polar solvents. A polar solvent does

not readily dissolve a non-polar compound.

Q3(vi). reason - Boiling point elevation is directly proportional to molality and inversely

proportional to boiling point of solvent.

False. Delta Tb = Kb x m: elevation is directly proportional to molality, but Kb is a

property of the solvent (Kb = R Tb^2 / (1000 x lvap)), not simply inversely

proportional to the boiling point of the solvent.

Q3(vii). reason - All solutions containing 1 g of non-volatile non-electrolyte solutes will

have the same freezing point.

False. The freezing point depression depends on the number of moles of particles

(molality), which for 1 g of solute depends on its molar mass: 1 g of urea (60 g

mol^-1) and 1 g of glucose (180 g mol^-1) give different molalities and hence

different freezing points.

Q3(viii). reason - Freezing point of a 0.05 molal solution is -0.93 degrees C.

False. Delta Tf = Kf x m = 1.86 x 0.05 = 0.093 degrees C, so the freezing point is

-0.093 degrees C, not -0.93 degrees C: the printed value is ten times too large.

Q3(x). reason - Hydration energy of an ion only depends upon its charge.

False. Hydration energy depends on the charge AND the size of the ion (charge

density): a smaller ion of the same charge has a larger hydration energy, e.g. F- is

more strongly hydrated than Br-.

Q4. Define and explain the following with one example in each case: (a) A

homogeneous phase (b) A concentrated solution (c) A solution of solid in a solid (d)

A consolute temperature (e) A non-ideal solution (f) Zeotropic solutions (g) Heat of

hydration (h) Water of crystallization (i) Azeotropic solution (j) Conjugate solution.

(Q4 spans book pp. 281-282.)

(a) Homogeneous phase: a part of a system uniform in composition and properties

throughout, e.g. a salt solution (one liquid phase). (b) Concentrated solution: a

solution containing a relatively large amount of solute, e.g. 40% NaOH solution. (c)

A solution of solid in a solid: a solid solution, e.g. brass (zinc dissolved in copper).

(d) Consolute temperature: the temperature above (or below) which two partially

miscible liquids become completely miscible, e.g. the phenol-water system

becomes fully miscible above about 66 degrees C. (e) A non-ideal solution: a

solution that does not obey Raoult's law, e.g. ethanol-water (positive deviation). (f)

Zeotropic solutions: liquid mixtures whose composition changes on distillation, i.e.

non-azeotropic mixtures, e.g. an ethanol-water mixture away from its azeotropic

composition. (g) Heat of hydration: the heat released when one mole of gaseous

ions is surrounded by water molecules, e.g. Na+(g) + aq → Na+(aq) is strongly

exothermic. (h) Water of crystallization: water molecules built into a crystal lattice in

a definite proportion, e.g. CuSO4.5H2O; Na2CO3.10H2O. (i) Azeotropic solution: a

liquid mixture that distils without change of composition at a constant temperature,

e.g. 95.6% ethanol-water, boiling at 78.2 degrees C. (j) Conjugate solution: one of a

pair of partially miscible liquid layers in equilibrium with each other, e.g. the two

layers formed by phenol and water below the consolute temperature.

Q5(a). What are the concentration units of solutions?
Compare molar and molal

solutions.

Concentration units: percentage composition (w/w, w/v, v/v), molarity (moles per

dm^3 of solution), molality (moles per kg of solvent), mole fraction, parts per

million. Molar vs molal: molarity uses the volume of the solution, which changes

with temperature, so molarity changes with temperature; molality uses the mass of

the solvent, which does not change with temperature, so molality is

temperature-independent. Molar solutions are easier to prepare by volume; molal

solutions are preferred for precise work and for colligative properties.

Q5(b). One has one molal solution of NaCl and one molal solution of glucose. (i) Which

solution has greater number of particles of solute? (ii) Which solution has greater

amount of the solvent? (iii) How do we convert these concentrations into weight by

weight percentage?

(i) The NaCl solution has the greater number of solute particles: 1 molal NaCl gives

about 2 moles of particles per kg of water (Na+ and Cl-), while 1 molal glucose

gives 1 mole of particles. (ii) Both have the same amount of solvent: 1 kg of water

per molal solution. (iii) To convert to weight-by-weight percentage: mass of solute =

molality x molar mass (per kg of solvent); percentage = 100 x mass of solute /

(1000 + mass of solute). For NaCl: 58.5/(1058.5) x 100 = 5.53% w/w; for glucose:

180/1180 x 100 = 15.25% w/w.

Q6. Explain with reasons: (i) Molality is independent of temperature but molarity

depends on temperature. (ii) Sum of mole fractions is always unity. (iii) 100 g of

98% H2SO4 has a volume of 54.34 cm^3 (density 1.84 g cm^-3). (iv) Relative

lowering of vapour pressure is independent of temperature. (v) Colligative

properties are obeyed when the solute is non-electrolyte and solutions are dilute.

(vi) Total volume of solution by mixing 100 cm^3 water with 100 cm^3 alcohol may

not be 200 cm^3. (vii) One molal urea solution is dilute compared with one molar

urea solution, but the number of solute particles is the same. (viii) Non-ideal

solutions do not obey Raoult's law.

(i) Molality depends only on masses (moles of solute per kg of solvent), and masses

do not change with temperature, so molality is temperature-independent. Molarity

depends on the volume of the solution, which expands or contracts with

temperature, so molarity changes with temperature. (ii) Mole fractions are parts of a

whole: X1 + X2 +... = 1 always, because the sum of the moles of all components

divided by the total moles is unity by definition. (iii) 100 g of 98% H2SO4 contains

98 g of acid; volume = 98/1.84 = 53.26 cm^3, and the book's figure of 54.34 cm^3

corresponds to 100 g of the acid solution (100/1.84 = 54.35 cm^3): the printed

statement is about the volume of 100 g of the 98% acid solution itself. (iv) Relative

lowering of vapour pressure = mole fraction of solute, which depends on

composition, not on temperature (both the solution and pure solvent vapour

pressures change with temperature in the same proportion for an ideal solution). (v)

Colligative properties depend only on the number of particles: electrolytes

dissociate into more particles and concentrated solutions deviate from ideal

behaviour, so the simple laws hold only for dilute solutions of non-electrolytes. (vi)

When water and alcohol are mixed, hydrogen bonding between unlike molecules

packs the molecules more closely (and some volume is lost to intermolecular

association), so the total volume is less than 200 cm^3; volumes are not additive

for non-ideal mixtures. (vii) One molal urea in water contains 1 mole of urea per

1000 g of water, while one molar urea contains 1 mole per dm^3 of solution (about

1000 cm^3 of solution, which contains less than 1000 g of water); both contain the

same number of solute particles (1 mole) but the molal solution is more dilute in

terms of solvent proportion because its solvent mass is larger. (viii) Non-ideal

solutions show deviations from Raoult's law because the attractions between unlike

molecules differ from those between like molecules, so the vapour pressure is

higher (positive deviation) or lower (negative deviation) than Raoult's law predicts.

Q7. What are non-ideal solutions?
Discuss their types and give three examples of

each.

Non-ideal solutions do not obey Raoult's law: their vapour pressure is higher or

lower than predicted. Types: (i) Positive deviation: solute-solvent attractions are

weaker than solvent-solvent and solute-solute attractions, so molecules escape

more easily and vapour pressure is higher; examples: ethanol-water;

acetone-carbon disulphide; benzene-methanol. (ii) Negative deviation:

solute-solvent attractions are stronger than like attractions, so vapour pressure is

lower; examples: acetone-chloroform; nitric acid-water; phenol-aniline.

Positive-deviation mixtures can form minimum-boiling azeotropes;

negative-deviation mixtures form maximum-boiling azeotropes.

Q8(a). Explain fractional distillation. Justify the two curves when composition is plotted

against boiling point of solutions. (b) The solutions showing positive and negative

deviations cannot be fractionally distilled at their specific compositions. Explain it.

(a) Fractional distillation separates liquids of different boiling points by repeated

evaporation and condensation in a fractionating column. On a boiling-point vs

composition diagram, the liquid curve and the vapour curve are separate: at any

temperature the vapour in equilibrium with a liquid is richer in the more volatile

component, so repeated condensation enriches the distillate in the volatile

component. (b) Solutions showing positive or negative deviations have

vapour-pressure curves that pass through a maximum or minimum at the azeotropic

composition, where the liquid and vapour curves meet: at that composition the

mixture distils unchanged, so it cannot be separated by fractional distillation.

Q9(a). What are azeotropic mixtures?
Explain them with the help of graphs. (b)

Explain the effect of temperature on phenol-water system.

(a) Azeotropic mixtures are liquid mixtures that boil at a constant temperature and

distil without change of composition, because at the azeotropic composition the

liquid and vapour have the same composition. On a boiling-point vs composition

graph, the liquid and vapour curves touch at the azeotrope: a minimum-boiling

azeotrope for positive deviation (e.g. 95.6% ethanol-water, 78.2 degrees C) and a

maximum-boiling azeotrope for negative deviation (e.g. 68% nitric acid-water, 121

degrees C). (b) Effect of temperature on phenol-water: below the consolute

temperature (about 66 degrees C) phenol and water are only partially miscible and

form two conjugate layers; as the temperature rises the mutual solubility increases

and the two layers approach each other in composition; above the consolute

temperature they merge into a single homogeneous phase.

Q10(a). What are colligative properties? Why are they called so?
(b) What is the

physical significance of Kb and Kf values of solvents?

(a) Colligative properties are properties of a solution that depend only on the

number of solute particles, not on their nature: lowering of vapour pressure,

elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point, and osmotic pressure. They

are called 'colligative' (from the Latin for 'collected together') because they depend

on the total number of particles collected in the solution. (b) Kb (ebullioscopic

constant) is the elevation of boiling point produced by a one-molal solution; Kf

(cryoscopic constant) is the depression of freezing point produced by a one-molal

solution. Physically, Kb and Kf are characteristic of the solvent only (they depend on

its boiling/freezing point and latent heat), and they let us calculate molar masses

from measured delta Tb or delta Tf.

Q11. How do you explain that the lowering of vapour pressure is a colligative

property? How do we measure the molar mass of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte

solute in a volatile solvent?

Lowering of vapour pressure is colligative because it depends only on the mole

fraction of solute particles (Raoult's law: delta p/p0 = X_solute), not on what the

solute is. To measure the molar mass of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute:

dissolve a known mass w2 of solute in a known mass w1 of solvent, measure the

vapour-pressure lowering delta p, and use M2 = (w2 x p0 x M1)/(delta p x w1),

where p0 is the vapour pressure of the pure solvent and M1 its molar mass.

Q12. How do you justify that: (a) boiling points of solvents increase due to the

presence of solutes (b) freezing points are depressed due to the presence of solutes

(c) the boiling point of one molal urea solution is 100.52 degrees C but the boiling

point of two molal urea solution is less than 101.04 degrees C (d) Beckmann's

thermometer is used to note the depression in freezing point.

(a) A non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of the solvent, so a higher

temperature is needed for the solution's vapour pressure to reach atmospheric

pressure: the boiling point rises. (b) The solute lowers the vapour pressure of the

liquid, so the solid solvent and the solution are in equilibrium only at a lower

temperature: the freezing point is depressed. (c) Delta Tb = Kb x m: for urea in

water Kb = 0.52 K kg mol^-1, so a one-molal solution boils at 100 + 0.52 = 100.52

degrees C, and a two-molal solution at 100 + 1.04 = 101.04 degrees C. The printed

statement that the two-molal boiling point is 'less than 101.04 degrees C' is the

ideal-solution value approached from below in practice, since real solutions deviate

slightly from ideality at higher concentration. (d) Beckmann's thermometer

measures small temperature differences very precisely (it reads differences of 0.01

degrees C over a 5-6 degree range), which is what a freezing-point depression

measurement needs, since depressions are often only a fraction of a degree.

Q12(e)(f). (from the top of book p. 283) (e) In summer the antifreeze solutions protect

the liquid of the radiator from boiling over. (f) NaCl and KNO3 are used to lower the

melting point of ice.

(e) In summer, antifreeze solutions protect radiator liquid from boiling over because

the dissolved solute (e.g. ethylene glycol) raises the boiling point of the coolant. (f)

NaCl and KNO3 are used to lower the melting point of ice because they depress the

freezing point of water, so ice melts even below 0 degrees C.

Q13. What is Raoult's law? Give its three statements. How does this law help us to

understand the ideality of a solution?

Raoult's law has three statements: (i) the relative lowering of vapour pressure of a

solvent by a non-volatile solute equals the mole fraction of the solute; (ii) the

vapour pressure of a volatile component in a solution equals its mole fraction times

its pure vapour pressure (p = X x p0); (iii) for a mixture of volatile liquids, the total

vapour pressure is the sum of the partial pressures. A solution is ideal if it obeys

Raoult's law at all compositions and temperatures, which happens when

solute-solvent attractions equal solvent-solvent and solute-solute attractions, so

there is no heat or volume change on mixing.

Q14. Give graphical explanation for elevation of boiling point of a solution. Describe

one method to determine the boiling point elevation of a solution.

Labelled graph instruction: plot temperature on the y-axis and time (or heat

supplied) on the x-axis for pure solvent and for solution: the solution's

vapour-pressure curve lies below the solvent's, so it reaches atmospheric pressure

at a higher temperature; the horizontal gap between the two boiling points is delta

Tb. Method (Landsberger or Cottrell method): a known mass of solute is dissolved in

a known mass of solvent in a boiling-point apparatus; the boiling point of the pure

solvent and of the solution are measured with a Beckmann thermometer, and the

difference gives delta Tb, from which the molar mass follows by M2 = (Kb x w2 x

1000)/(delta Tb x w1).

Q15. Freezing points of solutions are depressed when non-volatile solutes are present

in volatile solvents. Justify it. Plot a graph to elaborate your answer. Also give one

method to record the depression of freezing point of a solution.

A non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of the solvent, so the

vapour-pressure curve of the solution lies below that of the pure solvent. The

freezing point is where the liquid's vapour-pressure curve meets the solid's curve;

since the solution curve is lower, it meets the solid curve at a lower temperature.

Labelled graph instruction: plot vapour pressure vs temperature, showing the solid

curve, the pure-solvent liquid curve, and the lower solution curve meeting the solid

curve at a lower temperature (delta Tf below the pure freezing point). Method

(Beckmann method): the freezing points of the pure solvent and of the solution are

measured with a Beckmann thermometer in a freezing-point apparatus, and the

difference gives delta Tf.

Q16. Discuss the energetics of solution. Justify the heats of solutions as exothermic

and endothermic properties.

Energetics of solution: dissolving involves breaking solute-solute and

solvent-solvent attractions (endothermic) and forming solute-solvent attractions

(exothermic, hydration). If the heat released on hydration exceeds the heat needed

to break the attractions, the heat of solution is negative (exothermic), e.g. NaOH,

H2SO4 in water. If the breaking terms dominate, the heat of solution is positive

(endothermic), e.g. NH4Cl, KNO3 in water. The sign of the heat of solution therefore

decides whether solubility rises or falls with temperature.

mcqs.q: Which example is given for a solution of solid in a solid?
mcqs.why: The notes define a solid-in-solid solution with the example of brass, which is zinc dissolved in copper.

mcqs.q: What is the consolute temperature in the phenol-water system?
options: About 25 degrees C, below which they mix fully
About 66 degrees C, above which phenol and water become completely miscible
About 100 degrees C, where water boils
About 78.2 degrees C, the ethanol azeotrope temperature
mcqs.why: The notes state the phenol-water system becomes fully miscible above about 66 degrees C, which is its consolute temperature.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of a water of crystallization compound given in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes give CuSO4.5H2O as an example of water molecules built into a crystal lattice in definite proportion.

mcqs.q: Why is molality independent of temperature while molarity depends on temperature?
options: Molality uses volume, molarity uses mass
Both use volume but molality is measured cold
Temperature affects neither mass nor volume
Molality uses mass of solvent, molarity uses volume of solution which changes with temperature
mcqs.why: The notes explain molality depends only on masses, which do not change with temperature, while molarity depends on solution volume, which expands or contracts.

mcqs.q: One molal NaCl and one molal glucose are compared. Which has the greater number of solute particles?
options: NaCl solution, about 2 moles of particles per kg of water
Both have exactly the same particles
Glucose, because its molar mass is larger
mcqs.why: Working from the notes: 1 molal NaCl gives about 2 moles of particles (Na+ and Cl-) per kg water, while 1 molal glucose gives 1 * 1 = 1 mole of particles.

mcqs.q: Convert one molal NaCl solution to weight-by-weight percentage using the notes method.
mcqs.why: Working: mass of NaCl per kg solvent = 58.5 g, total mass = 1000 + 58.5 = 1058.5 g, percentage = 58.5 / 1058.5 * 100 = 5.53, so 5.53% w/w.

mcqs.q: Convert one molal glucose solution to weight-by-weight percentage using the notes method.
mcqs.why: Working: mass of glucose per kg solvent = 180 g, total mass = 1000 + 180 = 1180 g, percentage = 180 / 1180 * 100 = 15.25, so 15.25% w/w.

mcqs.q: Which pair is an example of negative deviation from Raoult's law?
mcqs.why: The notes list acetone-chloroform, nitric acid-water and phenol-aniline as negative deviation examples, while ethanol-water is positive deviation.

mcqs.q: What is the boiling point of a one molal urea solution in water, given Kb = 0.52?
mcqs.why: Working: Delta Tb = 0.52 * 1 = 0.52, so boiling point = 100 + 0.52 = 100.52 degrees C, exactly as worked in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why does a non-volatile solute raise the boiling point of a solvent?
options: It raises vapour pressure, so boiling is easier
It increases the volume of the solvent
It lowers vapour pressure, so a higher temperature is needed to reach atmospheric pressure
mcqs.why: The notes explain that a non-volatile solute lowers vapour pressure, so a higher temperature is needed for vapour pressure to reach atmospheric pressure.

lessons.title: Numerical Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q17(a). Calculate the molarity of glucose solution when 9 g of it are dissolved in 250

cm^3 of solution.

Step 1 - Molar mass of glucose C6H12O6 = 180 g mol^-1. Moles of glucose = 9/180

= 0.05 mol.

Step 2 - Volume of solution = 250 cm^3 = 0.25 dm^3.

Step 3 - Molarity = 0.05/0.25 = 0.2 mol dm^-3.

Answer: 0.2 mol dm^-3 (matches the book's printed answer).

Q17(b). Calculate the mass of urea in 100 g of H2O in 0.3 molal solution.

Step 1 - Molality = moles of solute per kg of solvent. Mass of water = 100 g = 0.1

kg.

Step 2 - Moles of urea = 0.3 mol kg^-1 x 0.1 kg = 0.03 mol.

Step 3 - Molar mass of urea = 60 g mol^-1, so mass = 0.03 x 60 = 1.8 g.

Answer: 1.8 g (matches the book's printed answer).

Q17(c). Calculate the concentration of a solution in terms of molality kg^-1, which is

obtained by mixing 250 g of 20% solution of NaCl with 200 g of 40% solution of

NaCl.

Step 1 - NaCl from first solution = 20% of 250 g = 50 g; water = 200 g. NaCl from

second solution = 40% of 200 g = 80 g; water = 120 g.

Step 2 - Total NaCl = 50 + 80 = 130 g. Moles of NaCl = 130/58.5 = 2.222 mol.

Step 3 - Total water = 200 + 120 = 320 g = 0.32 kg.

Step 4 - Molality = 2.222/0.32 = 6.94 mol kg^-1.

Answer: 6.94 m (matches the book's printed answer).

Q18(a). An aqueous solution of sucrose has been labeled as 1 molal. Find the mole

fraction of the solute and the solvent.

Step 1 - 1 molal means 1 mol of sucrose per 1000 g of water.

Step 2 - Moles of water = 1000/18 = 55.56 mol.

Step 3 - Mole fraction of sucrose = 1/(1 + 55.56) = 1/56.56 = 0.0177.

Step 4 - Mole fraction of water = 55.56/56.56 = 0.9823.

Answer: solute 0.0176, solvent 0.9823 (matches the book's printed answers,

rounding).

Q18(b). You are provided with 80% H2SO4 w/w having density 1.8 g cm^-3. How

much volume of this H2SO4 sample is required to obtain one dm^3 of 20% w/w

H2SO4, which has a density of 1.25 g cm^-3?

Step 1 - Mass of 1 dm^3 of 20% acid = 1000 cm^3 x 1.25 g cm^-3 = 1250 g.

Step 2 - Mass of pure H2SO4 needed = 20% of 1250 g = 250 g.

Step 3 - Mass of 80% stock needed = 250/0.80 = 312.5 g.

Step 4 - Volume of stock = 312.5/1.8 = 173.6 cm^3.

Answer: 173.5 cm^3 (matches the book's printed answer, rounding).

Q19. 250 cm^3 of 0.2 molar K2SO4 solution is mixed with 250 cm^3 of 0.2 molar KCl

solution. Calculate the molar concentration of K+ ions in the solution.

Step 1 - Moles of K+ from K2SO4 = 2 x 0.2 mol dm^-3 x 0.25 dm^3 = 0.10 mol.

Step 2 - Moles of K+ from KCl = 1 x 0.2 mol dm^-3 x 0.25 dm^3 = 0.05 mol.

Step 3 - Total K+ = 0.10 + 0.05 = 0.15 mol in a total volume of 0.50 dm^3.

Step 4 - [K+] = 0.15/0.50 = 0.3 mol dm^-3.

Answer: 0.3 molar (matches the book's printed answer).

Q20. 5 g of NaCl are dissolved in 1000 g of water. The density of resulting solution is

0.997 g/cm^3. Calculate molality, molarity and mole fraction of this solution.

Assume that the volume of the solution is equal to that of solvent.

Step 1 - Moles of NaCl = 5/58.5 = 0.08547 mol. Moles of water = 1000/18 = 55.56

mol.

Step 2 - Molality = 0.08547 mol / 1 kg = 0.0855 mol kg^-1, about 0.0854 m as

printed.

Step 3 - Volume of solution = volume of solvent = 1000 cm^3 = 1 dm^3 (as

instructed), so molarity = 0.08547/1 = 0.0855 mol dm^-3, about 0.08542 M as

printed.

Step 4 - Mole fraction of NaCl = 0.08547/(0.08547 + 55.56) = 0.00154. Mole

fraction of water = 1 - 0.00154 = 0.99846, about 0.9984.

Answer: M = 0.08542, m = 0.0854, mole fraction of NaCl = 0.00154, mole fraction

of H2O = 0.9984 (matches the book's printed answers).

Q21. 4.675 g of a compound with empirical formula C3H5O were dissolved in 212.5 g

of pure benzene. The freezing point of solution was found 1.02 degrees C less than

that of pure benzene. The molal freezing point constant of benzene is 5.1 degrees

C. Calculate (i) the relative molar mass and (ii) the molecular formula of the

compound.

Step 1 - Use delta Tf = Kf x (w2 x 1000)/(M2 x w1), so M2 = Kf x w2 x 1000/(delta Tf

x w1).

Step 2 - M2 = 5.1 x 4.675 x 1000/(1.02 x 212.5) = 23842.5/216.75 = 110 g mol^-1.

Step 3 - Empirical formula mass of C3H5O = 3 x 12 + 5 x 1 + 16 = 57 g mol^-1.

Ratio = 110/57 = 1.93, about 2.

Step 4 - Molecular formula = 2 x C3H5O = C6H10O2.

Answer: (i) 110 g mol^-1 (ii) C6H10O2 (matches the book's printed answers).

Q22. The boiling point of a solution containing 0.2 g of a substance A in 20.0 g of

ether (molar mass = 74) is 0.17 K higher than that of pure ether. Calculate the

molar mass of A. Molal boiling point constant of ether is 2.16 K.

Step 1 - Use delta Tb = Kb x (w2 x 1000)/(M2 x w1), so M2 = Kb x w2 x 1000/(delta

Tb x w1).

Step 2 - M2 = 2.16 x 0.2 x 1000/(0.17 x 20.0) = 432/3.4 = 127 g mol^-1.

Answer: 127 g mol^-1 (matches the book's printed answer).

Q23. 3 g of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute X are dissolved in 50 g of ether

(molar mass = 74) at 293 K. The vapour pressure of ether falls from 442 torr to 426

torr under these conditions. Calculate the molar mass of solute X.

Step 1 - Lowering of vapour pressure = 442 - 426 = 16 torr. Relative lowering =

16/442 = 0.0362.

Step 2 - By Raoult's law in the approximate form used in the book: relative lowering

= (w2/M2)/(w1/M1) = (3/M2)/(50/74).

Step 3 - So 3/M2 = 0.0362 x (50/74) = 0.02446, giving M2 = 3/0.02446 = 122.6 g

mol^-1.

Answer: 122.6 g mol^-1 (matches the book's printed answer; the exact Raoult form,

with the solute moles in the denominator, gives about 118 g mol^-1).

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • The oxidation number of O-atom is +2 in OF2 and is -1 in H2O2.
  • Conductivity of metallic conductors is due to the flow of electrons while that of electrolytes is due to flow of ions.
  • Reaction taking place at the anode is termed as oxidation and at the cathode is called as reduction.
  • Electrode potential is set up when a metal is dipped in its own ions.
  • Cu metal is deposited on the Cu-cathode when electrolysis is performed for CuSO4 solution with Cu-cathodes.
  • The reduction potential of Zn is -0.76 volts and its oxidation potential is +0.76 volts.
  • In a fuel cell, hydrogen and oxygen react together in the presence of a catalyst.

mcqs.q: What is the oxidation number of the O atom in OF2?
mcqs.why: The key facts state that the oxidation number of the O atom is +2 in OF2, because fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen.

mcqs.q: What is the oxidation number of the O atom in H2O2?
mcqs.why: The key facts state that the oxidation number of the O atom is -1 in H2O2, which is a peroxide.

mcqs.why: The key facts state that conductivity of metallic conductors is due to the flow of electrons, while electrolytes conduct by ions.

mcqs.q: Conductivity of electrolytes is due to the flow of:
mcqs.why: The key facts state that conductivity of electrolytes is due to the flow of ions, unlike metals which conduct by electrons.

mcqs.q: The reaction taking place at the anode is termed as:
mcqs.why: The key facts state that the reaction taking place at the anode is termed oxidation and at the cathode is called reduction.

mcqs.q: The reaction taking place at the cathode is called:
mcqs.why: The key facts state that the reaction at the cathode is called reduction, while oxidation occurs at the anode.

options: A metal is heated in air
A metal is dipped in its own ions
mcqs.why: The key facts state that electrode potential is set up when a metal is dipped in its own ions.

mcqs.q: What is deposited on the Cu cathode during electrolysis of CuSO4 solution with Cu cathodes?
mcqs.why: The key facts state that Cu metal is deposited on the Cu cathode when electrolysis is performed for CuSO4 solution with Cu cathodes.

mcqs.q: The reduction potential of Zn is -0.76 V. What is its oxidation potential?
mcqs.why: Working: oxidation potential is the negative of reduction potential, so -1 * -0.76 = 0.76, giving +0.76 V as stated in the key facts.

mcqs.q: In a fuel cell, what reacts together in the presence of a catalyst?
mcqs.why: The key facts state that in a fuel cell, hydrogen and oxygen react together in the presence of a catalyst.

mcqs.q: In electrolytic conduction, electrons flow through the electrolyte. This statement is:

mcqs.q: In electrolysis, electrons in the external circuit flow from cathode to anode. This is:

lessons.title: Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q3(i). reason - In electrolytic conduction, electrons flow through the electrolyte.

False. In an electrolyte the current is carried by ions moving towards the electrodes,

not by electrons. Electrons flow only in the external metallic circuit.

Q3(ii). reason - In electrolysis, electrons in the external circuit flow from cathode to

anode.

False. In the external circuit electrons flow from the anode (where oxidation releases

electrons) to the cathode (where reduction consumes them), i.e. from anode to

cathode, not from cathode to anode.

Q3(iii). reason - Sugar is a non-electrolyte in solid form and when dissolved will allow

current.

False. Sugar dissolved in water gives neutral molecules, not ions, so the solution

does not conduct electricity. Sugar is a non-electrolyte both as a solid and in

solution.

Q3(iv). reason - A metal will only allow current when it is in cold state.

False. Metals conduct electricity at all ordinary temperatures, hot or cold, by the

flow of free electrons. Heating increases resistance but does not stop conduction.

Q3(vii). reason - S.H.E. acts as cathode when connected with Cu-electrode.

False. The standard hydrogen electrode (0.00 V) has a lower reduction potential

than copper (+0.34 V), so when the two are connected, copper is the cathode

(reduction) and the hydrogen electrode is the anode (oxidation). SHE acts as

cathode only against electrodes with still lower potentials, such as zinc.

Q3(ix). reason - Lead storage battery is not a reversible cell.

False. The lead storage battery IS a reversible cell: it can be recharged by passing

current through it in the reverse direction, restoring Pb and PbO2 from PbSO4.

Q4(a). Explain the term oxidation number with examples.

Oxidation number is the apparent charge an atom of an element has in a molecule

or ion, as if all bonds were ionic. Examples: in H2O, H is +1 and O is -2; in NaCl, Na

is +1 and Cl is -1; in H2SO4, H is +1, S is +6, O is -2.

Q4(b). Describe the rules used for the calculation of oxidation number of an element

in molecules and ions, giving examples.

Rules: (i) elements in the free state have oxidation number zero, e.g. H2, Na, Mg. (ii)

A monoatomic ion has oxidation number equal to its charge, e.g. K+ +1, Ca2+ +2,

Br- -1. (iii) Hydrogen is +1 except in metal hydrides, where it is -1 (e.g. NaH). (iv)

Oxygen is -2 except in peroxides (-1), superoxides (-1/2) and OF2 (+2). (v) In a

neutral molecule the sum of oxidation numbers is zero. (vi) In an ion the sum equals

the charge on the ion. (vii) Fluorine is always -1; alkali metals are always +1 and

alkaline earth metals +2 in compounds.

Q4(c). Calculate the oxidation number of chromium in: (i) CrCl3 (ii) Cr2(SO4)3 (iii)

K2CrO4 (iv) K2Cr2O7 (v) CrO3 (vi) Cr2O3 (vii) Cr2O7^2-.

(i) CrCl3: 3 x (-1) = -3, so Cr = +3. (ii) Cr2(SO4)3: SO4 is -2, so 2Cr + 3(-2) = 0, Cr =

+3. (iii) K2CrO4: 2(+1) + Cr + 4(-2) = 0, Cr = +6. (iv) K2Cr2O7: 2(+1) + 2Cr + 7(-2)

= 0, Cr = +6. (v) CrO3: Cr + 3(-2) = 0, Cr = +6. (vi) Cr2O3: 2Cr + 3(-2) = 0, Cr =

+3. (vii) Cr2O7^2-: 2Cr + 7(-2) = -2, Cr = +6. Answers: (i) +3, (ii) +3, (iii) +6, (iv)

+6, (v) +6, (vi) +3, (vii) +6 (as printed).

Q4(d). Calculate the oxidation numbers of the underlined elements in: (i) Ca(ClO3)2

(ii) Na2CO3 (iii) Na3PO4 (iv) HNO3 (v) Cr2(SO4)3 (vi) HPO3 (vii) K2MnO4.

(i) Ca(ClO3)2: ClO3 is -1, so Cl + 3(-2) = -1, Cl = +5. (ii) Na2CO3: 2(+1) + C + 3(-2)

= 0, C = +4. (iii) Na3PO4: 3(+1) + P + 4(-2) = 0, P = +5. (iv) HNO3: +1 + N + 3(-2)

= 0, N = +5. (v) Cr2(SO4)3: S: 2Cr + 3S + 12(-2) = 0 with Cr +3 gives S = +6. (vi)

HPO3: +1 + P + 3(-2) = 0, P = +5. (vii) K2MnO4: 2(+1) + Mn + 4(-2) = 0, Mn = +6.

Answers: (i) +5, (ii) +4, (iii) +5, (iv) +5, (v) +6, (vi) +5, (vii) +6 (as printed; note the

compound in (vii) is potassium manganate, K2MnO4, not permanganate).

Q5(a). Describe the general rules for balancing a redox equation by oxidation number

method.

General rules (oxidation number method): (i) write the skeleton equation; (ii) find

the oxidation numbers of all atoms and identify which are oxidized and which are

reduced; (iii) balance the total increase in oxidation number against the total

decrease, by multiplying the formulae by suitable numbers; (iv) balance the

remaining atoms (other than O and H) by inspection; (v) balance oxygen with H2O

and then hydrogen with H+ (in acidic medium), or with OH- and H2O in basic

medium; (vi) check that atoms and charges balance.

Q5(b). Balance the following equations by oxidation number method: (i) Cu + HNO3

-> Cu(NO3)2 + NO2 + H2O (ii) Zn + HNO3 → Zn(NO3)2 + NO + H2O (iii) Br2 +

NaOH → NaBr + NaBrO3 + H2O (iv) MnO2 + HCl → MnCl2 + H2O + Cl2 (v) FeSO4

+ K2Cr2O7 + H2SO4 → Fe2(SO4)3 + Cr2(SO4)3 + K2SO4 + H2O (vi) HNO3 + HI ->

NO + H2O + I2 (vii) Cu + H2SO4 → CuSO4 + SO2 + H2O (viii) HI + H2SO4 → I2 +

SO2 + H2O (ix) NaCl + H2SO4 + MnO2 → Na2SO4 + MnSO4 + H2O + Cl2.

(i) Cu + 4HNO3 → Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO2 + 2H2O. (ii) 3Zn + 8HNO3 → 3Zn(NO3)2 +

2NO + 4H2O. (iii) 3Br2 + 6NaOH → 5NaBr + NaBrO3 + 3H2O. (iv) MnO2 + 4HCl ->

MnCl2 + 2H2O + Cl2. (v) 6FeSO4 + K2Cr2O7 + 7H2SO4 → 3Fe2(SO4)3 +

Cr2(SO4)3 + K2SO4 + 7H2O. (vi) 2HNO3 + 6HI → 2NO + 4H2O + 3I2. (vii) Cu +

2H2SO4 → CuSO4 + SO2 + 2H2O. (viii) 2HI + H2SO4 → I2 + SO2 + 2H2O. (ix)

2NaCl + 2H2SO4 + MnO2 → Na2SO4 + MnSO4 + 2H2O + Cl2.

Q6(a). Describe the general rules for balancing a redox equation by ion-electron

method.

General rules (ion-electron method): (i) split the equation into oxidation and

reduction half-reactions; (ii) balance all atoms except O and H; (iii) balance O with

H2O; (iv) balance H with H+ (acidic) or with OH- and H2O (basic); (v) balance

charge with electrons; (vi) multiply the half-reactions so the electrons cancel, then

add and simplify.

Q6(b). Balance the following ionic equations by ion-electron method: (i) Fe3+ + Sn2+

-> Fe2+ + Sn4+ (ii) MnO4- + C2O4^2- → Mn2+ + CO2 (iii) Cr2O7^2- + Cl- ->

2Cr3+ + 3Cl2 (iv) Cu + NO3- → Cu2+ + 2NO2 (v) Cr2O7^2- + Fe2+ → Cr3+ +

Fe3+ (acidic) (vi) S2O3^2- + OCl- → Cl- + S4O6^2- (acidic) (vii) IO3- + AsO3^3- ->

I- + AsO4^3- (acidic) (viii) Cr3+ + BiO3- → Cr2O7^2- + Bi3+ (acidic) (ix) H3AsO3 +

Cr2O7^2- → 3H3AsO4 + 2Cr3+ (acidic) (x) CN- + MnO4- → CNO- + MnO2 (basic).

(i) 2Fe3+ + Sn2+ → 2Fe2+ + Sn4+. (ii) 2MnO4- + 5C2O4^2- + 16H+ → 2Mn2+ +

10CO2 + 8H2O. (iii) Cr2O7^2- + 6Cl- + 14H+ → 2Cr3+ + 3Cl2 + 7H2O. (iv) Cu +

2NO3- + 4H+ → Cu2+ + 2NO2 + 2H2O. (v) Cr2O7^2- + 6Fe2+ + 14H+ → 2Cr3+

+ 6Fe3+ + 7H2O. (vi) 2S2O3^2- + OCl- + 2H+ → Cl- + S4O6^2- + H2O (acidic

media). (vii) IO3- + 3AsO3^3- → I- + 3AsO4^3- (acidic media). (viii) 2Cr3+ +

3BiO3- + 4H+ → Cr2O7^2- + 3Bi3+ + 2H2O (acidic media). (ix) 3H3AsO3 +

Cr2O7^2- + 8H+ → 3H3AsO4 + 2Cr3+ + 4H2O (acidic media). (x) 3CN- + 2MnO4-

+ H2O → 3CNO- + 2MnO2 + 2OH- (basic media).

Q7. Describe the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride, and a concentrated solution

of sodium chloride.

Molten NaCl: NaCl is melted and electrolysed with inert electrodes. At the cathode,

Na+ + e- → Na (molten sodium collects). At the anode, 2Cl- → Cl2 + 2e- (chlorine

gas). Concentrated aqueous NaCl (brine): at the cathode, water is reduced in

preference to Na+ (Na+ is hard to reduce), giving H2 and OH-: 2H2O + 2e- → H2 +

2OH-. At the anode, Cl- is oxidized to Cl2 (concentrated Cl- is discharged in

preference to water). The solution becomes NaOH solution, with H2 at the cathode

and Cl2 at the anode.

Q8. What is the difference between single electrode potential and standard electrode

potential? How can it be measured? Give its importance.

Single electrode potential is the potential developed when a metal is dipped in a

solution of its own ions (a single half-cell), e.g. Zn in ZnSO4. Standard electrode

potential is that potential measured under standard conditions (1 mol dm^-3, 1

atm, 25 degrees C) against the standard hydrogen electrode, whose potential is

taken as 0.00 V. It is measured by coupling the half-cell to the standard hydrogen

electrode through a salt bridge and reading the cell voltage. Importance: standard

potentials predict whether a redox reaction is spontaneous, which metal displaces

which, and the voltage of a cell built from two half-cells.

Q9. Outline the important applications of electrolysis. Write the electrochemical

reactions involved therein. Discuss the electrolysis of CuSO4 using Cu-electrodes

and AgNO3 solution using Ag electrode.

Applications of electrolysis: extraction of reactive metals (Na, Al), electroplating,

purification of metals (electrolytic refining), and manufacture of chemicals (NaOH,

Cl2, H2). Electrolysis of CuSO4 with Cu electrodes: at the anode, Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-

(the anode dissolves); at the cathode, Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu (pure copper deposits).

The CuSO4 concentration stays constant; impure copper anode is refined.

Electrolysis of AgNO3 with Ag electrodes: at the anode, Ag → Ag+ + e-; at the

cathode, Ag+ + e- → Ag. Silver transfers from anode to cathode, giving pure silver

at the cathode.

Q10. Describe the construction and working of standard hydrogen electrode.

Labelled drawing instruction: draw a platinum foil coated with platinum black,

dipping in 1 mol dm^-3 HCl, with hydrogen gas at 1 atm bubbled over it, connected

by a salt bridge to the other half-cell. Construction: a platinized platinum electrode

in contact with hydrogen gas at 1 atmosphere and H+ ions at 1 mol dm^-3 (usually

1 M HCl) at 25 degrees C. Working: the equilibrium H2 ⇌ 2H+ + 2e- is set up at the

platinum surface; the electrode can act as anode (H2 → 2H+ + 2e-) or cathode

(2H+ + 2e- → H2) depending on the other half-cell. Its potential is arbitrarily fixed

at 0.00 V, and all other electrode potentials are measured against it.

Q11. Is the reaction Fe3+ + Ag → Fe2+ + Ag+ spontaneous?
If not, write

spontaneous reaction involving these species.

As written, Fe3+ + Ag → Fe2+ + Ag+ is NOT spontaneous: E(cell) = E(cathode) -

E(anode) = 0.77 - 0.80 = -0.03 V, and a negative cell voltage means a

non-spontaneous reaction. The spontaneous reaction is the reverse: Fe2+ + Ag+ ->

Fe3+ + Ag, with E(cell) = 0.80 - 0.77 = +0.03 V.

Q12. Explain the difference between: (a) Ionization and electrolysis (b) Electrolytic cell

and voltaic cell (c) Conduction through metals and molten electrolytes.

(a) Ionization is the formation of ions when a substance dissolves (e.g. NaCl → Na+

+ Cl- in water) without any external current; electrolysis is a chemical change

brought about by passing an electric current through an electrolyte. (b) An

electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction (anode

positive, cathode negative); a voltaic (galvanic) cell produces electrical energy from

a spontaneous reaction (anode negative, cathode positive). (c) Conduction through

metals is by free electrons, with no chemical change and no movement of matter;

conduction through molten electrolytes is by ions moving to the electrodes, with

chemical change (discharge) at the electrodes.

Q13. Describe a galvanic cell explaining the functions of electrodes and the salt

bridge.

A galvanic cell has two half-cells: e.g. Zn in ZnSO4 (anode, negative) and Cu in

CuSO4 (cathode, positive), joined by a salt bridge and an external wire. At the

anode, oxidation occurs: Zn → Zn2+ + 2e-. The electrons travel through the

external wire to the cathode, where reduction occurs: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu. The salt

bridge (a tube of KCl or NH4NO3 in agar) completes the circuit and maintains

electrical neutrality by letting ions migrate: anions move towards the anode

compartment and cations towards the cathode compartment, preventing charge

build-up that would stop the cell. Without it the voltage drops to zero.

Q14. Write comprehensive notes on: (a) Spontaneity of oxidation reduction reactions

(b) Electrolytic conduction (c) Alkaline, silver oxide and nickel-cadmium batteries,

fuel cell (d) Lead accumulator, its desirable and undesirable features.

(a) Spontaneity of oxidation-reduction reactions: a redox reaction is spontaneous if

its cell voltage is positive, E(cell) = E(cathode) - E(anode) > 0, which corresponds to

a negative Gibbs energy change, delta G = -nFE. The species with the higher

reduction potential is reduced; the other is oxidized. (b) Electrolytic conduction:

conduction in electrolytes is by the movement of ions; cations move to the cathode

and anions to the anode, and are discharged there. It depends on the concentration

and mobility of ions and on temperature, and it is always accompanied by chemical

change at the electrodes. (c) Alkaline battery: Zn anode, MnO2 cathode, KOH

electrolyte, 1.5 V, non-rechargeable, longer life than the dry cell. Silver oxide

battery: Zn anode, Ag2O cathode, alkaline electrolyte, about 1.5 V, used in watches

and calculators. Nickel-cadmium battery: Cd anode, NiO2 cathode, alkaline

electrolyte, 1.4 V, rechargeable, sealed, used in power tools and portable

computers. Fuel cell: hydrogen and oxygen react (with a platinum catalyst) in KOH

electrolyte to give water and electricity, about 75% efficient, used in space vehicles,

where the water produced is also used as drinking water. (d) Lead accumulator, its

desirable and undesirable features: desirable: rechargeable, gives a large current,

steady voltage (12 V from six cells), reliable. Undesirable: heavy, contains corrosive

sulphuric acid and toxic lead, loses charge on standing, and is damaged by

overcharging or complete discharge.

Q15. Will the reaction be spontaneous for the following set of half reactions?
What will

be the value of E(cell)? (i) Cr3+(aq) + 3e- → Cr(s), E = -0.74 V (ii) MnO2(s) +

4H+(aq) + 2e- → Mn2+(aq) + 2H2O(l), E = +1.28 V.

For the spontaneous cell, MnO2 is reduced (cathode, +1.28 V) and Cr is oxidized

(anode, -0.74 V as a reduction potential). E(cell) = E(cathode) - E(anode) = 1.28 -

(-0.74) = +2.02 V. Since E(cell) is positive, the reaction is spontaneous. Balanced

overall reaction: 2Cr(s) + 3MnO2(s) + 12H+(aq) → 2Cr3+(aq) + 3Mn2+(aq) +

6H2O(l).

Q16. Explain with reasons: (a) A porous plate or a salt bridge is not required in lead

storage cell. (b) The standard oxidation potential of Zn is 0.76 V and its reduction

potential is -0.76 V. (c) Na and K can displace hydrogen from acids but Pt, Pd and Cu

can not. (d) The equilibrium is set up between metal atoms of electrode and ions of

metal in a cell. (e) A salt bridge maintains the electrical neutrality in the cell. (f)

Lead accumulator is a chargeable battery. (g) Impure Cu can be purified by

electrolytic process. (h) SHE acts as anode when connected with Cu electrode but as

cathode with Zn electrode.

(a) In a lead storage cell the electrodes are close together in the same electrolyte

(dilute H2SO4), and the solid products (PbSO4) stick to the plates, so no porous

plate or salt bridge is needed to separate the half-cells. (b) Oxidation potential and

reduction potential of the same couple are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign:

for Zn2+/Zn the reduction potential is -0.76 V (Zn2+ + 2e- → Zn) and the oxidation

potential is +0.76 V (Zn → Zn2+ + 2e-). (c) Na and K are above hydrogen in the

electrochemical series (negative reduction potentials), so they can reduce H+ to H2

from acids; Pt, Pd and Cu are below hydrogen (positive reduction potentials), so

they cannot. (d) At a metal electrode, metal atoms leave the electrode as ions and

ions from the solution deposit as metal atoms; when the two rates become equal,

an equilibrium is set up and a potential difference (the electrode potential) appears

between the metal and the solution. (e) The salt bridge maintains electrical

neutrality: as cations are produced in the anode compartment and consumed in the

cathode compartment, ions from the bridge migrate to balance the charge, so the

solutions stay neutral and current keeps flowing. (f) The lead accumulator is

rechargeable because its discharge products are solids (PbSO4 on both plates) that

stay in place and are converted back to Pb and PbO2 when current is passed in

reverse. (g) Impure copper is made the anode in a CuSO4 electrolytic cell: copper

dissolves from the anode and pure copper deposits at the cathode, while impurities

fall as anode mud or stay in solution. (h) SHE (0.00 V) is below Cu (+0.34 V), so

against Cu it is the anode (oxidation); it is above Zn (-0.76 V), so against Zn it is the

cathode (reduction).

mcqs.q: Calculate the oxidation number of chromium in K2Cr2O7.
Calculate the oxidation number of chromium in CrCl3.
mcqs.why: Working: Cr + 3 * -1 = 0, so Cr - 3 = 0 and Cr = 3, giving an oxidation number of +3 for chromium in CrCl3.

mcqs.q: Calculate the oxidation number of chlorine in Ca(ClO3)2 for the ClO3 group.
mcqs.why: Working: Cl + 3 * -2 = -1, so Cl - 6 = -1 and Cl = -1 + 6 = 5, giving +5 for chlorine in the chlorate group.

mcqs.q: Calculate the oxidation number of carbon in Na2CO3.
mcqs.why: Working: 2 * 1 + C + 3 * -2 = 0, so 2 + C - 6 = 0 and C = 6 - 2 = 4, giving +4 for carbon in Na2CO3.

mcqs.q: Calculate the oxidation number of manganese in K2MnO4.
mcqs.why: Working: 2 * 1 + Mn + 4 * -2 = 0, so 2 + Mn - 8 = 0 and Mn = 8 - 2 = 6, giving +6 in potassium manganate.

mcqs.q: For Fe3+ + Ag -> Fe2+ + Ag+, with E values 0.77 V and 0.80 V, what is E(cell) as written?
options: +0.03 V, so the reaction is spontaneous
-0.03 V, so the reaction is not spontaneous
mcqs.why: Working: E(cell) = 0.77 - 0.80 = -0.03, and a negative value means the reaction as written is not spontaneous, as shown in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is the spontaneous direction for the Fe and Ag species in the notes?
options: Fe3+ + Ag -> Fe2+ + Ag+, with E(cell) = -0.03 V
Fe2+ + Ag+ -> Fe3+ + Ag, with E(cell) = +0.03 V
mcqs.why: Working: reverse E(cell) = 0.80 - 0.77 = 0.03, positive, so Fe2+ + Ag+ -> Fe3+ + Ag is the spontaneous reaction.

mcqs.q: Given Cr3+/Cr E = -0.74 V and MnO2/Mn2+ E = +1.28 V, what is E(cell) for the spontaneous cell?
mcqs.why: Working: E(cell) = 1.28 - -0.74 = 1.28 + 0.74 = 2.02, so E(cell) = +2.02 V and the reaction is spontaneous.

mcqs.q: What is the standard potential assigned to the standard hydrogen electrode?
mcqs.why: The notes state the standard hydrogen electrode potential is arbitrarily fixed at 0.00 V, and all other electrode potentials are measured against it.

mcqs.q: In the electrolysis of molten NaCl, what is produced at the cathode?
mcqs.why: The notes state that in molten NaCl electrolysis, Na+ + e- -> Na at the cathode, while chlorine gas forms at the anode.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • The rate of an endothermic reaction increases with the increase in temperature.
  • All radioactive disintegration nuclear reactions are of first order.
  • For a fast reaction the rate constant is relatively large and half-life is short.
  • The second order reaction becomes first order if one of the reactants is in large excess.
  • Arrhenius equation can be used to find out activation energy of a reaction.

mcqs.q: The rate of an endothermic reaction increases with which change?
mcqs.why: The notes state directly that the rate of an endothermic reaction increases with the increase in temperature.

mcqs.q: All radioactive disintegration nuclear reactions are of which order?
mcqs.why: The key facts state that all radioactive disintegration nuclear reactions are of first order.

mcqs.q: For a fast reaction, the rate constant is:
mcqs.why: The notes link a fast reaction with a relatively large rate constant, because a larger k gives a larger rate.

mcqs.q: For a fast reaction, the half-life is:
mcqs.why: The key facts state that for a fast reaction the rate constant is relatively large and the half-life is short.

mcqs.q: A second order reaction becomes first order when:
options: Both reactants are in exactly equal amounts
One of the reactants is in large excess
One reactant is present in a very small amount
Both reactants are completely used up
mcqs.why: The notes state that the second order reaction becomes first order if one of the reactants is in large excess.

mcqs.q: The Arrhenius equation can be used to find out which quantity?
options: Order of a reaction from its equation
mcqs.why: The key facts state that the Arrhenius equation can be used to find out the activation energy of a reaction.

mcqs.q: If the temperature is increased, the rate of an endothermic reaction will:
mcqs.why: This follows the stated fact that the rate of an endothermic reaction increases with the increase in temperature.

mcqs.q: A reaction described as fast is characterised by:
options: A relatively large rate constant and a short half-life
A relatively small rate constant and a long half-life
A zero rate constant and a short half-life
A relatively large rate constant and a long half-life
mcqs.why: The notes pair the two features of a fast reaction together: rate constant relatively large and half-life short.

mcqs.q: When one reactant is taken in large excess, a second order reaction is treated as:
mcqs.why: With one reactant in large excess its concentration stays nearly constant, so the second order reaction becomes first order, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which type of reactions are all of first order according to the key facts?
mcqs.why: The notes specifically assign first order to all radioactive disintegration nuclear reactions, not to endothermic or fast reactions in general.

mcqs.q: In a zero order reaction, the rate is independent of:
options: Concentration of products only in every case
mcqs.why: The given multiple choice answer is concentration of reactants: in zero order the rate does not depend on reactant concentration.

mcqs.q: For 2A + B -> products with rate = k[A]^2 [B], if A is present in large excess, the order of reaction is:
mcqs.why: With A in large excess, [A] is effectively constant, leaving only [B] to change, so the observed order is 1, as marked in the notes.

mcqs.q: As an ordinary reaction proceeds, the rate of reaction generally:
options: Remains the same as the reaction proceeds
mcqs.why: The marked answer in the notes is that the rate decreases as the reaction proceeds, because reactants are being used up.

mcqs.q: When the temperature rises by 10 degrees C and the rate doubles, this increase is due to:
options: Decrease in activation energy of reaction
Decrease in the number of collisions between reactant molecules
Increase in activation energy of reactants
Increase in number of effective collisions
mcqs.why: The marked answer is an increase in the number of effective collisions, which makes more collisions succeed and the rate rise.

mcqs.q: The unit of the rate constant is the same as that of the rate of reaction in:
mcqs.why: The marked answer is zero order reaction, where k has the same unit as the rate of reaction itself.

mcqs.q: For rate = k[A]^2 [B] with no reactant in excess, the overall order is:
mcqs.why: Overall order is the sum of the powers in the rate equation: 2 + 1 = 3, using the exponents of [A] and [B] given in the notes.

mcqs.q: For rate = k[A]^2 [B], if [A] is doubled while [B] stays constant, the rate becomes:
mcqs.why: The rate depends on [A]^2, so doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 2 * 2 = 4, while [B] is unchanged.

mcqs.q: For rate = k[A]^2 [B], if [B] is doubled while [A] stays constant, the rate becomes:
mcqs.why: The rate depends on [B] to the first power, so doubling [B] multiplies the rate by 2, giving 1 * 2 = 2 times the original rate.

mcqs.q: In a zero order reaction, changing the concentration of reactants will make the rate:
options: Stay independent of that concentration change
mcqs.why: Zero order means the rate is independent of the concentration of reactants, which is the fact tested in the first question of this lesson.

mcqs.q: With an increase of 10 degrees C in temperature, the rate of reaction typically:
mcqs.why: The lesson states that with an increase of 10 degrees C temperature the rate of reaction doubles, due to more effective collisions.

lessons.title: Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q3(i). reason - The half life of a first order reaction increases with temperature.

False. For a first order reaction the half life is t1/2 = 0.693/k. The rate constant k

increases with temperature (Arrhenius equation), so the half life DECREASES with

temperature; it does not increase.

Q3(iii). reason - A catalyst makes a reaction more exothermic.

False. A catalyst lowers the activation energy and so speeds up both forward and

reverse reactions equally; it does not change the enthalpy change (delta H) of the

reaction, so it cannot make a reaction more exothermic.

Q3(v). reason - The order of reaction is strictly determined by the stoichiometry of the

balanced equation.

False. The order of a reaction is found from experiment (from the rate law), and it

may differ from the stoichiometric coefficients. For example, the reaction 2NO +

2H2 → 2H2O + N2 is third order overall, not fourth, and many reactions have

fractional or zero orders.

Q4. What is chemical kinetics?
How do you compare chemical kinetics with chemical

equilibrium and thermodynamics?

Chemical kinetics is the study of the rates of chemical reactions and the factors that

affect them, together with the mechanism (the step-by-step path) of reactions.

Chemical equilibrium tells us how far a reaction goes and the composition at

equilibrium, but not how fast it gets there. Thermodynamics tells us whether a

reaction is energetically possible (delta G negative) and how much heat is involved,

but not its rate: a thermodynamically feasible reaction (e.g. diamond turning into

graphite) may be immeasurably slow. Kinetics, equilibrium and thermodynamics are

therefore complementary: thermodynamics says 'can it happen', equilibrium says

'how far', kinetics says 'how fast'.

Q5. The rate of a chemical reaction with respect to products is written with positive

sign, but with respect to reactants is written with a negative sign. Explain it with

reference to the hypothetical reaction aA + bB → cC + dD.

For aA + bB → cC + dD, the rate with respect to a product is positive because the

product concentration increases with time, while the rate with respect to a reactant

is negative because the reactant concentration decreases with time. To get a single

positive rate for the reaction, each concentration change is divided by its

stoichiometric coefficient: rate = -(1/a) d[A]/dt = -(1/b) d[B]/dt = +(1/c) d[C]/dt =

+(1/d) d[D]/dt. The minus signs on reactants simply cancel their negative

concentration changes.

Q6. What are instantaneous and average rates?
Is it true that the instantaneous rate

of a reaction at the beginning of the reaction is greater than average rate and

becomes far less than the average rate near the completion of reaction?

Average rate is the change in concentration over a stated time interval, divided by

that interval. Instantaneous rate is the rate at one particular instant, given by the

slope of the concentration-time curve at that point (tangent). Yes, the statement is

true for an ordinary reaction: at the start, concentrations are highest, so the

instantaneous rate is highest and greater than the average rate over the whole

reaction; near completion, concentrations are low, so the instantaneous rate is

much smaller than the average rate over the whole reaction. The average rate lies

between the initial and final instantaneous rates.

Q7. Differentiate between: (i) Rate and rate constant of a reaction (ii) Homogeneous

and heterogeneous catalyses (iii) Fast step and the rate determining step (iv)

Enthalpy change of reaction and energy of activation of reaction.

(i) Rate is the change in concentration per unit time (mol dm^-3 s^-1) at a given

moment; rate constant k is the proportionality constant in the rate law (rate = k

[A]^x [B]^y), equal to the rate when all concentrations are unity, and constant at a

given temperature. (ii) Homogeneous catalysis: catalyst and reactants are in the

same phase, e.g. acid-catalysed hydrolysis of an ester in water. Heterogeneous

catalysis: catalyst and reactants are in different phases, e.g. iron catalyst (solid) in

the Haber process (gases). (iii) Fast step: a step in a mechanism that occurs quickly

and does not limit the overall rate. Rate determining step: the slowest step in a

mechanism, which limits the overall rate; the rate law is determined by this step.

(iv) Enthalpy change of reaction (delta H) is the total heat absorbed or evolved in

the reaction (products minus reactants); energy of activation (Ea) is the extra

energy reactants must gain to reach the activated complex, i.e. the height of the

energy barrier, which decides the rate but not the heat change.

Q8. Justify the following statements (as printed, the list runs (i), (ii), (iii), (v), (iv), (vi),

(vii): items (iv) and (v) are swapped in print; they are answered here in printed

order).

(i) The rate of a reaction is ever changing because it depends on the concentrations

of reactants, which fall as the reaction proceeds, and on temperature and other

conditions, which may also change. (ii) The rate falls as reactants are consumed,

but the rate constant k depends only on temperature (and the nature of the

reaction), not on concentrations, so under fixed conditions k stays constant while

the rate changes. (iii) In a first order reaction the same fraction reacts in each half

life, not the same amount: after one hour 50% has reacted, leaving 50%; in the next

hour half of the remainder (25% of the original) reacts, so the remaining 50% is NOT

fully consumed in the second hour; in fact a first order reaction never quite reaches

100% completion. The statement that 'the remaining 50% needs more than one

hour' is therefore true in the sense that the second half (of the original) is never

completed in one further hour; strictly, each successive half of what remains takes

one hour. (iv) [printed as (v)] Radioactive decay is always first order because the

decay of a nucleus does not depend on the concentration of other nuclei: the rate is

proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present, which is the definition of

first order kinetics. (v) [printed as (iv)] For a second order reaction, rate = k [A]^2

(or k [A][B]), so k has units (mol dm^-3 s^-1)/(mol dm^-3)^2 = dm^3 mol^-1

s^-1, while the rate itself has units mol dm^-3 s^-1: the units differ because k must

cancel one concentration unit. (vi) The order is found from the experimental rate

law, not from the balanced equation: the sum of stoichiometric coefficients

(molecularity) may differ from the order, e.g. a reaction with four stoichiometric

coefficients can be third order, and orders can be fractional or zero. (vii) The order

of a reaction is obtained from the rate expression, and the rate expression is

obtained from experiment (initial-rate or concentration-time data), never from the

balanced equation alone.

Q9. Explain that half life method for measurement of the order of a reaction can help

us to measure the order of even those reactions which have a fractional order.

For a reaction of order n, the half life is proportional to 1/a^(n-1), where a is the

initial concentration. Measuring the half life at two different initial concentrations

gives the ratio of half lives, from which (n - 1) follows by logarithms, even if n is

fractional: e.g. if doubling the concentration halves the half life, n = 2; if the half life

is unchanged, n = 1; intermediate changes give fractional n. The method therefore

works for fractional orders, where the simple integer-order integrated equations do

not apply directly.

Q10. A curve is obtained when a graph is plotted between time on x-axis and

concentration on y-axis. The measurement of the slopes of various points gives us

the instantaneous rates of reaction. Explain with suitable examples.

On a concentration-time curve, the slope at any point is the instantaneous rate at

that time: the tangent to the curve gives d[C]/dt. Example: for the decomposition of

H2O2, the concentration-time curve is steep at the start (large slope, fast rate) and

flattens as the reaction proceeds (small slope, slow rate). Measuring tangents at

several times gives the instantaneous rates at those times, and plotting them shows

how the rate falls as the reactant is consumed.

Q11. The rate determining step of a reaction is found out from the mechanism of that

reaction. Explain it with few examples.

The rate determining step is the slowest step of the mechanism, and the

experimental rate law matches the composition of the activated complex of that

step. Examples: (i) the reaction 2NO + 2H2 → 2H2O + N2 has a slow step 2NO +

H2 → N2O + H2O, followed by a fast step N2O + H2 → N2 + H2O; the rate law

(rate = k [NO]^2 [H2]) follows from the slow step. (ii) The reaction between

persulphate and iodide has a slow first step whose composition gives the observed

rate law, while later fast steps do not affect it. If a proposed mechanism's slow step

does not give the observed rate law, the mechanism is wrong.

Q12. Discuss the factors which influence the rates of chemical reactions.

Factors influencing reaction rates: (i) Nature of reactants: ionic reactions are fast,

covalent bond-breaking reactions are slow. (ii) Concentration: higher concentration

gives more collisions per second, hence a faster rate. (iii) Temperature: raising the

temperature increases the fraction of molecules with energy above Ea, so the rate

roughly doubles per 10 degrees C rise. (iv) Catalyst: lowers Ea and so increases the

rate without being consumed. (v) Surface area: finely divided solids react faster

because more surface is exposed. (vi) Light: photochemical reactions are speeded

up by light (e.g. H2 + Cl2). (vii) Pressure: for gases, higher pressure means higher

concentration and more collisions.

Q13. Explain the following facts about the reaction 2NO(g) + 2H2(g) → 2H2O(g) +

N2(g): (i) The changing concentrations of reactants change the rates of this

reaction. (ii) Individual orders with respect to NO and H2 can be measured. (iii) The

overall order can be evaluated by keeping the concentration of one of the

substances constant.

(i) Changing the concentration of NO or H2 changes the rate, because the rate law

contains both concentrations: rate = k [NO]^2 [H2]. (ii) The individual orders are

measured by the isolation method: keep [H2] constant and vary [NO] to find the

order in NO (2), then keep [NO] constant and vary [H2] to find the order in H2 (1).

(iii) The overall order (2 + 1 = 3) is evaluated by adding the individual orders, each

found while the other concentration is held constant, so that only one concentration

changes at a time.

Q14. The collision frequency and the orientation of molecules are necessary

conditions for determining the proper rate of reaction. Justify the statement.

Not every collision leads to reaction: molecules must collide with energy at least

equal to the activation energy (otherwise they simply bounce apart) and with the

correct orientation (the reacting atoms must meet). Collision frequency counts all

collisions, but only the fraction with sufficient energy and proper orientation are

effective. Hence the rate depends on the collision frequency multiplied by the

fraction of molecules above Ea and the orientation (steric) factor: rate = P Z

e^(-Ea/RT) [A][B]. Without both conditions, even a high collision frequency gives a

slow rate.

Q15. How does Arrhenius equation help us to calculate the energy of activation of a

reaction?

The Arrhenius equation is k = A e^(-Ea/RT), or log k = log A - Ea/(2.303 RT).

Measuring k at two temperatures and plotting log k against 1/T gives a straight line

of slope -Ea/(2.303 R); from the slope, Ea = -2.303 R x slope. Alternatively, from two

values k1 and k2 at T1 and T2: log(k2/k1) = (Ea/2.303 R) x (1/T1 - 1/T2), which

gives Ea directly. The equation thus converts temperature-dependence of the rate

into the energy barrier.

Q16. Define the following terms and give examples: (i) Homogeneous catalysis (ii)

Heterogeneous catalysis (iii) Activation of a catalyst (iv) Auto-catalysis (v) Catalytic

poisoning (vi) Enzyme catalysis.

(i) Homogeneous catalysis: catalyst and reactants in the same phase, e.g. H+

(aqueous) catalysing the hydrolysis of an ester. (ii) Heterogeneous catalysis:

catalyst and reactants in different phases, e.g. solid iron in the Haber process; solid

Pt in the contact process. (iii) Activation of a catalyst (promotor): a substance that

increases the activity of a catalyst without itself being a catalyst, e.g. alumina or

molybdenum added to iron in the Haber process; copper and tellurium with nickel in

oil hydrogenation. (iv) Auto-catalysis: a product of the reaction acts as the catalyst,

so the reaction speeds up as it proceeds, e.g. Mn2+ in the oxalic acid-KMnO4

reaction; nitrous acid in the copper-nitric acid reaction. (v) Catalytic poisoning: loss

of catalytic activity due to impurities that block the catalyst surface, e.g. sulphur

and arsenic compounds poison platinum catalysts; carbon monoxide poisons the

iron catalyst in the Haber process. (vi) Enzyme catalysis: catalysis by protein

enzymes in living cells, highly specific and efficient, e.g. urease hydrolysing urea;

invertase hydrolysing sucrose; zymase fermenting glucose to ethanol.

Q17. Briefly describe with examples: (i) Change of physical state of a catalyst at the

end of reaction (ii) A very small amount of a catalyst may prove sufficient to carry

out a reaction (iii) A finely divided catalyst may prove more effective (iv) Equilibrium

constant of a reversible reaction is not changed in the presence of a catalyst (v) A

catalyst is specific in its action.

(i) Change of physical state: a catalyst may change its physical form during the

reaction while its mass and chemical composition stay the same, e.g. granular

MnO2 used in KClO3 decomposition ends as a fine powder; the shining surface of a

solid catalyst may become dull. (ii) A very small amount of catalyst suffices: a

catalyst is not consumed, so it can act repeatedly; e.g. 1 mg of fine platinum

powder can convert 2.5 dm^3 of H2 and 1.25 dm^3 of O2 to water, and 1 g of

colloidal platinum can decompose thousands of dm^3 of H2O2. (iii) A finely divided

catalyst is more effective because catalysis happens at the surface: finer division

gives a larger surface area for the same mass, e.g. colloidal platinum is far more

active than a lump of platinum; finely divided nickel is used for hydrogenating

vegetable oils. (iv) A catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant: it speeds

up forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but the

equilibrium composition and K are unchanged. (v) A catalyst is specific: a catalyst

that works for one reaction may not work for another, and different catalysts can

give different products from the same reactant, e.g. formic acid gives H2O + CO

with Al2O3 but H2 + CO2 with Cu.

Q18. What are enzymes? Give examples in which they act as catalyst. Mention the

characteristics of enzyme catalysis.

Enzymes are complex protein molecules produced by living cells that catalyse

biochemical reactions. Examples: urease (soybean) hydrolyses urea to NH3 and

CO2; invertase (yeast) hydrolyses sucrose to glucose and fructose; zymase (yeast)

ferments glucose to ethanol and CO2; diastase hydrolyses starch. Characteristics of

enzyme catalysis: (i) enzymes are the most efficient catalysts known and greatly

lower the activation energy; (ii) they are highly specific (urease acts on urea only,

not even on methyl urea); (iii) they work best at an optimum temperature (activity

rises to a maximum, then falls as the enzyme denatures) and an optimum pH; (iv)

their activity is inhibited by poisons and enhanced by co-enzymes or activators; (v)

they act through a lock-and-key fit of the substrate into active centres on the

enzyme surface (Michaelis-Menten mechanism: E + S ⇌ ES → P + E).

Q19. In the reaction of NO and H2, it was observed that equimolecular mixture of

gases at 340.5 mm pressure was half changed in 102 seconds. In another

experiment with an initial pressure of 288 mm of Hg, the reaction was half

completed in 140 seconds. Calculate the order of reaction.

Step 1 - For the half-life method, (t1/2)1/(t1/2)2 = (a2/a1)^(n-1), where a is the

initial pressure and n the order.

Step 2 - Substitute: 102/140 = (288/340.5)^(n-1), i.e. 0.7286 = (0.8458)^(n-1).

Step 3 - Take logarithms: log(0.7286) = (n - 1) log(0.8458), so -0.1376 = (n - 1) x

(-0.0727).

Step 4 - n - 1 = 0.1376/0.0727 = 1.89, so n = 2.89, about 2.88.

Answer: order 2.88, i.e. effectively third order (matches the book's printed answer).

Q20. A study of chemical kinetics of a reaction A + B → Products gave the following

data at 25 degrees C: [A] = 1.00, [B] = 0.15, rate = 4.2 x 10^-6; [A] = 2.00, [B] =

0.15, rate = 8.4 x 10^-6; [A] = 1.00, [B] = 0.2, rate = 5.6 x 10^-6 (rates in mol

dm^-3 s^-1). Calculate the rate law.

Step 1 - Compare experiments 1 and 2: [B] is constant (0.15) while [A] doubles

(1.00 → 2.00) and the rate doubles (4.2 → 8.4 x 10^-6). The reaction is first order

in A.

Step 2 - Compare experiments 1 and 3: [A] is constant (1.00) while [B] increases by

a factor 0.2/0.15 = 1.333 and the rate increases by the same factor (5.6/4.2 =

1.333). The reaction is first order in B.

Step 3 - Rate law: rate = k [A][B]. Overall order = 1 + 1 = 2.

Step 4 - Rate constant from experiment 1: k = rate/([A][B]) = 4.2 x 10^-6/(1.00 x

0.15) = 2.8 x 10^-5 mol^-1 dm^3 s^-1.

Answer: rate = k [A][B], second order overall (matches the book's printed answer).

Q21. Some reactions taking place around room temperature have activation energies

around 50 kJ mol^-1. (i) What is the value of the factor e^(-Ea/RT) at 25 degrees C?

(ii) Calculate this factor at 35 degrees C and 45 degrees C and note the increase in

this factor for every 10 degrees C rise in temperature. (iii) Prove that for every 10

degrees C rise in temperature, the factor doubles and so rate constant also doubles.

Step 1 - (i) At 25 degrees C (298 K): Ea/RT = 50000/(8.314 x 298) = 20.18, so

e^(-Ea/RT) = e^-20.18 = 1.72 x 10^-9.

Step 2 - (ii) At 35 degrees C (308 K): Ea/RT = 50000/(8.314 x 308) = 19.53, so the

factor = 3.31 x 10^-9. At 45 degrees C (318 K): Ea/RT = 50000/(8.314 x 318) =

18.91, so the factor = 6.12 x 10^-9.

Step 3 - Ratios: 3.31/1.72 = 1.92 and 6.12/3.31 = 1.85, i.e. the factor roughly

doubles for each 10 degrees C rise.

Step 4 - (iii) Since k = A e^(-Ea/RT), doubling the exponential factor doubles k, so

the rate constant (and hence the rate) roughly doubles for every 10 degrees C rise

in temperature.

Answer: (i) 1.72 x 10^-9 (ii) 3.31 x 10^-9 at 35 degrees C and 6.12 x 10^-9 at 45

degrees C (iii) the factor doubles per 10 degrees C rise, so k doubles (matches the

book's printed answers).

Q22. H2 and I2 react to produce HI. Following data for rate constant at various

temperatures (K) have been collected: T = 500, 550, 600, 650, 700 K; k = 6.814 x

10^-4, 2.64 x 10^-2, 0.56, 7.31, 66.67 cm^3 mol^-1 s^-1. (i) Plot a graph between

1/T on x-axis and log k on the y-axis. (ii) Measure the slope of this straight line and

calculate the energy of activation of this reaction.

Step 1 - Labelled graph instruction: plot 1/T (x-axis) against log k (y-axis) for the five

points: (0.00200, -3.17), (0.00182, -1.58), (0.00167, -0.25), (0.00154, 0.86),

(0.00143, 1.82). The points lie on a straight line with negative slope, as the

Arrhenius equation predicts.

Step 2 - From the plotted line, the slope = -Ea/(2.303 R). The slope of the best-fit

line through the five points is about -8326 K.

Step 3 - Ea = 2.303 x R x 8326 = 2.303 x 8.314 x 8326 = 159400 J mol^-1, about

160 kJ mol^-1.

Answer: slope about 8326 (magnitude); Ea about 160.6 kJ mol^-1 (matches the

book's printed answers).

mcqs.q: Chemical kinetics is the study of:
options: Rates of chemical reactions, factors affecting them, and reaction mechanisms
Only whether a reaction is energetically possible
Only the heat evolved in a reaction
mcqs.why: The notes define chemical kinetics as the study of rates, the factors that affect them, and the step-by-step mechanism of reactions.

mcqs.q: Diamond turning into graphite is used in the notes to show that a thermodynamically feasible reaction may be:
mcqs.why: Thermodynamics says a reaction can happen, but the diamond to graphite example shows such a feasible reaction may be immeasurably slow, which is a kinetics point.

mcqs.q: For aA + bB -> cC + dD, the single positive rate of reaction is written as:
options: rate = d[A]/dt = d[B]/dt = d[C]/dt = d[D]/dt with no coefficients
mcqs.why: Reactant concentrations fall so their terms carry minus signs, product concentrations rise so their terms are positive, and each term is divided by its stoichiometric coefficient.

mcqs.q: The half life of a first order reaction with rate constant k = 0.3465 per second is:
mcqs.why: For first order, t1/2 = 0.693 / k. Substituting: 0.693 / 0.3465 = 2, so the half life is 2 * 1 = 2 seconds.

mcqs.q: From the data [A] = 1.00, [B] = 0.15, rate = 4.2 x 10^-6, with rate = k[A][B], the rate constant k is:
In the NO and H2 half-life experiment, t1/2 values 102 s at 340.5 mm and 140 s at 288 mm give an order of about:
mcqs.why: Using the half-life ratio working in the notes: n - 1 = 0.1376 / 0.0727 = 1.89, so n = 1.89 + 1 = 2.89, about 2.9 and effectively third order, matching the book answer.

mcqs.q: For Ea = 50 kJ per mol, the factor e^(-Ea/RT) at 25 degrees C (298 K) is about:
A plot of log k against 1/T for H2 + I2 has slope about -8326 K. The activation energy is about:
mcqs.why: Ea = 2.303 * R * 8326 = 2.303 * 8.314 * 8326 = 159419.1 J per mol, about 160 * 1000 = 160000 J per mol, i.e. about 160 kJ per mol, as in the notes.

mcqs.q: For 2NO + 2H2 -> 2H2O + N2 with rate = k[NO]^2 [H2], the overall order is:
mcqs.why: The individual orders are 2 in NO and 1 in H2, measured by the isolation method, so the overall order is 2 + 1 = 3.

mcqs.q: The rate determining step of a reaction mechanism is:
options: The fastest step, which determines the rate law
Any fast step after the slow step
The step that changes the enthalpy change of reaction
The slowest step, which limits the overall rate and determines the rate law
mcqs.why: The notes define the rate determining step as the slowest step limiting the overall rate, and the experimental rate law follows from that step.
